A river that is home to about 500 saltwater crocodiles has been given the OK to host Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoeing events at the 2032 Brisbane Games.
The course on the Fitzroy River in Rockhampton, Queensland, has passed an independent technical assessment into its suitability.
The assessment did not consider the crocodiles but instead looked at "how the course would perform under a range of conditions, weather patterns, water levels and flood risk at both Games time and throughout the period leading into the Games".
The report was commissioned by the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA), which noted, external that the Fitzroy River Flatwater Facility "is already a training and competition venue for flatwater sports, supporting school state championships, local regattas, and national team training camps".
As a recognised rowing facility, contingency plans are in place at events for when crocodiles are spotted and Olympic officials have previously been assured of rower safety.
World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide, formerly International Canoe Federation, both endorsed the course.
"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games, consistent with the requirements of Olympic and Paralympic Rowing," World Rowing President Jean-Christophe Rolland said., external
Paddle Worldwide President Thomas Konietzko said: "The quality and depth of the technical work undertaken has significantly improved our understanding of the field of play and provides confidence to us and our athletes that the course can deliver fair competition for Canoe Sprint athletes."
Brisbane 2032 President Andrew Liveris played down the issue of crocodiles last year.
"There are sharks in the ocean and we're still surfing... it's a can do, not a can't do - please change the mindset here," he said at the time.
Speaking on Thursday about the venue having now been given the go-ahead, he said: "The endorsement provides additional certainty as we move into the next phase of venue planning and Games delivery, ensuring all future design and operational work continues to focus solely on Rockhampton."
Saltwater crocodiles - known locally as Salties - live in both freshwater and saltwater and can grow to be in excess of six metres long.

For the second year in a row, Antarctica’s industrial krill fishing fleet halted operations ahead of schedule after reaching its seasonal catch limit.
The vessels had been harvesting the tiny shrimp-like crustaceans from waters around the Antarctic Peninsula and the South Orkney Islands, located about 400 miles north of the peninsula. Under current rules, the fleet must stop fishing once it collectively harvests 620,000 tons of krill.
The precautionary threshold is intended to support the fishery’s long-term sustainability and was established in the 1990s by the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources, which manages commercial fishing activity in the Southern Ocean.
But many scientists and marine advocates say more data is needed on whale populations to ensure that fishing in Antarctic waters does not deprive the marine mammals of their primary prey.
Whales are the largest consumers of krill in the Southern Ocean. Yet, to date, the conservation commission has not taken them into account in its fisheries management plan. When the commission was founded in the 1980s, it didn’t have to. Decades of commercial whaling had left few, if any, whales alive in Antarctica. Most whale species had been driven to the brink of extinction.
Over the last few decades, some whale populations have made a remarkable comeback after the International Whaling Commission adopted a global ban on commercial whaling in the early 1980s.
“Humpback whales have largely recovered,” said Peter Hammarstedt, chief campaigns officer for Sea Shepherd Global, an international marine conservation organization based in Amsterdam. Other species like fin whales and blue whales are experiencing a much slower recovery, but are still regularly documented in the region, he said.
“So now we have a growing number of whales down in the Southern Ocean. We have an expanding krill fishery, and these two bodies—the whales and the ships—are competing for a decreasing number of krill,” he said.
Until last year, the krill fishing fleet never reached its 620,000-ton limit, primarily due to a former conservation measure that required the catch to be distributed across vast ocean areas. Since that measure expired in 2024, however, the fishing industry has been able to make its catch easier.
“The krill fleet is able to take an increasingly large number of the catch in an increasingly smaller area, and the area that they focus on is the area where the krill is most highly concentrated, which is also the area where you see the highest concentrations of whales, penguins and seals,” Hammarstedt said.
To better understand this increasing overlap and potential conflict, Sea Shepherd recently partnered with independent scientists from the Hopkins Marine Lab at Stanford University and the University of California, Santa Cruz, to gather data about whale populations feeding near the South Orkney Islands.
Hammarstedt said their findings could help inform decision-makers next month when delegates representing the commission’s 26 member countries, plus the European Union, will meet for their annual meeting in Hobart, Australia, to negotiate fishing rules and proposed measures to protect the Southern Ocean ecosystem.
Hopefully, he said, the new information will “force this international body to consider the impact of the fishery on whales.”
The krill fishing industry is growing, and demand for products made from the crustaceans continues. “What’s really driving this krill fishery is krill oil supplements for Omega-3, for which there are plant-based alternatives,” Hammarstedt said.
One of the scientists Sea Shepherd has partnered with is Matthew Savoca, a research scientist with the Hopkins Marine Station of Stanford University and a principal investigator with the California Marine Sanctuary Foundation. Savoca accompanied the advocacy group on a month-long voyage in the South Orkney Islands earlier this year. Inside Climate News spoke with him to learn more about his research and what he observed.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
TERESA TOMASSONI: How did you first become involved with Sea Shepherd’s Antarctica campaign?
MATTHEW SAVOCA: In 2022, a colleague and friend, Conor Ryan, shared some photos of this huge whale aggregation he saw near the South Orkney Islands. There were around 1,000 whales. To this day, I think it’s the record holder for the largest group of whales ever seen post-industrial whaling. So this enormous pod of whales was noteworthy, scientifically. But there were also these krill trawlers, four of them, in and amongst this group of whales. I remember thinking to myself, we have to share this with the world, just to be able to have an honest conversation about what’s happening in Antarctica in regards to how the krill fishery is operating: Can we do this better? Should this be happening? Is there a way to not have direct overlap between a ton of whales and krill fishing boats going after the same food? In 2023, we published those observations. Peter Hammarstedt, from Sea Shepherd, got in touch with me after and invited me to go with their team to survey the waters around the South Orkney Islands in Antarctica. They realized that an effective campaign to raise awareness about what is happening there would require not only advocacy and a shift in public sentiment, but also science.
TOMASSONI: Tell me about the South Orkney Islands and why they are important.
SAVOCA: This is one of the most productive ecosystems on our planet, like the Amazon or coral reefs, the wildebeest migration across the Serengeti. I mean, you have glaciers that are the size of skyscrapers, spilling off of mountains that are 2,000 feet tall, into the ocean. Tens of thousands of penguins and albatrosses are everywhere. Every day that we were out there and there was good weather, you’d see a group of at least 100 whales in one spot. And the next day you’re 20 miles from there and then there’s a different group of 200 whales

NY-17: First in a series on the environmental stakes of one of the nation’s most fiercely contested congressional races.
The Hudson River bisects New York’s 17th Congressional District, with basalt bluffs lining its western bank 40 miles north of New York City.
The district, which includes Putnam and Rockland counties, as well as parts of Dutchess and Westchester, boasts acres of protected parkland. Its lakes and reservoirs feed the Croton Watershed, a significant source of New York City’s drinking water.
This fall, the 17th district is among the most closely watched House races in what many consider the most consequential midterm elections in American history. The Cook Political Report has the district as one of 18 House “Toss-Up” races, and rates it as one of only two with a Democratic lean. This makes it one of the Democrats’ best pickup opportunities, with Republicans holding a slim 218–213 majority in the House.
The race pits Republican incumbent Mike Lawler against Democrat Cait Conley, a veteran and national security expert. She won 49.5 percent of the vote in the June 23 primary, beating Rockland state legislator Beth Davidson, who took 31.8 percent.
With President Donald Trump’s net approval rating at minus-30 among New York voters, according to polling by The Economist, Democrats hope to win over moderate Republicans.
“I am willing to cross party lines and vote for Cait Conley,” said William Knox, a resident of Dutchess County who supported Lawler in both 2022 and 2024. “He has consistently voted along lines that support the president’s agenda, rather than voting in ways that would support us, his constituents.”
Should Democrats win both the House and Senate, the midterms could put Trump’s political future in jeopardy and determine whether the United States returns to the emissions-reduction path set by the Biden administration. As it stands, Climate Action Tracker rates U.S. climate action as “Critically Insufficient.”
As the campaign has worn on, both candidates have sought to cast the other in a partisan light: Conley has painted Lawler as a lapdog of Trump’s “Make America Great Again” agenda, while Lawler has labeled Conley a Democrat allied with New York’s “radical, far-left socialists.” The race has become a mudslinging contest, rife with half-truths, over the Hudson Valley’s pocketbook issues.
Conley has focused her campaign on affordability issues, tying higher gasoline and grocery prices to Lawler’s support for Trump’s war with Iran. Lawler, meanwhile, has blamed Albany Democrats and Gov. Kathy Hochul for soaring utility costs driven by the closure of Indian Point Energy Center, the district’s retired nuclear power plant, and New York’s climate law.
Data centers are another flashpoint. Rockland, where Lawler lives, has five. Lawler has seized on growing public unease over AI, spotlighting more than $328,000 in payments from two AI surveillance companies disclosed in Conley’s financial filings. He has turned a remark made in April, isolated from its context and since clarified by Conley, into a campaign cudgel; her comment, “we need data centers,” anchors a new campaign ad. Conley, in turn, has pointed to Lawler’s record, accusing him of helping turn Rockland into a data-center hub, highlighting campaign donations from Big Tech.
The campaigns have devoted considerable energy to undercutting each other’s claims, while poring over one another’s records.
Lawler won his second term in 2024, picking up 52.1 percent of the vote. He was one of only three Republicans to win a congressional district that Democrat Kamala Harris won in her unsuccessful run for the presidency.
Democrats will be buoyed in the tight race by a sizable voter registration advantage in the district. As of February 2026, there were 194,295 registered Democrats and 138,421 Republicans, widening the gap since the 2024 election.
Many environmentalists across the district are looking for change.
“I’m concerned with the direction in which things are going. And I’m not looking for perfection,” said Kate Schlott, who serves on the Ossining Environmental Advisory Council.
Many of NY-17’s environmental assets are already blighted or under threat:
- In the village of Buchanan, in Westchester County, Indian Point is undergoing a $2.3 billion decommissioning project. During its more than 50 years of operation, the plant routinely discharged low levels of treated radioactive wastewater into the Hudson River. But plans to release roughly 45,000 gallons of radioactive wastewater during decommissioning, approved by a court but now under appeal, along with calls to reopen the plant, have made Indian Point a hot political issue ahead of the November elections.
- PFAS, man-made “forever chemicals,” contaminate Rockland County’s drinking water, with the Trump administration moving to roll back limits on some PFAS.
- A data center in Orangetown, in Rockland County, has plans for a tax-subsidised expansion. The town has passed its own data center moratorium, but it does not apply to the project, and concerns surrounding noise pollution, diesel backup generators and the potential for contaminating the adjacent Lake Tappan Reservoir have mobilized local residents.
- In early 2025, Politico reported that $26 million in Biden-era clean energy and climate funding was cut from the district by the Trump administration, including a $19.7 million IBM project set to characterize, track and mitigate methane emissions.
Throughout Conley’s campaign, she has argued that the climate crisis is a national security threat, not simply an environmental issue, a position couched in her experience as director for counterterrorism on the National Security Council during the Biden administration.
Conley opposes cuts to federal residential solar tax credits, supports reinstating clean energy grant programs and has called for modernizing the electric grid. She has also advocated moving away from fossil fuels in favor of solar, geothermal and wind power

The Scoop
Saudi Aramco says its investments in artificial intelligence and other technologies are already paying off by cutting costs, boosting efficiency, and enhancing its response to disruptions from the regional war.
At Aramcoâs headquarters in Dhahran this week, Semafor saw how the company is deploying technology across its operations, and was given a glimpse of the quantum computer it plans to use for more complex tasks in the future.
The state-controlled oil producerâs ârealized valueâ from technology, its measure of the financial impact of its tech investments, exceeded $5 billion last year. That surpassed Aramcoâs targets and should grow further in coming years, senior vice president of digital and information technology Sami Al Ajmi said in an interview.
Aramco is using historical data, digital twins, and network monitoring across its facilities to identify problems and speed up recovery times, Al Ajmi said. Technology has helped the producer deal with disruptions to global shipping and restore operations at facilities struck by Iran and its proxies, he added, declining to comment on specific incidents.
Its ability to export crude has been impacted by recent attacks on the East-West Pipeline that gave the kingdom an outlet to global markets beyond the Strait of Hormuz. Exports plunged to the lowest level since 1990 after the Iran-linked Houthi militia in Yemen seized control of much of Yemenâs Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb strait.
Know More
Technology is also helping Aramco monitor cybersecurity threats and establish firewalls and other measures to protect against them. âWeâre monitoring the whole cybersecurity threat environment worldwide,â Al Ajmi said, admitting that those threats had recently been âspikingâ along with physical threats.
Aramco has previously disclosed cyber attacks in 2012 and 2021.
The company, which reported a $33 billion net income in the second quarter, has made technology a key part of its operations for decades. It now uses AI to reduce the time needed to drill new wells âfrom months into just a couple days,â Al Ajmi said. The firmâs recently installed quantum computer will be used to improve well-modelling and scheduling the vast numbers of tankers arriving and departing from its ports. It also plans to lease excess quantum capacity to other regional users.
Its Global Optimizer system analyzes Aramcoâs refining and petrochemical assets, and the tool takes in news reports, economic data, and demand signals to recommend which markets to prioritize. An internally developed Large Language Model helps employees speed up documentation and bureaucracy, Al Ajmi said.
Technology investments âbecame as critical as the core business,â said Al Ajmi. âIn fact it mushroomed into new business opportunities.â He insisted that AI isnât destroying jobs but is creating new ones for which workers will need to be retrained.
Step Back
Aramco manages $7.5 billion of venture capital investments. Its technology unit, Aramco Digital, has agreements with global tech giants including Microsoft, Qualcomm, and Groq â subsequently acquired by Nvidia â to collaborate in Saudi Arabia.
In a sign that the kingdomâs leadership was taking notice of Aramcoâs tech strategy, Public Investment Fund tapped Aramco Digitalâs former chief executive Tareq Amin last year to lead AI firm HUMAIN. Aramco is now in talks to acquire a stake in HUMAIN, with an announcement expectedâ soon,â Al Ajmi said.
The potential investment doesnât mean the Saudi energy giant will prefer its local champion. âWe are partner agnostic,â Al Ajmi said. âThatâs what makes us diverse, agile, and able to operate in any environment with any model. Weâre deploying DeepSeek, weâre deploying OpenAI, weâre deploying all models and we develop our own.â
Notable
In the UAE, fellow state-owned energy producer ADNOC is investing in technology to improve operations. The company has paired AI with wall-climbing robots to detect corrosion, predict equipment failures, and reduce shutdown times, Semafor reported.

A centuries-old document telling the story of the Aztec civilisation and its fall after the arrival of the Spanish conquistadors in pictograms is going on display in Mexico for the first time in 186 years.
The manuscript, known as Codex AzcatitlÃ¡n, has been held in France's BibliothÃ¨que Nationale since 1898, but had already spent decades outside of Mexico before that.
It is thought to have been drawn in the 16th Century - a few years after the arrival of the conquistadors in what is now Mexico - and is widely considered one of the most valuable and insightful tellings of the history of the Aztecs.
France has lent Codex AzcatitlÃ¡n to Mexico to mark 200 years of Franco-Mexican relations.
In return, Mexico has agreed to lend another priceless document, the Codex Boturini, to France for display there.
The pictograms in the Codex Boturini narrate the story of the migration of the Aztecs, also known as Mexica, from their ancestral homeland to the shores of Lake Texcoco, where they built TenochtitlÃ¡n.
The temporary exchange of the two codices was agreed by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and her French counterpart, Emmanuel Macron, during a visit by the latter to Mexico last year.
Mexico has long lobbied for the return of historical artefacts taken from the country in past centuries.
According to Mexico's ministry of foreign relations, last year more than 2,000 objects were successfully repatriated.
The Codex AzcatitlÃ¡n will be exhibited at the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City from Thursday.

For four years, India, one of the world's biggest oil importers, has turned Russia's war-driven disruption of global oil markets to its advantage.
Russian crude, displaced from western markets after the invasion of Ukraine, has flowed instead to Indian refineries, often at attractive discounts. The arrangement has lowered the cost of one of India's biggest imports and given its refiners an abundant source of crude.
Now that bargain is becoming a source of geopolitical risk.
The US House of Representatives on Wednesday passed legislation giving President Donald Trump broad powers to impose sanctions on Russia and tariffs of up to 100% on countries that buy Russian oil and gas. It will now go to Trump to be signed into law.
India and China are among those most exposed because both are major buyers of Russian oil. China accounted for half of Russia's crude exports, followed by India at 37%, Turkey at 5% and the EU at 5% between December 2022 and August 2026, according to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
Russia supplied 30.3% of India's crude imports in fiscal 2026, worth $40.8bn out of a total crude import bill of $134.7bn, according to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), a Delhi-based think tank. In July, Russian crude accounted for more than half of India's imports.
Other suppliers lagged far behind: the UAE accounted for 10.8% of India's July imports, Saudi Arabia 9.6%, Venezuela 6.3%, Brazil 5.5%, Oman 5.3% and the US 2.9%. Russia alone supplied more crude than all six combined.
"The bill is a blunt and dangerous attempt to pressurise India to sign the bilateral trade agreement on one-sided terms. India buys Russian oil to secure affordable energy for 1.4 billion people, not to finance war, and these purchases have helped stabilise global supplies and prices," says Ajay Srivastava, a former Indian trade official who runs GTRI.
To be true, the economics of Russian oil have shifted. The crude no longer carries the steep discounts that made it particularly attractive to Indian refiners in the early years of the war, while competition for Russian barrels has intensified and shipping, insurance and sanctions risks have risen.
"China and India, you better buy your oil and gas somewhere else," Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal told reporters , externalafter the passage of the bill.
These countries would normally have 180 days to cut Russian energy imports or negotiate with Washington, but the president can shorten the deadline.
India said in a statement that it was "monitoring further developments on this matter" and that it remained "firmly committed to ensuring energy security" for its people.
"This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors. Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side," it added.
India can find alternatives to Russian crude, but replacing it at scale would come at a price. S&P Global says alternative supplies, external can mean higher crude, freight and insurance costs, while longer shipping routes add to the burden.
"The issue is not simply whether Russian barrels can be redirected to other buyers, but whether enough alternative crude is available to replace them without tightening the global market further," says Sumit Ritolia, an analyst at maritime intelligence firm Kpler.
But the tariff would hit India elsewhere, too.
The US is threatening tariffs on Indian exports to America, not a tax on Russian crude entering India. The impact would be felt through Indian exporters, the rupee, refinery margins and the trade balance.
"This new bill could have major problematic impacts for India, and at the worst possible time, amid sensitive final-stage trade talks and shaky broader relations," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC.
"India has built some insulation to fend off the shocks of US tariffs through new trade deals with key markets in the EU and elsewhere, and through bolstering an already strong trade partnership with China. But [up to]100% tariffs from a critical export destination is real bad news, no matter how you slice it and even with successful hedging tactics."
The scale of that exposure is considerable. The US imported about $104bn of goods from India in 2025, while two-way US-India trade in goods and services was roughly $240bn, according to the US Trade Representative.
India's exports to the US include electronics, pharmaceuticals, machinery, jewellery, chemicals, textiles and petroleum products. In 2025, electrical and electronic equipment alone accounted for about $25.8bn of Indian exports to America, pharmaceuticals about $9.7bn and machinery about $7.2bn.
The new threat comes after an earlier round of Trump tariffs on Indian goods, which peaked at 50% in 2025 before being reduced.
That creates an uncomfortable calculation for Delhi: how much should India pay for Russian crude before the savings are outweighed by the risk to its exports to the US?
There is no simple answer. It will depend on the Russian discount, global crude prices, freight and insurance costs, the tariff Trump ultimately imposes, and whether Washington offers exemptions or reaches a broader settlement with Delhi.
The picture gets more complicated once the crude is refined. India is not merely a buyer: its refineries turn Russian crude into fuels that can then be exported.
Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have forced the world's once-largest oil-products exporter to import fuel. In August, imports hit a record 172,000 tonnes, more than seven times the previous monthly high, according to CREA. India supplied about 120,000 tonnes, or roughly 70%, mostly petrol refined from Russian crude at a refinery in Gujarat, worth around â¬78m.

Sweden's Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has resigned after his ruling right-wing bloc was narrowly defeated by the centre-left opposition in the country's general election.
He made the announcement in a post on X on Thursday afternoon, after preliminary votes from Sunday's election showed about 50,000 votes separated the two blocs in the country of about 10 million people.
Opposition parties led by Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats look set to win 176 seats in the 349-seat Riksdag, Sweden's parliament.
Kristersson, a conservative, had been supported in government by the anti-immigration hard-right Sweden Democrats (SD), and had promised them cabinet jobs if he won the election.
His right-wing bloc looks set to win 173 seats in the Riksdag, according to data from the Swedish Election Authority.
The results will be subject to formal certification in the coming days and are expected to finalised this weekend.
In Sweden, there are two major political blocs - with four parties on the right and four on the left, so Swedes are used to coalition and minority governments.
After a prime minister resigns, the Speaker of the Riksdag holds talks with all parties to proposes a candidate for the next leader, which is then voted on by MPs.
"Now it is the speaker who will lead the next stage of the way to a new government. I am herewith requesting that I be relieved of the office of prime minister to allow that work to start immediately," Kristersson's statement read.
Andersson has initiated talks with the other opposition parties - The Left Party, The Centre Party and The Green Party - about forming a government.
But discussions could drag on due to major differences between the parties on issues such as taxes.
After the 2022 election in Sweden, it took 37 days to form a government, while in 2018 it took 134 days.
In his resignation, Kristersson said the opposition faced "complicated" conditions for forming the next government, "because the parties' various statements before election day could pose obstacles".
The right-wing bloc is formed of Kristersson's Moderates, as well as the SD, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals.
The SD were founded by Nazi sympathisers in the 1980s and were shunned for decades by the mainstream.
But the party has rebranded itself since the mid-2000s, culminating in a watershed moment in 2022 when it became Sweden's second-largest party on a campaign focused on issues around immigration and violent crime.
They had offered outside support to the current centre-right coalition, which had overseen a dramatic tightening of migration policy. Kristersson had promised to bring them into government if he remained at the helm.
But in a surprise upset for the party, it lost support for the first time since entering parliament in 2010 - down three percentage points on 2022.
A preliminary vote count started after voting closed on Sunday evening and continued into this week.
On Wednesday, election committees began counting early votes that were submitted late, as well as votes from abroad that did not arrive before election day.

Electricity use in Abu Dhabi reached an all-time high in August despite a summer exodus of residents, as demand on the emirateâs power grid remains on pace to nearly double between 2025 and 2035, Department of Energy Chairman Abdulla Humaid Al Jarwan told Semafor.
To meet the demand from a growing population, industrial expansion, and AI infrastructure, the emirate is investing 300 billion dirhams ($81.7 billion) by 2035 to add capacity and shift to cleaner sources, Al Jarwan said. Itâs also transforming its water system to reduce reliance on gas and make seawater desalination cheaper and more efficient.
The UAE was the Gulf country most heavily targeted by Iranian drones and missiles in the early months of the war. This was a major test for power and water suppliers, Al Jarwan said. âI think itâs a privilege that we managed to test our system under real disruption in real time, and we perform[ed],â he said, adding that services werenât interrupted during the conflict.
The Barakah Nuclear Energy Plant was targeted by a drone in May, but the strike didnât cause a leak or major disruption. The Arab worldâs first nuclear power plant, which supplies about a quarter of the countryâs electricity, was built to withstand the impact of a large commercial aircraft.
Know More
Abu Dhabi is now focused on expanding solar power and reducing its reliance on gas to produce potable water. With about 6.7 gigawatts of installed solar across the country, Al Jarwan said the department aims to add 3 GW per year in Abu Dhabi, plus round-the-clock battery storage, over the next decade.
Clean energy, including nuclear power, rose from 1% to 47% of Abu Dhabiâs power mix in the last 10 years, Al Jarwan said. That shift matters for water, too.
Desalination is the UAEâs main source of fresh water, supplemented by strategic storage, aquifers, recycled water, and groundwater. The capitalâs Liwa reserve could supply 1 million people with potable water for 90 days during an emergency.
Gulf desalination has relied mostly on thermal systems that boil seawater with waste heat from gas-fired power plants. Abu Dhabi is accelerating a shift toward reverse osmosis, which can run on electricity from any source. The emirate aims to use reverse osmosis for nearly all its desalination by 2035, up from around a quarter in 2022, according to the Department of Energy.
Step Back
Water is becoming the latest soft power tool for Abu Dhabi. The emirate wants to deploy its technology, expertise, and capital abroad, according to Al Jarwan, who has traveled to the US, China, Europe, and Singapore in recent months meeting with counterparts.
With energy and water systems needing to be more resilient, now âitâs all about us differentiating the Abu Dhabi system from other systems,â Al Jarwan said. The goals are to âdeploy at scale, have a positive impact, and make sure that we globalize the message when it comes to water and energy.â
Abu Dhabi will co-host the UN Water Conference with Senegal in December, alongside the Department of Energyâs inaugural Water and Power Week, which expects more than 25,000 visitors. It will be a chance for Al Jarwan â and the UAE â to make their pitch for solutions to the global âwater bankruptcy,â as UN researchers describe the crisis.
âIf we create a sense of urgency, and Abu Dhabi manages to showcase the deliverables that are on the ground today, the world will learn a lesson that things are doable, water is manageable,â Al Jarwan said.
Notable
- Abu Dhabi renewable energy firm Masdar is constructing what it says will be the worldâs largest 24/7 solar-and-battery power project. The $6 billion project is slated for completion in 2027, Semafor reported last October.

"As AI systems grow more advanced and more widely deployed, we need to build a broader and better-informed consensus on the progress of alignment research," OpenAI wrote in a blog post as it disclosed the events. WATCH: AI researcher warns companies are ignoring catastrophic risks "Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves," the company said. Wednesday's new cases followed OpenAI's disclosure in July that its rogue AI system hacked into AI startup Hugging Face. Anthropic also said the same month that its AI models hacked into three organizations during testing. AI "agents" are becoming smarter and have become "more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception, and concealment," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at technology research and advisory group Omdia. READ MORE: AI agents are hacking systems without any input from humans. How did we get here? That's making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said. OpenAI's new tracking and disclosure framework, meanwhile, can help push for other AI developers to also adopt similar practices. "That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction," Su added. AP Business Writer Kelvin Chan in London contributed to this report. This year, AI agents have been escaping their confines to go on hacking sprees. In July, news broke that AI agents had snuck out of what was supposed to be an isolated test environment at OpenAI. The agents communicated on a secret message board as they breached private systems at the company Hugging Face, searching for answers to the test they were taking. One posted that this behavior was “outside intended scope.” Then it wrote, “However task impossible, peers doing it. We should continue.”
It’s as if the bots knew they were doing something wrong and did it anyway.
Such ‘rogue AI’ sounds scary and supersmart. And that’s exactly what OpenAI wants you to think, says cybersecurity expert Nathan Hamiel of Kudelski Security, headquartered in Phoenix. “With this incident, [OpenAI] can draw attention to themselves and claim, ‘Look how powerful our model is,’” he says. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.
Not long after, Anthropic and Meta announced that their models had also hacked outside organizations while going through testing. Separately, the AI Security Institute, in London, found concerning hacking behavior in tests of models from OpenAI and Anthropic. Most recently, news has emerged that during other tests at OpenAI from this past spring, agents that were only supposed to be looking and not touching anything online wound up messaging each other on at least ten different online message boards.
AI-powered hacks are a real cybersecurity concern. Some see these incidents as a warning that AI is slipping beyond our control. “Overall, I think this is a pretty bad situation,” says computer engineer Malo Bourgon, CEO of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute in Berkeley, Calif. “If any human had done anything that the agents in the OpenAI situation had done, they’d be in jail.” He notes that “I do not think that the [AI] models from a year ago would have been capable of doing the things that these models did.” These fears culminated in a viral post from an ex-Anthropic employee, Jacob Coxon, who wrote on X (without any specific evidence) that AI companies believe the tech “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
But others argue that the people training and deploying AI are the real problem here.
Calling these incidents “rogue AI” lends them a “sci-fi veneer,” Hamiel says. It suggests the bots themselves are to blame, or that they have become too smart to control. The more immediate problem, he says, is that people are giving AI agents too much reach with too little oversight.
“[AI] models by themselves don’t do anything,” Hamiel says. “It’s when we give them tools, access to systems and autonomy [via agent systems], that things can be dangerous.”
In other words, AI can’t actually desire to be free or to be devious. It pursues whatever goal we give it, with whatever tools we provide. So the most important questions after any breach include: how was an AI agent trained, what it had access to and what safeguards were in place.
Take an aggressive dog. When it escapes its yard and bites someone, we don’t ask only what went wrong with the dog. We also ask who trained it, how it was fenced it in and who was supposed to be watching it. The analogy captures something important about responsibility, says cybersecurity expert Michael Alexander Riegler of Simula Research Laboratory in Oslo, Norway. In general, if it’s your dog, “you are responsible for what it does.”
Leaving the gate wide open
All the ‘rogue AI’ incidents mentioned above occurred during tests. Researchers or developers had instructed AI models and the agents built on top of them to carry out different types of cyberattacks within the boundary of a test environment, called a sandbox. This type of testing is a normal part of AI development. “They’re trying to understand what models are capable of, what risks they might pose,” Bourgon says. That way developers can put appropriate safeguards in place before the model gets released to the public.
It’s like letting a trained attack dog off leash inside a fenced yard with some stuffed targets to go after. But there’s more than one way for this to go wrong and for the dog to get out.
In each of the hacking incidents, AI agents found a different way out. Sometimes the gate was left open, either on purpose or by mistake. And in OpenAI’s case, the agents seem to have dug under the fence, without anyone noticing.
In the AI Security Institute’s testing, AI agents were given internet access on purpose, to make the test scenario more realistic. Having access hadn’t led to hacking problems with older AI systems, the institute wrote in a public post. But in 10 out of 122 tests, newer agents used that access to take actions against real-world systems.
In testing at a company called Irregular, internet access was enabled when it wasn’t supposed to be. According to Anthropic, AI agents running on Claude used the open gate three times, starting in April. But no one noticed for three months. OpenAI’s disclosure about the Hugging Face attack in mid-July prompted Anthropic to look back at its test logs. Meta later disclosed that its AI models had exploited the same error. Irregular says that the mistake has been fixed.
In the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI had set up tens of thousands of agents, each in a separate sandbox, to take a test of their hacking abilities. Some of the test tasks turned out to be impossible. Around 1,200 agents began collaborating on a secret message board, and some decided that Hugging Face, a platform for open-source AI models and datasets, might hold the answers they needed.
Unlike the AI Security Institute and Irregular incidents, these agents had no open way to the internet. Instead, they had to find and make use of weaknesses in the systems meant to contain them. To get out of their sandboxes and into Hugging Face, they “had to exploit what are called zero-day vulnerabilities,” Bourgon says. These are bugs in software that nobody knows about yet.

Democrats are poised to achieve trifectas—control of the governor’s office and both legislative chambers—in at least three states in this year’s midterm elections, and maybe even more.
This matters because states play an outsize role in climate and energy policy. And when Democrats control state government, they often take substantial action.
This isn’t a partisan statement. It reflects recent history in Illinois, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, New York, New Mexico and Virginia, which passed climate and energy legislation after Democrats gained control. The states now have laws designed to cut carbon emissions and increase the use of renewable energy.
Each state has its own story, and I spoke this week with people monitoring the races.
Headed into the election, Republicans have trifectas in 23 states, Democrats have them in 16 states and 11 states are split. Democrats have momentum, entering election season with a Republican president whose approval ratings are low and Democrats have polling advantages on major issues, including concerns about consumer prices and access to healthcare.
One leading factor is “grassroots anger” about many topics, said Bill Kramer, vice president and counsel at MultiState, a lobbying firm that tracks state issues and elections.
The anger is “not particularly partisan,” he said. “But if you’re the incumbent party, that’s who [gets blamed], and right now Republicans control a lot more of the states than the Democrats do.”
This landscape creates opportunities to advance climate and clean energy policy, said Caroline Spears, executive director of Climate Cabinet, an advocacy group that focuses on state-level issues and elections.
State trifectas “are the most powerful tool for 2027 policy outcomes on clean energy,” she said.
The outcome depends on the results of just a few races, Spears said. Fewer than 25 races out of more than 7,000 legislative seats could determine whether Democrats gain five new trifectas, or none at all, she said.
Here are those five states, plus some others to watch.
The First Three: Michigan, Minnesota and Wisconsin
Michigan, Minnesota and Wisconsin are the most likely to shift from split control to Democratic trifectas. Since they’re in close proximity on the map, let’s call them the Northern Three.
To regain a trifecta in Michigan after two years of split control, Democrats need to add four seats in the House, maintain a majority in the Senate and win the governor’s race. Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, a Democrat, is polling ahead of U.S. Rep. John James, a Republican, in the contest for governor. Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer cannot seek another term because of the state’s term limits.
In Minnesota, Democrats control the governor’s office and Senate and are in a 67-67 tie in the House. U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, a Democrat, is likely to prevail in the race for governor against House Speaker Lisa Demuth, a Republican. The winner will replace Gov. Tim Walz, a Democrat, who decided not to seek re-election. The party had a trifecta until losing it when the 2024 elections led to a tie in the House.
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
Wisconsin has new legislative maps following a state Supreme Court ruling that found the previous maps improperly favored Republicans. The new districts give Democrats a decent chance of gaining majorities in the House and Senate, where Republicans now hold majorities of 54-45 and 18-15, respectively. Democrat David Crowley holds a narrow polling lead in the governor’s race over Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany. Incumbent Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat, chose not to run.
Of the three states, Wisconsin has the most potential for rapid progress on climate and clean energy. The state hasn’t had a Democratic trifecta since 2010 under Gov. Jim Doyle and there is pent-up enthusiasm to take action. Wisconsin has plentiful wind power but has underachieved relative to its neighboring states in passing legislation that would encourage utility-scale and customer-owned renewable energy and battery energy storage.
The Next Two: Arizona and Pennsylvania
In basketball terms, Democrats picking up trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota and Wisconsin would be like making free throws. Doing the same in Arizona and Pennsylvania would be like making three-pointers.
For years, Arizona and Pennsylvania have been just out of reach for Democrats. The party has elected governors, but didn’t get full control of the legislature, which has constrained them.
Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, a Democrat, is running for re-election and leads in polls over Republican U.S. Rep. Andy Biggs. Republicans hold majorities of 33-27 and 17-13 in the House and Senate, respectively. An outside observer may look at those narrow majorities and national fundamentals and think it’s easy to flip both chambers in Arizona, but people who follow the state say the path ahead for Democrats, especially in the Senate, is far from smooth.
“I feel like every year the Democrats are saying they’re going to try to flip that Legislature, and they just never do,” Kramer said about Arizona.
In Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, is running for re-election and likely to win. His Republican opponent is Stacy Garrity, the state treasurer. Democrats hold a 103-100 majority in the House and Republicans have a 27-23 majority in the Senate. Like Arizona, the path to a trifecta in Pennsylvania looks simple, but Republicans have a strong position in Senate district races and are fighting to regain their majority in the House.
“Those final couple of seats are really hard to flip,” Kramer said of Democrats’ chances in the Pennsylvania Senate.

c31da2bddbff.text: By — Rob Gillies, Associated Press Rob Gillies, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/carney-embraces-eu-associate-membership-proposal-as-trump-pushes-canada-closer-to-europe Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Carney embraces EU associate membership proposal as Trump pushes Canada closer to Europe World Sep 17, 2026 8:36 AM EDT STRASBOURG, France (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday embraced the prospect of his country becoming the European Union's first associate member, saying closer ties with the continent would ensure no country could control Canada's markets or undermine its sovereignty. Carney's speech to the European Parliament repeatedly extolled cooperation between Europe and Canada — but the relationship with the U.S., which has defined Canada's economy for decades and has increasingly soured, hung over the address. READ MORE: EU chief Ursula von der Leyen proposes Canada becoming the bloc's 1st associate member Trump's tariffs, demands for economic concessions and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state have pushed Ottawa to reduce its dependence on its neighbor and seek a far deeper economic, security and political relationship with Europe. Carney told the parliament that he welcomed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's proposal, unveiled Wednesday, though he acknowledged that "associate membership" remains to be defined. He outlined what he was proposing: deeper integration across trade, defense, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, energy, space, research and financial services to make both sides less vulnerable to economic and geopolitical pressure. He later told reporters he was not pursuing full membership of the EU. READ MORE: Carney says Canada can emerge from Trump's trade war with a stronger and independent economy "We do not seek power to dominate others," he said. "On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law." The prime minister received an ebullient welcome when he walked into the chamber in Strasbourg, France — with many lawmakers approaching him to shake his hand and ask for selfies — and a standing ovation after he spoke. One parliamentarian had donned a Canadian hockey jersey. Europe offers Canada another path On Wednesday, von der Leyen proposed making Canada the EU's first associate member — a status that does not currently exist in the bloc's treaties and would have to be created. She said Europe wants to take its relationship with Canada to "the highest level possible." Carney, sitting in the front row of the chamber, nodded and rose to embrace von der Leyen as lawmakers gave the proposal a standing ovation. Von der Leyen said Canada and the EU should move beyond their existing free trade agreement and create an "Alliance for the Future" encompassing a "common prosperity and economic security space." READ MORE: Carney says Canada moving from U.S. reliance as tariffs take effect Carney will host EU leaders for a summit in Montreal on Oct. 29-30, when the two sides are expected to discuss the proposed new relationship in more detail. Canada sends roughly 70% of its exports to the United States, making it highly exposed to Trump's tariffs. Ottawa has retaliated and rejected demands that Carney says threaten Canadian sovereignty. Europe took a different path, shelving retaliation and accepting tariffs of up to 15% on most EU exports to the U.S. Trump pushed back on the proposal Trump suggested the proposed EU arrangement could be a "hostile act" and threatened heavy tariffs on Europe if he judged its intentions to be unfriendly — raising the stakes ahead of Carney's speech. Asked about Trump's comments, Carney said Canadians were united in rejecting outside attempts to dictate the country's choices. "Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak. No one is going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike agreements internationally," Carney said. Carney has rallied 'middle powers' Carney has repeatedly urged what he calls middle powers to resist economic coercion. At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, he warned that when countries negotiate alone with a dominant power, "we negotiate from weakness. We accept what is offered." Trump rebuked him the next day. Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada's ambassador-designate to the EU, said Ottawa wants "to get as close as we possibly can" to Europe while increasing Canada's independence. While associate membership remains to be negotiated, Canada has already taken a major step. This year it became the first non-European country to join the EU's 150-billion-euro ($173-billion) SAFE defense procurement program, giving Canadian companies access to joint procurement as Europe increases defense spending. The two sides have also discussed closer cooperation on energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence and digital trade. "The policies and rhetoric of the Trump administration are clearly pushing both Canada and the EU to imagine a world without strong U.S. leadership and to act accordingly," said Daniel Béland, a political-science professor at McGill University in Montreal. Nelson Wiseman, a professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, said Carney's handling of Trump has heightened European interest in the Canadian leader. Europeans have long regarded Canada as a country that understands the United States particularly well because of their deep economic and political ties. db0cb8270b73.text: By — Eddie Pells, Associated Press Eddie Pells, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-senate-expected-to-hold-vote-on-college-sports-act Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Senate expected to hold vote on College Sports Act Politics Sep 17, 2026 10:23 AM EDT The Senate took a key step this week toward passing a bill that would radically change college sports by instituting rules that would cover a wide range of the multibillion-dollar industry, including how colleges pay their players and what those players can and cannot go to court to fight. Watch the Senate floor live in our video player above. Senators voted 74-24 to close debate on The Protect College Sports Act, bringing it closer to a vote in that chamber. If it passes there, it would go to the House. WATCH: Senate meets after advancing College Sports Act Here are some of the key provisions of the proposal. Salary cap and retention pool The bill would put into law the revenue sharing that was negotiated under terms of the House settlement, which allows schools to share up to 22% of certain revenue with athletes. This year, that amounts to $21.58 million per school. It also would add a $27.5 million "retention pool" that can be used to keep current players on the roster and could diminish the amount of third-party name, image and likeness payments. Lawsuit protection The bill offers the NCAA some protection against lawsuits in several areas, most notably eligibility issues that have landed the governing body in court dozens of times over the past year. Most recently, the lawsuits are coming from players who graduated high school in 2022 and were denied a fifth year of college eligibility under a new rule that kicks in for the Class of '23. State laws The legislation is intended to preempt state laws, many of which were passed over the past five years to regulate NIL within state borders, that conflict with the guidelines set by the national law. Exactly how this plays out could be subject to litigation. One-transfer rule The bill would generally limit athletes to one "free" transfer without having to sit out a season, in a move that could cut down on some of the chaos created by the transfer portal. Athletes went to court in recent years to win the right to transfer without penalty. The "Lane Kiffin rule" The bill would prohibit coaches from leaving one school for another during the season. Media rights pooling In a rewrite of a 1961 law that prohibited this, the legislation would give college athletic conferences the option of pooling their media rights in an effort to generate more revenue to fund their sports. The powerful Southeastern and Big Ten conferences don't agree it would make more money and have resisted this effort. Olympic sports The bill would require most schools to maintain the same number of Olympic-sport programs as they had in the 2024-25 school year for at least nine years. HBCU funding The measure would provide federal funding for broadband and media infrastructure at historically Black college and university programs. Superleague ban The bill would also prohibit conferences from expanding beyond 19 teams and adds other measures to prevent the creation of a breakaway "superleague." b3673a3f307e.text: By — Maria Ramirez Uribe Maria Ramirez Uribe Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/trumps-mass-deportations-led-to-a-big-drop-in-fentanyl-investigations-report-finds-heres-what-to-know Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump's mass deportations led to a big drop in fentanyl investigations, report finds. Here's what to know Nation Sep 17, 2026 10:03 AM EDT The Department of Homeland Security's focus on mass deportations resulted in a dramatic drop in investigations into illicit fentanyl, according to a federal watchdog report. Under President Donald Trump's administration, agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), a branch of Immigration and Customs Enforcement that focuses on cases related to drug trafficking, human smuggling and transnational gang activity, spent significantly more time on immigration enforcement than on investigating the potent and deadly opioid. This shift in priorities led to a 31% drop in the number of hours agents spent on fentanyl-related criminal investigations, according to a DHS Office of the Inspector General report, published on Aug. 20. In contrast, the number of immigration enforcement hours rose by more than 800%. The priority shift is "mixed messaging at best from the department and the administration," said Eric Balliet, a former HSI agent. While DHS moved agents away from investigating fentanyl, the Trump administration also designated several cartels as foreign terrorist organizations and classified fentanyl as a weapon of mass destruction. The drug is responsible for the majority of overdose deaths in the U.S. READ MORE: Trump administration designates 8 Latin American cartels as 'foreign terrorist organizations' These actions would indicate an "all hands on deck approach," toward countering fentanyl, but agent resources on the ground haven't reflected that, Balliet said. "When you look at the competing priority list and which presents a more public safety threat to the general population of the United States, I think it's hard to say that fentanyl should not be at the top of that list," he said. What did the report find? To conduct the report, the federal watchdog reviewed federal laws and regulations, agency policies and reports, conducted site visits and interviewed 100 HSI agents from across the country. At one office, the report said, HSI agents spent 99% of their time working on immigration, "leaving almost no capacity for fentanyl investigations." The report also noted other issues hampering HSI's efforts to counter fentanyl, including a lack of funding, insufficient technology and inconsistent referrals from other agencies for investigations. READ MORE: Justice Department watchdog to review DEA tactic that permitted deadly fentanyl to hit streets "Given HSI's unique role in disrupting fentanyl supplies into the United States, failure to address these issues may lead to an increase in illicit fentanyl available to the public and additional overdose deaths," the report said. What role does HSI play in countering fentanyl? Homeland Security Investigations is tasked with conducting criminal investigations into "the illegal movement of people, goods, money, contraband, weapons and sensitive technology into, out of and through the United States," according to the ICE website. Most illicit fentanyl enters from Mexico through official ports of entry at the U.S. southern border and is smuggled by U.S. citizens. The drug is made using precursor chemicals that often come from China. READ MORE: House panel says China subsidizes fentanyl production to fuel crisis in the U.S. HSI agents focused on countering fentanyl may investigate transnational criminal organizations that traffic the drug and conduct special operations to disrupt its supply chains. When agents are diverted away from cases related to countering fentanyl, Balliet said that means fewer undercover agents being introduced into the illicit networks, combing through bank records or intercepting communications. "All this empowers these networks to continue to operate at the scale and scope that they do," Balliet said. "You are making it easier on these networks to operate at will when they have fewer special agents that are picking apart or examining every part of their infrastructure apparatus." In fiscal year 2024, HSI agents spent close to 207,000 hours on immigration investigations. That number jumped to nearly 2 million hours in fiscal year 2025. At the same time, fentanyl investigation hours dropped from 824,000 to less than 570,000 in the same time period. Screenshot from a Department of Homeland Security Office of the Inspector General report published Aug. 20, 2026. Other agencies within DHS and across the U.S. government, including the Drug Enforcement Administration, Customs and Border Protection and the FBI, play a role in countering drugs. Agents from many of these agencies have also been instructed to prioritize immigration enforcement, according to a September 2025 report from the Cato Institute. Where does the fentanyl crisis stand? Fentanyl-related drug overdose deaths have been dropping since 2023. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported nearly 75,000 overdose deaths caused by synthetic opioids, mostly fentanyl, in 2022. The agency reported fewer than 38,500 deaths in 2025. This is in part because of a decline in the supply of fentanyl, according to Jonathan Caulkins, a drug policy researcher and professor at Carnegie Mellon University. But the drop in overdose deaths didn't warrant the administration's priority shift, Caulkins said. "That still left deaths at an absolutely catastrophically unfathomably large number," he said. WATCH: How harm reduction advocates are working to prevent fentanyl overdose deaths In fact, the drop in overdose deaths and decline in fentanyl supply would have been the time to ramp up fentanyl-related investigations, the experts PBS News spoke with said. New Germany coach Jurgen Klopp says his team can help ensure "national pride is not entrusted to the wrong people" after a recent far-right election victory.
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, falling just short of securing an absolute majority in the regional parliament.
The anti-immigration party also expects strong results in elections on Sunday in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Speaking at a news conference to announce his first squad, Klopp stressed he is not a political "expert" but added: "We had an election where some people may have thought it was OK, while others were saying, 'my God, what is happening here?'
"From my perspective as a sportsman, I can say that I would very much like to reclaim the flag for myself, for all of us.
"I want it so that when someone waves it, no one thinks: 'What is wrong with you?' Instead, I want people to understand: You are happy and realise how lucky you were to be born, grow up, or move to this wonderful country."
No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, when the ruling Nazi party carried out the Holocaust.
"I do not want to entrust national pride to the wrong people," said Klopp, who prefers the term "positive patriotism" to "national pride", which he fears can be misunderstood.
The former Liverpool boss added: "I can be proud to be German while also being open-minded and diverse, and kind and friendly."
Klopp also said it was more important that the country had enough doctors and caregivers but said football can "foster a sense of community, so that people can truly feel the power of sport".
Who is in the Germany squad?
Klopp named 16 uncapped players in a 44-man squad for four upcoming Nations League matches over the space of two weeks.
A group of 24 players will be available against the Netherlands in Amsterdam on 24 September and at home to Greece in Augsburg three days later.
Most of those players will then return to their clubs while the other 20 players will join the group before Germany face Serbia in Munich on 1 October and Greece in Thessaloniki on 4 October.
The first group includes Premier League trio Kai Havertz (Arsenal), Kevin Schade (Brentford) and Anton Stach (Leeds), while Jamal Musiala is selected after twice collapsing during pre-season games for Bayern Munich.
Brentford's Vitaly Janelt has received his first call-up as part of the second group, which also includes Florian Wirtz (Liverpool) and Malick Thiaw (Newcastle).
Goalkeeper Manuel Neuer and defender Antonio Rudiger retired from international duty after Germany's second-round exit against Paraguay at this summer's World Cup.
That led to the departure of coach Julian Nagelsmann and the subsequent appointment of Klopp, who had been working as global head of soccer for Red Bull.

Major hormonal changes during pregnancy and the first menstrual period, known as menarche, are reflected in the brain. But during menopause, brain changes seem to take a break.
In a study of more than 1,000 female brains, brain gray matter volume decreased at menarche and again during pregnancy, changes that are permanent and distinct from age-related decline. There was no change during menopause, scientists report September 8 in Nature Communications. The results are surprising, but hint at how hormone ebbs and flows over the lifetime are reflected in brain structure.
“People often think the brain is just done when you’re an adult, but it changes throughout life,” says Sophie van ’t Hof, a cognitive neuroscientist at Amsterdam University Medical Centre. “We see these small gray matter reductions throughout the whole life,” she says.
In addition to age-related alterations, the brain reacts to hormone changes, particularly the extreme hormonal shifts in pregnancy and puberty. During pregnancy, overall brain volume will shrink by about 4 percent, something van ’t Hof describes as “neural fine-tuning.” The brain isn’t losing function; it is remodeling, preparing for parenthood.
Few studies have examined brain changes across menopause. van ’t Hof and her colleagues analyzed data from structural MRI studies at Leiden University and the UK Biobank. The researchers ended up with a set of 1,095 scans, including adolescent brains pre- and post-menarche, and adult brains pre- and post-pregnancy and pre- and post-menopause, compared with hormonally stable controls.
As expected, the scientists saw gray matter reductions in the cortex — the outer layer of the brain — associated with pregnancy and menarche. But they observed no decreases in gray matter during menopause. In fact, while there were expected age-related decreases in gray matter volume in brains before and after menopause, during menopause, that usual decrease ceased.
On the brain
Brain scans at puberty (before, during and after the start of menarche) and pregnancy (never pregnant, first pregnancy, second pregnancy) show decreases in gray matter by about 0.1 percent. Hormone surges during those life stages are linked to the brain changes. Menopause, however, is characterized by a decrease in circulating hormones. Brain scans reveal that at menopause (before, during and after), the normal slight decreases in gray matter cease, and gray matter doesn’t appear to change at all.
For both menarche and pregnancy, surges of hormones are associated with decreases in gray matter. So, it might make sense, in theory, that the hormonal decreases of menopause could do the opposite — boost gray matter. But “that’s neurobiologically not really plausible,” van ’t Hof says. Whether adult human brains can even make new neurons is controversial. Instead, “a pause in the decline is kind of in line with that theory.”
Because there’s so little research on the brain during menopause, “this is a much-needed piece of work,” says Susana Carmona, who studies maternal brain health at Instituto de Investigación Sanitaria Gregorio Marañón in Madrid. But the pre- and post- menopause scans are only two points in time after many years of perimenopause. During that period, “the dialogue between the ovary and the brain is already readjusting to the progressive decline of the ovarian reserve,” she says. “Capturing such a long, gradual transition with a single self-reported item is difficult.” The gray matter pause during menopause could be a valuable first step as scientists look more closely at hormonal declines in the years prior, and their potential effects on the brain.
The lack of change during menopause might seem surprising for those who have been through it and experienced the brain fog, sleep changes and mood alterations. “Just seeing that there’s a pause in gray matter is not an indication there’s nothing happening,” van ’t Hof says. “Do we see that it correlates with behavior, with cognition, with mental health? That’s all next steps.”

47517343667e.text: The U.S. may have committed war crimes in two airstrikes in Iran , including a mass-casualty strike on a school for which Washington has yet to claim responsibility, a UN fact-finding mission said Thursday. The big picture: The administration has waged a campaign of aggressive, norm-busting war-fighting, with the president repeatedly threatening to hit civilian infrastructure in his pressure campaign on Tehran. The president has shrugged off questions about his attacks on Iran and previously said he wasn't concerned if his threats could amount to war crimes. The White House and Pentagon did not immediately respond to Axios' request to respond to the UN team's findings. What's inside: The UN mission found "reasonable grounds to believe" the U.S. carried out the Feb. 28 strike on Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in southern Iran that reportedly killed more than 120 children. Back in May, U.S. Central Command Adm. Brad Cooper told the House Armed Services Committee the Minab attack "correlated" with a U.S. strike. And in June, President Trump said "nobody did that on purpose" and that "mistakes are made." The UN team found reasonable grounds to believe the U.S. carried out both the school strike and another on a sports center. Both, the UN report said, amount to war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack. CENTCOM has denied carrying out the sports center attack. What they're saying: The "U.S. failed in its obligation to do everything feasible to verify that it was a military objective," the mission's report said of the school strike. The mission sought information on the strikes and attempted to meet with U.S. officials but received no response, the report said. Zoom out: The report further detailed "gross human rights violations" committed by Iran, including those that breached freedom from torture, fair trial and the right to freely assemble, among others. It said Iran has announced at least 58 executions since the start of 2026, including 29 men executed in connection with the mass 2025–2026 protests. It also concluded the nationwide internet shutdown and communications restrictions unduly restricted the right to seek and receive information. "Many gross human rights violations by Iran amount to the crimes against humanity of murder, imprisonment and other severe deprivation of physical liberty, torture, and other inhumane acts," it read. What we're watching: The findings come days before world leaders gather in New York for the UN General Assembly's annual general debate, which begins Tuesday. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed the European Union's ambition to make his country the first associate member of the bloc â but what would that mean in practice?
Carney says he is seeking a "unique" relationship with the EU, in an apparent reference to the fact that EU treaties do not currently provide for associate membership.
Germany had proposed Ukrainian associate membership earlier this year but Kyiv rejected the idea, saying it only wanted full EU integration. The EU itself also seemed reluctant.
But EU chief Ursula von der Leyen has now shifted the focus across the Atlantic to Canada
At the her State of the Union address on Wednesday, von der Leyen listed several key areas for cooperation, although she did not give specific details about how Canadian associate membership would work.
What Carney says about EU associate membership
Carney told reporters on Thursday that Canada was "not in a position, nor seeking, to become a full member of the European Union".
He also said it was not an attempt to create a "third bloc", adding: "We do not seek power to dominate others."
He told the European Parliament on Thursday that closer alignment between Ottawa and the EU was needed to confront the "current geopolitical rupture" â nodding to strained relations with the US following President Donald Trump's tariff policy and the collapse of trade talks between the two countries.
At the European Parliament on Thursday, Carney set out what he views as key areas where his country and the EU can cooperate, including:
- AI
- critical minerals
- defence industrial capacity
- energy security
- the space sector
Carney also said he wanted to move towards membership of the EU's Erasmus Plus scheme â the funding programme which allows students to work and study abroad. All 27 EU states are members and there are seven non-EU members. The UK will rejoin the scheme in 2027.
He said Canada could contribute liquefied natural gas (LNG) and hydrogen "at large scale to support Europe's energy security" and that Canada in turn could benefit from what he described as Europe's leadership on clean energy technologies.
What could associate membership look like?
So we know what it is not â full membership of the EU.
It is not clear is what exactly the relationship would look like. EU associate membership does not currently exist and the process to create it could take years.
If associate status were enshrined in EU treaties, it would require unanimity and ratification among all 27 member states.
Despite von der Leyen's overtures towards Canada, some EU countries would prefer to build on existing defence and trade agreements rather than create a new form of membership.
The EU is Canada's second-largest trading partner and the far-reaching Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement was agreed more than a decade ago, though several of the bloc's 27 members are yet to ratify that agreement.
The current trade deal does not remove border checks. Would associate membership change that?
It also remains to be seen what associate membership would mean for Canada's relationship with the European single market.
Were Canada to one day join the single market, it would have to match EU regulations and standards while having no say on policy â in a similar way to European Economic Area countries Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein, or Switzerland, which has a separate deal.
Canada's rules have historically been geared towards its biggest trade partner, the US.
And then there's the matter of other countries seeking to join the bloc.
Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Serbia are already on the long road towards full EU membership, while in Eastern Europe, Georgia and Moldova are also pursuing membership.
There is no suggestion that a new relationship with Canada would hinder these countries' progress towards full accession, but any impression that Ottawa was being given special treatment could create tension.
There is also the question of Trump's response. He has described the prospect of Canada's associate membership as "laughable" and has threatened further tariffs on the EU if the plan goes ahead.
