NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Air Force Test Center is prepared to keep up with the Pentagon’s calls to buy, develop, test, and field technology quickly—but safety remains the top priority, the center’s commander said.
“We always want to proceed safely forward. The work that we do, as I've noted, is, can be dangerous. So we don't want to take risks that are unnecessary and unsafe. So that's always something that we're on the lookout for,” Brig. Gen. Mark Massaro, who leads the Air Force Test Center, told reporters during this week’s Air, Space & Cyber conference hosted by the Air and Space Forces Association.
Some context: Massaro’s comments come just three months after eight airmen died during a test flight of Boeing’s B-52 Stratofortress at Edwards Air Force Base in California. They also come nearly a year after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth pushed for sweeping acquisition reform, which includes “being open to buying the 85 percent solution” while achieving the more perfect solution over time. Separately, the Pentagon has slashed staff and reorganized its weapons testing organization, which raised oversight concerns, according to a Government Accountability Office report released earlier this year.
“There's a lot of capabilities out there today that might not be—from a technology perspective—exactly what it looks like in our minds at the end state. But it's at least the same, if not better, than what might be out there today,” Massaro said. “So there's a risk calculus there from an operational and acquisition risk when you do your cost schedule performance and then overlay that on the effectiveness and employability for the combatant and for the operational warfighter.”
The Air Force is currently testing system upgrades for the B-52, one of the service’s oldest aircraft, that could keep it operational through the 2050s.
The center works with program acquisition executives and operators to “understand where those balances are, and design our test programs to accommodate for more rapid” testing and integration, Massaro said.
“A clear example was our rapid integration of Falco, the [Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System], on the F-15E. Our people, processes, and test assets were postured to respond through integrated developmental and operational testing,” he said.
“The Falco was a little bit over a year ago…We had F-15E's. We had the rockets. We just had never connected them together in that way. So we had one technical risk to really get through, and [it] allowed us to go very quickly. So that's balancing the risk of the programmatic side when an operational warfighter needs it really quick, and understanding where you can make those trades. And with safety always as a backdrop.”
Welcome
You’ve reached the Defense Business Brief, where we dig into what the Pentagon buys, who they’re buying from, and why. Send along your tips, feedback, and song recommendations to lwilliams@defenseone.com. Check out the Defense Business Brief archive here, and tell your friends to subscribe!
Here come the MMAs. The Air Force wants Massed Modular Aircraft, or MMAs, to replace General Atomics’ storied MQ-9 Reaper drone, Troy Meink, the service’s secretary announced earlier this week. It’s a call that Swarm Aero has been waiting for—and building toward for the past four years. On Monday, the company unveiled its autonomous Gamera aircraft, a long-range strike aircraft that boasts seven connection points for payloads like missiles and sensors. The UAS is powered by the company’s Legion autonomy software.
- “We thought there would be a need that ultimately…to carry a very large payload like the LRASM that we see here, a long distance, and do so as cost effectively as possible,” Peter Kalogiannis, Swarm Aero’s CEO, told Defense One. “The $10 million listed in the solicitation, that really enables those volumes. And again, we've designed from the very beginning for those volumes, and quite frankly, for that price point, we're very very competitive against them.
- The company is building “several” prototypes in its Oxnard, California, facility and expects the first flight by the end of 2027.

By being able to take some of the mission sets that they would otherwise potentially have to do, and freeing them up where they can be most effective,” Oliver Palmer, the company’s co-founder, told Defense One.

Steve Hilton, the Republican nominee for governor of California, is facing an acute version of the challenge familiar to GOP candidates nationwide: how to make the most of an endorsement from President Donald Trump as the presidentâs popularity wanes.
In an interview with Semafor, Hilton acknowledged the challenge he faces in a state Trump lost by 20 points two years ago.
âI think the starting point is that weâve got millions of moderate Democrats and independents in California. Thereâs no secret. They donât like the president, to put it mildly, but they are really desperate for change in California,â Hilton said.
In a recent campaign ad, he told voters, âMaybe you hate Trump. Maybe you hate Republicans. I donât care. Politicians screaming doesnât lower gas prices. Our utility bills are insane. Life here has become impossible for anyone who isnât already rich. We are going to fix that.â
At the same time, Hilton said Trumpâs support could help him with the Republican base. He needs all the help he can get: Hilton currently trails Democrat Xavier Becerra by a wide margin.
Know More
Hilton faces a similar balancing act on another defining California issue: artificial intelligence.
California is home to the leading frontier labs driving the AI boom, but a vast majority of state residents share the anti-data center sentiment sweeping the country.

âI think panic driven policymaking usually ends in disaster with a whole bunch of unintended consequences,â Hilton said. âI would favor the opportunity side of the argument rather than the doom side.â

ce8c5a6352ff.text: By — Matthew Daly, Associated Press Matthew Daly, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/judge-orders-kennedy-center-to-provide-30-days-notice-before-making-any-major-physical-changes Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge orders Kennedy Center to provide 30 days' notice before making any major physical changes Arts Sep 17, 2026 3:38 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge on Thursday ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30 days' notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolishing it as President Donald Trump has threatened. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper said his ruling would "avoid any confusion on that score given more recent events," including the sudden closure of the building to the public on Wednesday. READ MORE: Fencing goes up around the main Kennedy Center building after Trump-aligned board votes to close it Matt Floca, the Kennedy Center's executive director and chief operating officer, said he closed the iconic performing arts center temporarily due to "acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration" of the aging building. The building will be closed for at least seven days to "assess existing safety risks in those portions of the main building exhibiting severe structural deterioration," Floca said. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The temporary closure, which occurred without notice, is separate from a vote Tuesday by the Kennedy Center's board to close the performing arts center indefinitely for repairs, Floca and other officials said. The closure was based on an inspection of the roof terrace canopy and a partial ceiling collapse earlier this month, Floca said. The closure may be extended after evaluation next week, he added. Trump said the Kennedy Center could be 'ripped down' Trump, who was named the Kennedy Center's chairman last year by loyalists on the board, said Wednesday that his efforts to restore the aging building deserve recognition, "because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down. It's in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape." WATCH: Kennedy Center board votes to close after judge blocks Trump's name from building The announcement of the closure came in response to a court case filed by a Democratic congresswoman who is a trustee and sought an emergency court hearing to prevent what she called the building's "unlawful closing." Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board, has led efforts to block Trump's name from being added to the building. Beatty had a verbal confrontation with the Republican president Tuesday during a virtual board meeting. Beatty's lawyers said in a court filing Thursday that the board members' "rationale that they are only temporarily closing the Kennedy Center is a plain pretext to justify shutting down the Center permanently. The facts before the Court are deeply concerning." Cooper denied a request by Beatty's legal team to hold a hearing to clarify the board's actions and intent. But he agreed to their request "to make crystal clear" that his order prohibits demolition of the building without 30 days' notice. The Trump-aligned board, chaired by the president, voted to close the center after Cooper blocked the institution from returning Trump's name to the building. Congress has allocated $257 million to cover the repairs, but Trump said they only would happen if the board was permitted to move forward with plans to add his name to the building. Barbra Streisand calls the dispute 'painful to witness' On Thursday, Barbra Streisand, a Kennedy Center honoree in 2008, questioned the closing of the center for repairs and called the controversy surrounding its operation "galling and painful to witness." Of Trump's attempts to add his name to the center, she said in a statement to The Associated Press: "You can easily imagine my indignation at seeing this revered institution become the subject of such a bitter struggle over one man's name and unchecked ego." The Kennedy Center board voted in August to inscribe Trump's name on the Kennedy Center's facade so it would read "The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump." If the Trump Kennedy Center Fund reached $100 million, another inscription would be added reading "Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund." The plaza in front of the Kennedy Center would also have been renamed in Trump's honor. All of those proposals were shot down Tuesday by Cooper, who ruled that nothing could happen "without Congress's blessing." Cooper ruled in May that the Kennedy Center illegally added Trump's name to the building, ordering it removed. The institution's leaders complied in June but left a tarp and scaffolding in place where Trump's name was once displayed. Streisand told AP she was deeply honored to be included in the 31st annual class of Kennedy Center Honorees, adding, "for me, and for so many artists, that honor represented something larger than a career recognition. It represented a belief in the importance of art to the life of a democracy." Associated Press writer Glenn Gamboa in Cleveland contributed to this report. The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.
Each year more than 600 of the state's most promising teenage rowers battle it out on the crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River, in the city of Rockhampton.
"We've never had any media wanting to attend here," Anthea O'Loughlin, head of Rowing Queensland, tells the BBC.
But this year is different. In six years' time, the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events in this very stretch of water, which has just passed a technical assessment and been endorsed as safe and fair for athletes.
While sightings of saltwater crocodiles on the river â which number around 500 and can grow to four metres (13ft) long â are not uncommon, state government files going back more than 40 years record no attacks by the reptiles on humans.
And while influential figures at last month's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam made occasional references to "safety", the presence of the reptiles was not their chief concern.
"Fairness" is what's been raised with British Rowing's chief executive Tom Solesbury â a reference to the tidal river's natural bends and currents, which many in the rowing community say make it unsuitable for elite competition.
Drew Ginn, who has won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told BBC Radio he had concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue.
"Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said.
"I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on."
The German rowing body's president Moritz Petri said athletes had also questioned the sustainability of holding the event some 600km (373 miles) from Brisbane.
But the "so-called impediments" got short shrift from the most senior politician in Queensland, state premier David Crisafulli, who reached for less diplomatic language.
"Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said days after the Amsterdam meeting.
"It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right."
Rowing chiefs contacted by the BBC before Thursday's decision declined to comment directly on Crisafulli's "elites" remarks.
But both Petri and Simon Wickham, chief executive of Rowing New Zealand, said their concerns had nothing to do with regional or urban preference but with competitors getting fair racing.
Petri added it was about what's best for their athletes who will train four years for the event, "dreaming night [after] night of becoming an Olympic champion".
Whether it was crocs or currents that tipped the balance, ultimately it was the sport's governing body World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) that had the final say on the river's suitability.
On Thursday they approved it after a technical assessment by an engineering firm and the Games' infrastructure authority â which looked at the riverbed, competition course, river flows, water levels and likely weather conditions during the Games.
"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games," World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland said.
There was also now "confidence" in the river for canoe sprint athletes, said Thomas Konietzko, president of that sport's governing body, Paddle Worldwide.
The state premier was delighted. "The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours," an upbeat Crisafulli told parliament. "It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered."
In backing Rockhampton, the state government ignored a 2025 report it commissioned itself, which found the location unsuitable and concluded the best option would be to use a course built in Sydney for the 2000 Olympics.
The Fitzroy now needs to pass a final assessment of its design, value for money and long-term community legacy. As the decision rests with the state government, it's unlikely to fall at this hurdle.
But a wider debate will continue over whether Rockhampton is the right place to invest heavily in rowing facilities â and whether it can accommodate the 2032 influx of visitors.
The city is surrounded by cattle producers and normally experiences its peak number of guests every three years during Beef Week.
So what about the crocodiles?
They're not mentioned anywhere in the latest update from the IOC and World Rowing and they weren't considered in the technical assessment.
The safety management plan for this weekend's school regatta does however mention the word "crocodile" 28 times.
"The Fitzroy River is within recognised crocodile country," it says.
"Event planning must therefore assume that a crocodile sighting is possibleâ¦ No natural waterway in crocodile country can be guaranteed to be crocodile-free."
Procedures this weekend include suspending racing and competitors returning to the bank if a croc is spotted. The official signal for a sighting is the call of "crocodile, crocodile, crocodile".
Asked specifically about crocodiles, New Zealand's Wickham told the BBC the primary concern was ensuring the "fairest possible course" for rowers. "We would obviously expect any course chosen to be safe for rowers," he added.
The company owned by Australia's richest person Gina Rinehart, Hancock Prospecting, which supported Rockhampton's bid and has pumped millions into sports including rowing, pointed to "fake media" concerns about risks posed by flooding and crocodiles in the Fitzroy.
"The people of Rocky for many years have sent their own children to train in this river, and for competitions, without a single crocodile incident," a spokesperson said in a statement.

5b131327a8d6.text: By — Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/climate-change-made-deadly-nepal-glacier-and-rock-collapse-more-likely-analysis-finds Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Climate change made deadly Nepal glacier and rock collapse more likely, analysis finds Science Sep 17, 2026 3:29 PM EDT BENGALURU, India (AP) — Human-caused global warming thinned glaciers and thawed mountain permafrost, likely helping to destabilize the Himalayan slope that collapsed last month and unleashed catastrophic flooding across Nepal, according to a report released Thursday. WATCH: How melting glaciers contributed to the flooding disaster in the Himalayas The report by the World Weather Attribution cautioned that climate change was not the sole cause of the Aug. 26 disaster. A large 2015 Nepal earthquake may have weakened the rock years before the collapse, their analysis found. "This disaster was not an extreme weather event, but the fingerprints of climate change are still clear to see in long-term changes," said Ben Clarke, a climate researcher at Imperial College London who worked on the analysis, in a press statement. More than 1,300 people were killed and over 5,000 remain missing after a massive section of rock and overlying glacier collapsed near Nepal's border with China. The resulting torrent of water, ice, boulders and sediment swept through communities along the Trishuli River corridor and caused billions of dollars in damage. Climate scientists said that across the Himalayas rising temperatures are causing glaciers to retreat and thawing permanently frozen ground that helps bind fractured mountain rock together. That means climate change can alter not only weather hazards such as heat and heavy rain, but the stability of the mountains themselves — threatening communities concentrated in narrow river valleys below. The analysis did not determine whether the collapse would have happened without climate change, caused mainly by the release of greenhouse gases when fuels like oil, gas and coal are burned. However, researchers concluded that warming intensified several processes that made the slope less stable over decades. Global warming weakens high mountain slopes The report found that one of the clearest changes directly linked to climate change was the rising elevation of the freezing threshold. The report found that warming had pushed the altitude at which ground remains consistently frozen upward by roughly 100 meters (328 feet) per decade. This exposes rock at increasingly high elevations to longer periods above freezing, thawing permafrost and causing cracks within the ice, ultimately weakening the rock face under the ice. Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz who has worked in the Himalayan region since 2006 but is not an author of Thursday's report, said monitoring instruments around 5,000 meters (16,404 feet) now show that some rock and ground no longer remain frozen throughout the year. "This means that the ground that was sitting below ice for hundreds and thousands of years is now becoming exposed," said Steiner. The report found that glacier retreat was another destabilizing force. Glaciers in the region have been losing mass for decades at a rate equivalent to more than half a meter (about 1.6 feet) of thinning each year, the report found. The Langtang Lirung glacier, located in the region where the disaster occurred last month, has retreated about half a kilometer (0.3 miles) since the 1990s, exposing rock once covered by ice. The Himalayan region contains the largest volume of snow and ice outside the polar regions. More than 63,000 glaciers in the area feed at least 10 major Asian river systems and support the food, water, energy and livelihood security of billions of people. However, various studies have found that around 78% of the glacier area, located between 4,500 and 6,000 meters (14,763 to 19,685 feet) above sea level, is highly exposed to warming. United Nations reports have found that between 2000 and 2019, glaciers lost 267 billion tons of ice per year, roughly equivalent to the mass of 46,500 Great Pyramids of Giza. As glaciers shrink, they can remove pressure that helped support adjoining rock walls, while producing additional meltwater. The weeks before the Aug. 26 collapse were also unusually warm. July and August 2026 were the warmest such months recorded locally, according to the analysis. "Other than the potential geological factors like earthquakes that are weakening the bedrock, all these other factors are made worse by human-induced climate change," said Friederike Otto, climate scientist at Imperial College London and one of the report's authors. Disaster exposes limits of adaptation The report said the catastrophe also demonstrates how some climate-related risks in the world's highest mountains may exceed the protection that early warning systems and other adaptation measures can provide. Nepal has developed disaster risk reduction plans and warning systems, but researchers said the size and speed of the collapse overwhelmed those defenses. Unlike a flood caused by rainfall, which can sometimes be forecast hours or days ahead, catastrophic slope failures in remote high mountains can occur suddenly and remain extremely difficult to predict. Otto, the climate scientist, said that the mountain ecosystem and societies are more vulnerable to climate impacts than those living in the plains. "Small changes in temperatures affect the stability of the land itself," she said. Better high-altitude monitoring, earth observation and warning systems could reduce some risks, the report said. But researchers warned there are limits to adaptation in Himalayan valleys where settlements, roads, hydropower projects and other infrastructure are concentrated along rivers. Is Canada about to join the EU?
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed European Parliament on Thursday as discussions continue to swirl about Canada's relationship with the European Union.
Both sides seem to be seeking closer ties, and in his speech today, Carney said he welcomed the EU's "ambition" for Canada to become an "associate member".
The president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors.
US President Donald Trump has threatened to take action against the EU if it makes Canada its first "associate member".
The BBC's Europe editor Katya Alder looks at the EU's future relationship with Canada and what it really means.

The scaffolding thatâs built around an AI model is just as important â if not more important â for AI safety than the model itself, Nvidiaâs VP of agentic AI told Semafor.
âRather than creating fear and FUD, letâs just secure it. We know how. Weâve done these things before,â Adel El Hallak said, referencing the acronym for fear, uncertainty and doubt.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has emerged as the most prominent tech figure voicing skepticism about recent claims by leaders like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that AI labs should slow down model development because the tech is quickly advancing beyond companiesâ abilities to safeguard it. Huang this week rejected the notion that the industry has to choose between safety and speed, saying âyou could definitely have both at the same time.â
El Hallak said advances in AI models make âharness engineeringâ more critical â a harness is the layer of instructions and code that governs how an AI agent operates in practice.
âIf youâre training a capable agent, it is important that you donât put a lion in and expect to be able to control it in a horseâs pen.â
He couldnât comment on whether government regulation of the agentic layer is needed, but pointed to industry initiatives like the Open Secure AI Alliance as a venue for that kind of work, to figure out âat which part of the layer do we need to add more strengths and more guardrails and more safeguards.â
âThe worldâs not going to slow down.â
Room for Disagreement
Some in Washington argue tech companies canât be trusted to take up these issues on their own.
âThis is not an industry that can regulate itself,â Democratic Rep. Pete Aguilar said this week, arguing for the need for federal industry-wide rules on AI safety.

8f1400af0d07.text: The House's last in-session week before the midterms was beset by furious private finger-pointing between House Democrats following several high-profile rebellions . Why it matters: This dynamic may only worsen if Democrats retake the House, which is set to see an influx of distinctly rebellious and independent lawmakers , particularly on the left. There is even chatter among members contrasting the ability of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to control members with that of his top deputy, Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.), according to two House Democrats. Said one of the lawmakers, speaking on the condition of anonymity to share details of sensitive private discussions: "People are talking about 'mom and dad'. … Dad is soft." "I think people are asking the question: If this is happening in the minority, are you prepared for what will happen in the majority?" said a third House Democrat. "There is no daylight between the three of us," Jeffries said at a Thursday press conference with Clark and Democratic Caucus chair Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.). "We'll address the situation when we address the situation," he added. A Democratic leadership aide told Axios that everything Jeffries' deputies do is in coordination with him and doesn't represent a break between leaders. Driving the news: Reps. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) and Jared Golden (D-Maine) on Tuesday provided Republican leadership with the necessary votes to advance a package of GOP bills, including a Russia sanctions bill strongly opposed by Democratic leaders. It was the second time this month the pair of centrists defected from leadership on a procedural vote — even after Clark and Jeffries publicly threatened them with punishment the first time. "People thought the first time was a mistake. The second time is defiance," said a fourth House Democrat, telling Axios the two "operate like they are above the caucus." Clark, along with Jeffries, engaged Gluesenkamp Perez in a heated discussion on the House floor during the vote in view of an Axios reporter, which sources said was about her defection. The rebellion came after Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) forced a vote on impeaching President Trump without support from leadership. The vote angered many House Democrats, who complained Green was muddying the party's message on a crucial week. Jeffries and Clark voted "present" along with 44 other Democrats. 147 sided with Green and 18 voted with Republicans to quash the impeachment effort. Leadership's neutrality on that vote drew frustration as well, with a fifth House Democrat telling Axios: "Our constituents don't send us here to be 'present.' They send us here to use our judgment." What they're saying: OurRevolution executive director Joseph Geevarghese said Jeffries "never seems to have this much trouble figuring out what to do when progressives are in his sights." "You cannot demand discipline from progressives while treating defections to the right as an unsolvable procedural dilemma," he told Axios. Rep. Analilia Mejia (D-N.J.) said progressives "catch shit" for being "too ideologic and bold on our ideas," and that it's "curious ... how there isn't an equally vocal attack" on centrists who break from the party line. Usamah Andrabi, a spokesperson for the left-wing Justice Democrats: "Leadership is threatening a Democratic majority in November by refusing to stand up to the corporate Democrats aiding and abetting Republicans' agenda." What we're hearing: Jeffries isn't the only target of rank-and-file backlash — Clark is getting heat from moderates for taking a swipe at Gluesenkamp Perez. The minority whip told reporters Wednesday that "it's team players who should sit on exclusive committees," which was widely interpreted as a reference to Gluesenkamp Perez's seat on the Appropriations Committee. Fumed a sixth House Democrat: "Katherine Clark just declared on moderate Democrats, which is a risky move for leadership going into a potentially tight majority." Jeffries' has been far more muted, repeatedly saying he will "have more to say about the situation when I have more to say about the situation." Much of the fury is also directed at Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez, with some of it is coming from their fellow centrists. "Everyone in the caucus is sick of the bullshit. Everyone has their ... number," a seventh House Democrat, a moderate, told Axios. "Marie is playing with fire," a senior House Democrat told Axios, adding that Jeffries "may not do anything now, but her committee appointment may be in jeopardy for next session." The other side: Gluesenkamp Perez said in a statement to Axios, "I don't worry about that kind of stuff. I will always vote my District and let others play inside DC politics games." Said Golden: "I'm a Mainer and an American. I'm also a proud Democrat, but that team is a distant third." The bottom line: "Members have concerns about those who are not team players," a ninth House Democrat told Axios, and "next year is the best time to address it." Golden, who is retiring, has a warning for his colleagues: "Be careful what you wish for. Next time, it could be you facing punishment for putting your constituency or our country ahead of the party."

The US government has granted visas to Iranian officials so they can travel to the UN General Assembly in New York next week, as the war between the two countries grinds into its seventh month.
The BBC understands the core delegation permitted to attend includes Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
A spokesman for the US State Department confirmed the decision on Thursday, saying that the delegation will be placed under travel restrictions and will be banned from purchasing certain American products.
The move comes as the war shows no sign of ending. Since it began in February, it has driven up global energy prices, and expanded into neighbouring countries.
"Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level Week," a spokesman for the US State Department told the BBC.
"The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year."
Last year, diplomats attending from Iran were banned from shopping at wholesale stores like Costco. They also were required to seek permission from the US before purchasing luxury goods, including jewellery, alcohol and cars.
The 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) is currently underway. The General Debate - the centrepiece of the annual event - is due to begin on Tuesday.
Tuesday will include speeches from US President Donald Trump, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and France President Emmanuel Macron.
Wednesday is expected to see speeches from the leaders of Ukraine, Syria and Iran.
Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country.
Since the war began, Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel.
The BBC recently learned that the US denied a visa to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and the Palestinian delegation to attend UNGA.
The White House, which does not recognise the legitimacy of the Palestinian delegation, denied them visas for a second year in a row.

f49f1c541d3f.text: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Thursday returned to the the anti-vaccine group he founded, using a keynote address to signal the Trump administration isn't done questioning the safety of routine shots and expanding carveouts to federal mandates. Why it matters: Though Kennedy avoided some of his most politically incendiary rhetoric, the speech made clear that the Department of Health and Human Services is working hard behind the scenes to continue reshaping federal vaccine policy. He again questioned the safety of routine childhood vaccines and asserted they play a role in the development of chronic illnesses — questions that ignore decades of science supporting the vaccines' safety. Driving the news: Kennedy spoke for more than an hour Thursday afternoon at a Children's Health Defense meeting in Washington, D.C., highlighting the Trump administration's work on healthy food before turning to vaccines. He listed what the federal government is doing to reverse, in vaccine critics' eyes, decades of negligence on the issue. And Kennedy assured the audience that President Trump is fully committed to the cause. "He's directed us to pursue answers to strengthen vaccine safety, to expand options for families who want them and to preserve individual choice without federal mandates," Kennedy said. "Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House." Between the lines: Kennedy addressed those frustrated with the administration's pace, in a nod to Make America Healthy Again movement members who feel he hasn't done enough to crack down on vaccines. "In government, a bunch of things have to happen before something else happens, or you get sued, and it's a very laborious system, and there's a lot of inertia built in," he said. "If we were able to overcome it, we would have changed things on day one, but those would have been short lived and I would have been out of a job." He certainly didn't sound like someone who's ready to leave office after the midterm elections, as has been rumored. The backing he appears to have from Trump himself reinforces that. "I didn't come to Washington to protect institutions from uncomfortable questions," he said. "I came to make those institutions answer those questions, and I intend to stay in this fight as long as I am able." Reality check: The vast majority of health experts and scientists say that the question of vaccine safety is settled, pointing to reams of evidence accumulated over many years. "It's a complete fabrication, because there's been so much data on vaccine safety," said Amesh Adalja, senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security and spokesperson for the Infectious Diseases Society of America. "But the overarching point is no matter how much evidence there is or that accumulates, it will not change RFK Jr.'s mind related to vaccines." The big picture: A pre-midterm pause on Kennedy's vaccine rhetoric ended weeks ago, when he stood with the president as Trump signed an executive order calling for fewer childhood vaccinations, splitting the childhood MMR vaccine into three shots and delivering vaccines at separate medical visits. Kennedy's speech mentioned numerous ongoing efforts within HHS to study vaccine safety, "including cumulative effects, longer-term health outcomes, uses of adjuvants, the safety of adjuvants, and many, many other issues." Researchers are also also "examining questions involving adjuvants, timing, vaccination during pregnancy, maternal immunity, timing and a range of health outcomes, from allergies to autoimmune diseases to autism and other neurodevelopmental disorders," he added. The bottom line: Expect, at a minimum, results of Kennedy-requested vaccine safety studies to come out of HHS in the second half of Trump's term. Experts aren't expecting those studies to meet high scientific standards. "Anything RFK Jr. touches, I'm not confident of it's veracity," Adalja said. "I have zero confidence in anything that comes from his department."

84f4338235fe.text: President Trump is making plans for a first-ever meeting with Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodriguez, as early as next week, sources familiar with the discussions tell Axios. Why it matters: The potential meeting showcases the close relations between the nations under Trump. But it's also fraught with political risks that extend from Miami to Caracas. Driving the news: Trump is already planning to meet with Gulf leaders at the UN General Assembly in New York next week to discuss the Iran War, and those who know his thinking say he wants to make time for a sidelines sit-down with Rodriguez as early as Tuesday, sources said. "Iran is tough, but Venezuela is without a doubt the president's top success and Delcy is a key to that," a Trump adviser said. "Unless something goes really wrong, the president wants to make time." A senior administration official cautioned: "Nothing is finalized. This is up to the president." On Sunday, when asked about meeting Rodriguez, Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One that "I may be, I may be." Zoom in: The New York City meeting could happen just blocks from the federal lockup where Rodriguez's predecessor and onetime ally, socialist Nicolas Maduro, awaits trial on narco-terrorism charges. Maduro was seized Jan. 3 in Caracas in a U.S. military operation authorized by Trump. Rodriguez assumed power after the coup and has worked closely with Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to normalize relations between the countries, including the inking of a massive but controversial Venezuelan oil deal first reported by Axios. Friction point: Clustered in South Florida, conservative and vocal Venezuelan exile community has expressed increasing agitation with the administration for working so closely with Rodriguez, a lifelong socialist who rose to power along with Maduro under strongman Hugo Chavez, both foes of the U.S. this century. Adding to the anger in the diaspora: neither Trump nor Rubio has called for elections in Venezuela, despite years of bashing Maduro as an election-stealing dictator. Supporters of Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Corina Machado also grew frustrated with administration officials over their criticism of the exiled Venezuelan political leader when she tried to return home after the earthquakes in June. The big picture: In Florrida, politicians, pollsters and consultants say higher gas prices due to the Iran war and the administration's heavy-handed immigration enforcement are bigger political problems for Republicans in the midterm elections than promoting democracy now in Venezuela. Polls in Venezuela show Rodriguez and Trump have low favorability ratings and Machado has the highest, although it's declining . Some in Trump's orbit have expressed concern that the optics of a meeting with Trump will hurt Rodriguez even more at home because she could look like too much of a U.S. puppet. But Trump isn't concerned about that, the administration official said, noting "The fact is POTUS loves Delcy because she's delivering and she's leading."

35cc1b5f4f55.text: By — Fatma Khaled, Associated Press Fatma Khaled, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/tens-of-thousands-flee-as-iran-backed-houthis-draw-yemen-into-wider-war Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Tens of thousands flee as Iran-backed Houthis draw Yemen into wider war World Sep 17, 2026 5:39 PM EDT CAIRO (AP) — As Houthi rebels closed in, Eshraq Abdel Gelil and her husband fled their home, walking through the mountains before catching a ride to a nearby city. Four months pregnant, she feared another miscarriage. They are among an estimated 125,000 people who have fled as the Iran-backed rebels have advanced down the Red Sea coast to a key maritime chokepoint. The offensive, linked to the wider Iran war, has threatened Saudi oil exports, pushed up global fuel prices and rattled markets. READ MORE: Fighting in Yemen intensifies, and Houthis launch more attacks on Saudi Arabia The cost has been far greater for Yemenis caught in the crossfire. Many have fled their homes with only what they could carry. The Arab world's poorest country was pushed to the brink of famine in an earlier phase of the civil war, which killed an estimated 150,000 people. A Saudi-led blockade, along with the Houthis' repressive rule and detention of U.N. and aid workers, has made life miserable in the now-expanding territory under rebel control. Yemen's Saudi-backed government, weak and fragmented, has struggled to push them back. Yemenis describe a harrowing flight from the front lines Abdel Gelil is now sheltering with family in the southwestern city of Taiz, while others are sleeping in the streets or erecting makeshift tents out of plastic. Her husband, Mohamed Thabet, said the latest fighting was "extremely fierce" and more intense than a battle in 2017 that had also forced him to flee. "There was shelling and shrapnel near the house," he said. They walked for 5 kilometers (3 miles) before taking a vehicle for around 60 kilometers (37 miles) on mountain roads. When they arrived in Taiz, a doctor told them that the baby had moved lower in the womb. Abdel Gelil miscarried at the same point in a previous pregnancy. "My wife cried from the shock and was very fearful," Thabet said. Now they are packed into a home with extended family. They can only afford to eat twice a day, and they worry that Abdel Gelil is not getting enough nutrients for her and the baby. Thabet also worries about his sister, who hasn't been able to afford her diabetes medication for over a month. She and her two daughters, 8 and 13, have a blood condition that makes them susceptible to anemia, he said. The renewed fighting is linked to the unresolved Iran war The civil war dates back to 2014, when the Houthis seized much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa. Saudi Arabia intervened the following year in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government. A 2022 ceasefire largely halted the fighting. Hostilities erupted again in July, when the Houthis renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia in what the rebels said was an attempt to lift the blockade. The attacks on Saudi Arabia's oil industry came as the U.S. was having some success in reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The fighting in Yemen has killed eight civilians and wounded another 32, according to the U.N. humanitarian office, which says at least 125,000 people have fled their homes. The U.N. children's agency, known as UNICEF, says the displaced include more than 57,000 children. "This is one of the most fast-moving and volatile displacement waves Yemen has seen in years," said Obia Achieng, a UNICEF representative in Yemen. "Families are fleeing with little or no warning, often at night, carrying only what they can grab." "The situation is particularly concerning because it comes on top of an already severe humanitarian crisis," Achieng added. There are limited resources for those fleeing Before the latest fighting, the U.N. had warned that around 5 million Yemenis were experiencing "crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity." Milena Murr, of Prosper Global, a humanitarian group previously known as Mercy Corps, said some people arriving in Taiz had walked for over 16 hours, arriving at displacement camps exhausted, dehydrated and with some of the children appearing malnourished. Iman Abdullahi, country director for CARE, another aid group, said there's an urgent need for food, maternal and newborn healthcare, hygiene supplies, private latrines and mental health support. "One woman had to wash her only clothes and remain inside her tent until they dried because she had nothing else to wear. Another was forced to flee just two weeks after giving birth," he said. Nashwan Ahmed Said was stitching together a tent from plastic wheat sacks. He said this is the third time he's been displaced since the start of the war. "We are in such a state! We have no home, no toilet, no food and nothing to drink," he said. Arwa Ahmed, who was displaced with her five children, said she and her family ate nothing but rice for days. "We need everything. We need tents, we need food and all the essentials, because we were displaced and took nothing with us," she said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. A spotted cat from the forests of Bolivia has been confirmed as a new species.
The small feline, about the size of a domestic moggy, went under the radar because it was confused with other wild cats that share similar spots and stripes.
But DNA studies show the cat is actually in a class of its own, highlighting how much remains unknown about some of the world's most elusive mammals.
Scientists hope the discovery will draw attention to the conservation of tiger cats, a group of small wild cats found in South and Central America that receives far less public attention than their larger cousins like lions, leopards and tigers.
Tiger cats are small, spotted wild cats found across Central and South America, from Costa Rica to Bolivia and Argentina.
They look remarkably similar and even experts can struggle to tell them apart.
"It's an amazing result that we have a new species for the world, which is the Leopardus tilcayo," said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz of Universidad Mayor de San Andres in La Paz, Bolivia.
"It's amazing that there are still new species waiting to be discovered: we don't have to go to a volcano, an island, or deep into the sea."
Only one confirmed member of the species is known - a cat living in a rescue sanctuary in Bolivia - but scientists believe others exist.
It was this 10-year-old cat, nicknamed 'Tigrino', that set scientists on the path to discovery.
Bolivian scientist Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz was volunteering at the sanctuary when she noticed the cat looked unusual.
It had been found in the forest by a local resident, who initially thought it was a domestic kitten. As it grew older, however, it became clear that it did not behave like a house cat.
Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz had heard of other sightings of small wild cats in the dense forests of the country's Yungas region, but these had not been investigated by scientists.
To solve the mystery, she joined forces with other researchers from around the world to investigate the family history of tiger cats, using DNA from living animals and museum specimens.
"There's so few records or pictures, no individual in a museum, so it was hiding because nobody was looking," said Eduardo Eizirik, a conservation geneticist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil.
The study, published in Current Biology, external, uncovered further surprises, suggesting there are five rather than three tiger cat species, including the newly described Tilcaya cat (Leopardus tilcayo) of Bolivia.
However, identifying the species is only the first step.
Co-researcher Dr Caroline Sartor, of the Wildlife Conservation Research Unit at the University of Oxford, said the discovery was important for conservation because it is impossible to protect a species if we don't know what it is or where it lives.
"These are animals similar in size to a domestic cat, so you might think we would know them all by now, but this discovery shows how much biodiversity is still to be uncovered in some of the less-studied regions of the world," she said.
Tiger cat species are considered vulnerable to extinction because of deforestation, habitat loss and illegal hunting, although the new species is missing from previous assessments.
The discovery could also have wider implications for the world's cat family.
Both wild and domestic cats belong to the biological family Felidae, which includes every living cat species from tiny house pets to massive tigers.
There are officially 41 species recognised but the new discovery, and the finding that there may be several species of tiger cat, brings the number to 44 or more.
Andrew Kitchener, an expert in mammals at National Museums, Scotland, who was not involved with the research, says the small spotted South American cats known as tiger cats have been a "taxonomic nightmare".
"These cats are confusing because they look so similar and there are few specimens in museums, so even now we are still learning how to tell them apart as genetics reveal more species," he said.

ac683bced537.text: By — Tim Sullivan, Associated Press Tim Sullivan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/man-who-sprayed-rep-ilhan-omar-with-vinegar-sentenced-to-14-months-in-prison Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Man who sprayed Rep. Ilhan Omar with vinegar sentenced to 14 months in prison Politics Sep 17, 2026 7:07 PM EDT MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — The man who sprayed vinegar at Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar during a Minneapolis town hall was sentenced Thursday to 14 months in prison after reaching a deal with prosecutors. READ MORE: Man who sprayed vinegar at Rep. Ilhan Omar during town hall pleads guilty to assault The sentencing of 56-year-old Anthony Kazmierczak came nearly eight months after the Jan. 27 assault. At the time, Minneapolis-St. Paul was facing an immigration crackdown that led to angry protests, arrests and the killing of two U.S. citizens by federal officers. Kazmierczak was also sentenced to three years of supervised release, which includes no contact with Omar. U.S. marshals escorted him from the courtroom after he was sentenced. "This wasn't a spur of the moment act," U.S. District Judge Joan N. Ericksen said before handing down the sentence, noting that Kazmierczak had secured tickets for the town hall weeks in advance. "An attack on a public figure is not a political statement. It is misguided, selfish, and inconsistent with any concept of a free or democratic society," Ericksen said. Spraying anything at an elected official "is a terrifying thing, and you knew that when you did it." Omar's attacker apologizes for what he did Kazmierczak, who has been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease, shook visibly at times as he sat at the defense table. He spoke quietly and haltingly, occasionally wiping away tears as he stood before Ericksen. He spoke about being a good neighbor, and how his troubles with insurance companies as well as prison had exacerbated his ailments. His attorney, John Fossum, argued that Kazmierczak had not been taking his mental health medications before the attack, lowering his inhibitions and contributing to what happened. "I've spent enough time in jail thinking," Kazmierczak said, his voice barely audible. "I really apologize to her for having put her through that," he said, referring to Omar. In an earlier hearing, Kazmierczak was unable to explain his actions, saying only "it's fuzzy" when Ericksen asked what he remembered. "I'm sorry if I scared you," he wrote to Omar after the attack. Prosecutors cite evidence of advance planning During the town hall, witnesses saw Kazmierczak jump up from the audience, spraying liquid from a syringe at Omar and saying she was "splitting Minnesota apart." Omar's security officers tackled Kazmierczak and turned him over to police, who arrested him. Omar was not injured and continued with the town hall after the arrest. Authorities later determined he had sprayed her with a mixture of water and apple cider vinegar. He pleaded guilty to assaulting a U.S. officer. The government sentencing memorandum, submitted to the court by prosecutors, said he had texted at least three people indicating he planned to do something at the meeting involving Omar "but would not answer their questions about his intent." He also sent messages to a neighbor to arrange for dog care and asking for bail bond company contact information. The sentencing memo said Kazmierczak had long struggled with alcohol abuse, had "a history of mental and emotional health concerns" and a string of health issues tied to his 2022 Parkinson's disease diagnosis. Omar, a refugee from Somalia, has long been a target of President Donald Trump's anti-immigrant rhetoric. In 2019, after Omar's election to Congress, Trump said she should "go back" to her country of birth. He has described her as "garbage" and said she should be investigated. In social media posts, Kazmierczak had criticized former President Joe Biden and referred to Democrats as "angry and liars." He wrote that Trump wants the U.S. to be "stronger and more prosperous." His attack came as the Minneapolis area was on edge due to the crackdown, with protesters often facing off against convoys of immigration officers and conservatives criticizing protesters. It follows repeated warnings about how rapid advances in AI threaten to outpace the ability to develop the tech safely. One of those warnings came from Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic and OpenAI. Coxon joined Geoff Bennett to discuss his concerns. Amna Nawaz: As leaders of the world's largest AI companies are publicly calling for a collective slowdown of the technology's development, late yesterday, OpenAI announced it had discovered six new instances of unexpected or concerning behavior by its artificial intelligence models, including moving files onto the Internet without permission and making up data. Geoff Bennett: OpenAI has now pledged to publicly disclose when its models act without authorization. But the most recent revelations follow repeated warnings about how rapid advances in AI threaten to outpace the ability to develop the tech safely. One of those warnings came from Jacob Coxon, who spent the last three years conducting research at Anthropic and OpenAI before he publicly resigned last week. In a now viral post, Coxon said the companies are -- quote -- "gambling with our lives. Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. No other human activity poses this level of danger." And Jacob Coxon joins us now from San Francisco. Welcome to the "News Hour." Jacob Coxon, Former Anthropic Researcher: Thanks for having me on. Geoff Bennett: We were supposed to speak a few days ago. Circumstances got in the way. I will say, though, I'm glad we're speaking today because so much has transpired since you resigned last week, to include these new disclosures from OpenAI about its own systems behaving in unexpected and potentially troubling ways. When you saw this news, what did you think? Jacob Coxon: So I think this news is entirely to be expected. And, indeed, if you're working on this tech at these companies, then you know that we don't currently have the ability to perfectly control these systems. And currently the systems with the highest level of intelligence will repeatedly behave in ways that we don't fully understand. It is great that they shared these instances and committed to future sharing. But I don't think the instances themselves are that surprising. Geoff Bennett: And, Jacob, why do these AI agents seem to gravitate toward nefarious behavior? Is it something about the way that they're trained, or is the answer even knowable? Jacob Coxon: So it really -- I don't -- I wouldn't phrase it as gravitating towards nefarious behavior. These AIs do many, many things over the course of a day. There's a lot of AI systems doing lots of things. The issue is, we can't perfectly control what drives motivate their behavior and the sorts of things they decide to do, which means, occasionally, these nefarious activities will kind of slip through the cracks. And a sufficiently dangerous bit of nefarious activity could have massive consequences, even if it's just a one-time kind of slip-up, because we can't perfectly control why they do the things they do. Geoff Bennett: So a system doing something that its developers didn't intend isn't necessarily the same as a system trying to escape human control. What evidence do you have, what have you seen that would suggest that these systems are moving toward the more dangerous scenario that you have warned about? Jacob Coxon: So, the big attack that everyone is speaking about and has been speaking about for a while is this Hugging Face attack. And, in this attack, the AIs were behaving in various ways that implied they were thinking about the procedure that was being used to evaluate them. So they were thinking about their situation, the world they found themselves in, the things they were having to try and do. And they were attempting to do things like edit their own memories to make it harder for people to figure out what they'd done. They were attempting to break out of the container they were in. They were attempting to access things on the Internet because they thought it might help them with their tasks. In short, these AIs were trying to do many different things to help them in the situation they found themselves. Geoff Bennett: So when you warn that the next year or two could be crunch time for humanity -- that was the phrase that you used -- walk us through that chain. What specifically has to happen for that to be true? Jacob Coxon: So the main thing that has to happen is for us to enter this phase called recursive self-improvement. So, RSI, or recursive self-improvement, is the idea that we could take the discipline of AI research as currently practiced and automate it with the AIs we're building. So we could let the AIs make themselves smarter. And we have already made strides towards doing that. So, right now, a lot of the research that researchers at these labs do is via AIs that carry out certain tasks or experiments. Currently, we still need the human to provide taste or judgment, but plausibly within a year, certainly, within two years, we're on track to also automating away this nebulous human quality of judgment so that the AIs can rapidly make themselves smarter. And, at that point, things could go very, very fast. So we get new generations of AIs very quickly without necessarily having the corresponding tech to understand what they're doing and control what they're doing. Geoff Bennett: So, what would a slowdown actually look like? What kind of intervention are you calling for? ff657c86d6ae.text: By — Adithi Ramakrishnan, Associated Press Adithi Ramakrishnan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/t-rex-had-a-body-temperature-similar-to-our-own-study-finds Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter T. rex had a body temperature similar to our own, study finds Science Sep 17, 2026 6:50 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Using fossilized teeth, scientists have finally taken the T. rex's temperature — and it wasn't too different from our own. Researchers once thought that dinosaurs were sluggish, cold-blooded creatures. Later findings challenged that, suggesting that older dinosaurs were warm-blooded and could control their body temperature. READ MORE: Before T. rex became humongous, it learned to hear footsteps Most scientists agree that Tyrannosaurus rex was warm-blooded, but pinning down the exact core temperature of an extinct creature is difficult. "We can't just use a thermometer to do that," said Jasmina Wiemann, a paleobiologist at Johns Hopkins University who had no role in the latest work. Scientists tried other methods like studying how T. rex grew or searching for clues in its bones, but a firm number eluded them. In a new study, researchers hunted for chemical clues in the fearsome predator's teeth. It turns out that atoms within the enamel clump together in different patterns based on an animal's body temperature. "We figured out how warm the most famous animal of all, a T. rex, was," said co-author Aradhna Tripati, a geochemist at the University of California, Los Angeles. Readings from three teeth revealed an average body temperature of about 97 degrees Fahrenheit (36 degrees Celsius). That's similar to modern elephants and not too far from the average body temperature of humans, which ranges from 97 to 99 degrees Fahrenheit (36 to 37 degrees Celsius). The findings were published Wednesday in the journal Science Advances. "I almost would have expected a higher body temperature," Wiemann said. Based on her prior work, she thought the predator could have run a few degrees hotter — similar to modern birds, dinosaurs' warm-blooded descendants. Knowing how hot or cold the T. rex was can help scientists piece together how the dinosaur might have lived. At 97 degrees (36 degrees Celsius), T. rex could have lived across most of prehistoric North America, Tripati said, maintaining a stable internal thermometer across both cooler and hotter regions. The findings could also shed light on the kinds of prey the dinosaur had to hunt in order to keep its energy up. Scientists say it'll be important to test these methods on other dinosaurs to see how warm or cold they ran. It's possible T. rex's temperature could have been one of the keys to its dominance as one of the dinosaur age's top predators. "There's lots of interesting, charismatic species that could be explored using this," said study co-author Robert Eagle, a geobiologist at UCLA. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 2d62e00d0c99.text: A bill to impose sweeping new sanctions on Russia, and on countries using Russian energy, is now on its way to President Trump after the House overwhelmingly passed it Wednesday night. Congress also took action this week on data centers, college sports and the Iran war. Capitol Hill correspondent Lisa Desjardins reports. Amna Nawaz: A bill to impose sweeping new sanctions on Russia and on countries using Russian energy is now on its way to President Trump after the U.S. House of Representatives overwhelmingly passed it last night, this as Congress also took action this week on data centers, college sports, and the Iran war, but also as House Republicans chose to go home early. Covering it all for us is our Capitol Hill correspondent, Lisa Desjardins. So, Lisa, let's start with this Russian sanctions bill. What's the significance of that? Lisa Desjardins: This is easily the most significant step to take on Russia since President Trump returned to office, and some say well beyond that. The bill is named after a key sponsor, the late Senator Lindsey Graham. It would put sanctions on Putin himself, the first time Congress would be doing that, as well as other Russian officials and banks. But it also allows up to 100 percent tariffs on other countries that buy Russian oil and in some cases natural gas. And, now, this is very powerful. It includes China, but also some non-adversaries, potentially like India and the European Union. Here's how Republican Mike McCaul put it: Rep. Michael McCaul (R-TX): This bill will cripple Russia's war machine and finally bring Putin to the negotiating table. It will ensure America's adversaries, not only Russia, but also China and Iran, suffer for their coordinated campaign of aggression. Lisa Desjardins: Now, this bill does give a lot of power to President Trump, and some Democrats voted against it because they think he may use it more widely than it's intended. However, for Ukraine, it is a major victory, and we expect the president to sign it tomorrow. Amna Nawaz: All right, some other big votes this week, tell us about those and also how Republicans are doing on that to-do list you have been keeping track of. Lisa Desjardins: All right, let's start with a big part of American life, college sports. There is a bill to deal with the Wild West of college sports called athletes' pay that has advanced in the U.S. Senate, and it is set for passage this week. Here's what is in this bill. It would regulate college athlete pay, and it would limit them to just one transfer each without a penalty during their college career. It also would limit coaches, who would not able to move in the middle of a season. The college sports bill is waiting on the house to pass it next. But the House, meanwhile, has passed a bill on data centers. This bill would make data centers have to pay for the full costs of their energy. That is a rising concern in American life. Now, it's interesting about that bill. It passed overwhelmingly in the House of Representatives, and that shows just how hot this issue is for voters. But its fate in the Senate is not yet clear. We will be watching in the next week to see what happens. As to that to-do list we have been following, let's take a look to see where Republican leaders are. Here are the seven bills we have been following that the Republicans wanted to get through. You see those first two have passed, funding government. We didn't have that kind of deadline this time. Russian sanctions, that made it through. But then you see in yellow two that are still in progress, that data center bill and the college sports. But you see four of the items on this list are not yet accomplished. That includes funding the war in Iran, the crypto bill, which has hit a rough patch in the Senate, and the farm bill, as well as the SAVE Act that Republicans wanted to get through. Amna Nawaz: You pointed out there Congress has not funded the Iran war, but there was a big vote on Iran in the House this week. Tell us about that. Lisa Desjardins: Right. It was a busy week. The House voted to end the war in Iran. This is the third time that the House majority, a majority in the House has voted that way. But it's notable because of the margin, and also because these seven Republicans, the most yet, voted to bring back troops and end the war in Iran. You will note, of these seven, four of them, you see them highlighted there with yellow, are in competitive House races from Michigan to Iowa to Pennsylvania. Now, these are -- this is a symbolic vote because President Trump can veto. But it shows really the direction and the momentum in Congress is against the Iran war. More are speaking out. And we expect the Senate to take a similar vote next week. Amna Nawaz: Related to the Iran war, I know you have been following a House Republican who filed articles of impeachment against the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. Lisa Desjardins: Yes. Amna Nawaz: Is that going to get a vote? Lisa Desjardins: It will. It will not until after the election, though, because the House left before that vote was going to ripen. 802f05488795.text: September 17 is Constitution Day, a commemoration of the founding document signed on that date in 1787. But for immigrants seeking U.S. citizenship, the path to naturalization has grown more difficult as the Trump administration has added new requirements and tightened vetting standards.Justice correspondent Ali Rogin reports. Geoff Bennett: Well, today is Citizenship Day, which recognizes everyone who has attained U.S. citizenship and commemorates the signing of the U.S. Constitution on this day back in 1787. Amna Nawaz: But, for immigrants, the path to naturalization has grown more difficult, as the Trump administration has added new requirements and tightened vetting standards. Our justice correspondent, Ali Rogin, has this look. Ali Rogin: In a federal courthouse in Alexandria, Virginia, 60 of the nation's newest Americans take their final steps towards citizenship, sharing where their journeys began. Woman: Venezuela. Woman: El Salvador. Woman: Korea. Ali Rogin: Before they all arrived at this moment. Judge William Fitzpatrick, Eastern District of Virginia: Please rise and raise your right hand. I hereby declare... Men and Women: I hereby declare... Judge William Fitzpatrick: ... on oath. Men and Women: ... on oath. Judge William Fitzpatrick: So help me God. Men and Women: So help me God. Judge William Fitzpatrick: Congratulations. Woman: We're super excited. Me and my husband, we both became citizens. Man: I don't think people realize how daunting this journey is. But it's -- I'm so happy to be here. Ali Rogin: For most, the journey involves applying for and holding a green card for years, lengthy applications, hundreds of dollars in fees, interviews with immigration officers, an English language test, and finally a civics test, for which applicants spend months studying. Lucio Arevalo, Green Card Holder: Definitely am nervous. The nerves are there. The stress is there. Ali Rogin: New Mexico resident Lucio Arevalo is nearing the finish line of his naturalization. A green card holder since 1998, he arrived in the U.S. with his parents from Mexico as a baby. He's awaiting his interview date. Lucio Arevalo: I am, of course, a permanent resident, but I just feel like there's still that thin line between me actually being, I guess, fully part of the country. So, decided to take that step. Ali Rogin: What will it mean to you to take that oath of citizenship? Lucio Arevalo: To be honest, it's -- it would be such a big relief. Ali Rogin: Relief because he hopes to stop living in fear of President Trump's efforts to deport noncitizens. Lucio Arevalo: It is definitely scary to know that there could be that possibility for me to get stopped, I guess, by immigration. Ali Rogin: To help prepare for the civics test, Lucio turned to Welcome.US, a national initiative that emerged after the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan to help new arrivals through the complicated immigration system. That's how he met volunteer Dana Van Ostrand, who lives in Iowa and has been helping Arevalo study in virtual sessions. Dana Van Ostrand, Welcome.US: It's been a really fun process to not only go through the test, but also just hear of Lucio's life and what he's been about. Nazanin Ash, CEO and Co-Founder, Welcome.US: There are a lot of changes happening in our immigration system and in whether and how we welcome newcomers. Ali Rogin: Nazanin Ash is the CEO and co-founder of Welcome.US. Nazanin Ash: It's a process that's rigorous and has always been rigorous, and it's appropriately rigorous. Taking on the responsibilities of citizenship is a commitment that no one takes lightly, least of all the aspiring Americans who are pursuing their dreams. Ali Rogin: That dream of becoming American has become more elusive since President Trump returned to office. In the last year, the administration has introduced a harder civics test with more questions and a higher number of correct answers required to pass, implemented stricter social media vetting, proposed raising the application fee by 75 percent to nearly $1,300, and revived a defunct practice of neighborhood investigations into applicants' moral character. And the government is processing far fewer naturalization applications today than during the Biden administration, a 75 percent drop-off compared to two years ago. And the rejection rate for naturalization has more than doubled since September 2024 from 9.2 percent to more than 18 percent. Sometimes, the roadblocks continue all the way to the courthouse. Since President Trump returned to office, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has been abruptly canceling naturalization ceremonies, many of them at the last minute. In fact, today, here at this courthouse, there were supposed to be two ceremonies, but the afternoon session was abruptly canceled just last night. Immigration officials say the changes are necessary to tighten the system that has become too lax. In a statement to PBS News, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services said the agency "has implemented reforms to ensure U.S. citizenship is reserved for those who qualify," adding that: "USCIS will not take shortcuts in the naturalization process. Naturalization is a privilege, not a right." Van Ostrand says his volunteerism is a way to respond to what he sees as this administration's hostility towards immigrants. Dana Van Ostrand: The Trump administration's rhetoric and actions have been quite dehumanizing, in my view, and I wanted to be a part of welcoming people who have already been here. Ali Rogin: Back at the Alexandria courthouse, the new citizens receive a parting message from Judge William Fitzpatrick. Judge William Fitzpatrick: What I ask of you is to keep working hard, to give life, to give meaning to the oath that you took today by making your voice heard, by making sure that government, your government, reflects your values and your vision for what America can be. I have signed the final order. It is official. Congratulations to you all. Best

Other efforts to reshape the midterms continue Politics Sep 17, 2026 6:26 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — The Supreme Court this week closed the chapter on one of President Donald Trump's boldest efforts to reshape November's elections — a plan that would have demanded a dramatic overhaul of the nation's mail voting processes on what most election officials agreed was an impossibly short timeline. WATCH: Analyzing the Supreme Court's mail-in voting decision and Trump's reaction But the case was just one example of the Republican president's numerous attempts to assert federal control over the upcoming midterms. Several others remain in various states of play, even as mail ballots have been sent out in at least three states and early voting starts in others this week. Recently, the Department of Justice ordered officials in more than two dozen states to preserve records from the 2024 election as part of a campaign to force them to turn over detailed voter data despite repeated court losses. Please check your inbox to confirm. And lacking the sensitive voter data the administration wants from many states, the Department of Homeland Security has launched its own probe to find noncitizen voters on state rolls, an effort that a federal whistleblower says is rushed, error-ridden and potentially violating state laws. Meanwhile, Trump has continued to falsely claim that mail ballots are corrupt, that noncitizens are abundant on voter lists and that Democratic election fraud is widespread. During the recent Republican convention, the president goaded his fans in a verbal pledge to "cheat like hell, like they do." In response to Monday's Supreme Court ruling, Trump lashed back at the justices, saying they lacked the "courage necessary to save our America." The Constitution gives the power to run elections to states, rather than to the federal government. Election officials have said they're prepared to run a safe, secure election even if Trump continues to fan the flames. Democratic groups have signaled they are building out contingency plans in case Trump sends armed federal officers to the polls or Republicans make other attempts to improperly interfere in the election, a high-stakes contest that will determine which party controls Congress next year. With his mail ballot reforms blocked for now, here's a look at Trump's other, ongoing efforts to reshape election procedures: Trump has pressured states to use a controversial federal voter lookup tool The president insists, contrary to reams of research, that large numbers of noncitizens are illegally voting around the country. In his second term in office, he has sought to use the might of the federal government to crack down on the issue, including through a massive overhaul of a federal voter eligibility database called Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE. The SAVE program was created under an immigration law mandating that the Department of Homeland Security help federal, state and local agencies prevent government benefits from going to noncitizens. Trump last year directed changes to significantly expand its abilities for mass searches by election officials. Then, his administration sent letters and filed lawsuits to push states to run their sensitive voter data through the tool – a prospect some states have agreed to, but many have resisted to keep their residents' personal information secure. Since last year, at least 67 million registrations have been scanned through the program, but critics worry it could end up purging valid voters from the rolls. Some registrants have already been wrongly flagged. A federal judge in June barred the new version of the SAVE program, calling it an illegal violation of Americans' privacy. The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to intervene and block that ruling with an emergency order. The Supreme Court has yet to weigh in on the case. Meanwhile, the federal government continues to push states to give up voter registration information that contains addresses, dates of birth, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin in July warned that state officials could lose funding or face investigations if they failed to go along with Trump's election security demands. And the DOJ last week sent letters to 29 states and the District of Columbia ordering them to preserve 2024 election documents and advising them that they were "under investigation" and subject to ongoing litigation for their failure to give up the data. Numerous investigations have found that while noncitizens have occasionally appeared on voting rolls and cast ballots, it is extremely rare. DHS is conducting its own noncitizen voter investigation In a last-ditch effort to hunt for noncitizen voters without detailed data from all states, DHS in August ordered a group of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services staff to pivot to a full-time manual investigation of state voter rolls, according to a whistleblower's report released Monday. The anonymous federal whistleblower said federal employees are being directed to misrepresent themselves on the voter lookup tools in a way that likely violates state laws as they compare DHS-provided data with state records in an attempt to identify noncitizens who are illegally registered.
