The Drugs and Devices Have Been on the Market for Years. But FDA-Ordered Studies Still Aren’t Done.
When the FDA was deciding whether to approve the drug Tavneos several years ago to treat a set of rare autoimmune diseases, agency experts argued that would be a mistake, according to FDA records.
One problem cited: The manufacturer had provided only “limited safety data.”
As it often does, the FDA in 2021 approved the drug with a proviso: It required the manufacturer to conduct an additional years-long safety study once the drug was on the market.
Today, like many similar “postmarket” studies mandated by the FDA, that additional study is delayed, according to a federal database. As of last fall, only 21 of the planned 300 patients had been enrolled, the FDA said in an April letter and regulatory posting.
Meanwhile, the FDA has identified dozens of cases of liver damage “possibly” or “probably causally associated” with the drug. That was one of the potential side effects the postmarket study was meant to evaluate.
Tavneos illustrates the perils of the FDA’s approach to many drugs and medical devices — and the frequent lapses in follow-through.
A KFF Health News analysis of Food and Drug Administration data found hundreds of postmarket studies listed as delayed. In some cases, the work was delayed by more than a decade or the manufacturer was still developing a plan for the study.
As a result of delays, patients, doctors, and others could be left in a fog about the risks and benefits of the drugs or devices, even as they stake their money, their health, or their lives on the products.
Postmarket study requirements “have often proven toothless,” said cardiologist Sanket Dhruva, an associate professor of medicine at the University of California-San Francisco who has published related research.
The FDA’s reliance on postmarket studies reflects a balancing act.
Making new treatments available faster can save or improve lives, especially when patients with grim prognoses and no good options have little to lose. The full risks and benefits may be revealed only over the long term, and when therapies are used by far more people than even large clinical trials enroll.
But relying on post-approval studies to resolve questions risks exposing patients to products that do more harm than good. Whoever is paying the bills — patients, insurance companies, employers, or government health programs such as Medicare and Medicaid — can end up wasting money and rewarding manufacturers for useless or risky products.
“Doctors rely on this evidence, patients rely on this evidence, and if that evidence is not there, it’s going to lead to a lot of uncertainty,” Dhruva said.
Trump administration policy changes designed to hasten drugs through FDA review could leave more riding on postmarket studies, medical researchers say.
For example, in February, FDA leaders announced that “the default requirement” for agency approvals will be one clinical trial instead of two.
Reducing pre-approval testing “will inevitably put a lot of pressure on the post-approval system,” said Aaron Kesselheim, a professor at Harvard Medical School who has analyzed postmarket studies.
FDA officials said the new policy would “substantially reduce costs” for manufacturers and “speed drugs to market.” Writing in The New England Journal of Medicine, they denied the change would compromise safety or efficacy, saying that “erroneous conclusions may be reached even with two, three, or four studies.”
In response to questions for this article, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, which includes the FDA, said postmarket studies can experience delays for legitimate reasons. “Assessing the significance of any delay requires a case-specific review,” said the spokesperson, Emily Hilliard.
The fact that a study is delayed “should not be treated as evidence that a product has an unresolved safety or effectiveness issue,” Hilliard said.
Amgen, the company that makes Tavneos, is still working on the postmarket research the FDA mandated, company spokesperson Alison Chartan said, adding, “We remain committed to completing this important study.”
Behind Schedule
An FDA database downloaded by KFF Health News in August tracks the progress of postmarket studies that makers of drugs or biologics — such as vaccines and gene therapies — were required to perform or promised to perform.
The database showed almost 600 were running behind schedule.
Of those, more than 250 originally had final reports due before July 31, 2026 — the date that, according to an FDA webpage, the database last had been updated.
About a third of ongoing studies were listed as delayed.
In some cases, the FDA has granted extensions. In others, it has denied them. And in rare instances, the products were discontinued before the studies ran their course.
Postmarket studies can involve clinical trials or other analyses of patient data. They can look at safety or efficacy. A product can be the subject of more than one postmarket study.
The nearly 600 delayed studies involved almost 350 products, KFF Health News found.
The FDA has defined delayed as behind the original schedule. That can mean off track or overdue.
As of August, other FDA databases tracking medical devices listed dozens of postmarket studies as behind schedule.
Products included:
The CustomFlex Artificial Iris, a prosthesis implanted in the eye in place of damaged, defective, or congenitally missing irises. The protocol for a study in children was accepted in 2019, the database said. The study was meant to follow patients for five years. According to an FDA page downloaded in August, zero patients were enrolled.
Barbara Fant of Clinical Research Consultants, to whom the FDA’s 2018 letter approving the product was addressed, said the rarity of an eye disease called aniridia poses challenges for post-approval studies. Healthcare prices are likely to keep increasing next year. As midterm elections approach, candidates are laying out their plans to tackle these growing expenses.
KFF Health News chief Washington correspondent Julie Rovner joined WAMU’s Health Hub on Sept. 16 to explain how healthcare could play a critical role in the midterm elections. She said similar cost increases in the early 2000s led to the debate that became the Affordable Care Act.
“We’re seeing people have to pay more in their — not just premiums — but their deductibles, how much they pay before their insurance kicks in, and how much they pay when they go to the doctor,” said Rovner, host of the What the Health? From KFF Health News podcast.
In recent years, it’s not uncommon for healthcare providers to ask for payment upfront.
“Now you get there, and they say, ‘Can we have your credit card?’ before you even get to go in and get your care,” Rovner said.

The California valley with the most dairy farms in the state will follow stricter water pollution requirements following years of advocacy and a marathon six-hour meeting this week.
The State Water Resources Control Board unanimously agreed to adopt the regulations under what several environmental groups call a long overdue dairy order.
Nitrogen from the manure dairies produce turns into excess nitrate in soil, waterways and groundwater, and can eventually contaminate drinking water.
Families and children in the Central Valley “are living in crisis,” said Leslie Martinez, of the Leadership Counsel for Justice and Accountability and Defensores del Valle Central para el Aire y Agua Límpio (Central Valley Defenders of Clean Air and Water), a group of San Joaquin Valley residents.
“Low-income rural communities of color rely heavily on shallow groundwater and face the greatest exposure,” Martinez said during Tuesday’s meeting in Sacramento.
More than 700 dairies in the state—concentrated in the Central Valley—are within 1 mile of an area at high risk for nitrate groundwater contamination, according to state figures from last September.
A 2024 state tally estimated that more than 1.7 million cows generated over $8 billion worth of milk in California. But dairy farms here also pollute nearby waters.
In a 2017 study, the University of California, Davis, concluded that agricultural lands, including those with dairy operations, “are the largest contributor of nitrate to groundwater in the Central Valley.”
The 131-page order that was adopted Tuesday was released at the start of September as a draft and detailed the new requirements limiting water pollution from dairies. In the order, officials acknowledged the “outsized contribution” of dairies to nitrate pollution in the valley.
Environmental groups, while not satisfied with every aspect of the regulations, were happy to see them approved. Some advocates have fought since the early 2000s to increase oversight and management of water pollution from dairy facilities.
In an October 2024 first draft of the new regulations, water board officials proposed requiring that Central Valley dairies comply with a nitrate drinking water standard of 10 milligrams per liter and meet new rules for storing waste, applying manure to fields of crops and providing alternative drinking water to residents when nitrate levels in their water supplies are unsafe. Those requirements held in the newly approved order.
Still, during Tuesday’s meeting, even supporters of the new requirements worried about public participation and whether Spanish-first speakers had been given ample opportunity to comment on the rules being outlined.
The new dairy draft order was released online to the public Sept. 4 and feedback on the latest version was only gathered in-person or via video during the meeting Tuesday. No written comments were accepted.
Environmental groups were also uneasy about whether tribal communities got an appropriate chance to weigh in.
Dairy industry representatives in Sacramento were wary about the new regulations and what impacts they may have going forward.
Michael Boccadoro, executive director of the industry group Dairy Cares, worried the order was “inconsistent” with the Central Valley Salinity Alternatives for Long-Term Sustainability, a collaboration that has worked for 20 years to tackle nitrate and salt accumulation affecting water supplies in the region.
Kevin Abernathy, general manager of the Milk Producers Council, another industry group, believes the new rules will leave smaller dairy farms vulnerable to takeovers by bigger operations.
“This has the potential to further consolidate the dairy industry into the Costco and Walmart world that we all live,” said Abernathy, noting he was concerned about small- and medium-sized family dairies. “Mark my words, what you guys do here today will further consolidate the industry.”
He added, “Ag and dairy has always done our part to protect the environment for all of us and be good stewards of all of our land.”
A Long List of Health Risks
The Central Valley water board oversees dairy farms under a 2013 waste discharge rule. Current state estimates list between 900 and 1,000 regulated dairies in California.
Existing regulations of dairy farms were adopted at the urging of the Environmental Law Foundation and the Asociación de Gente Unida por el Agua, known as AGUA, which sued the regional board claiming its 2007 dairy regulations were inadequate.
A Sacramento court of appeals ruled in 2012 that the board was out of compliance with California’s law to protect clean water.
Under the state Safe Drinking Water Act, the maximum contaminant level for nitrate is 10 milligrams per liter, said Peter Thorne, an environmental health professor at the University of Iowa.
“There’s evidence that if you’re consuming water in the range of, say, 5 to 10 milligrams per liter there’s still an elevated risk of cancer that has been documented in a number of different studies,” Thorne said. “Especially for gastrointestinal cancers, stomach cancer and colorectal cancer.”
Earlier this year, Stanford University researchers released a white paper outlining frequently underreported levels of wastewater and manure from large dairy facilities in the Central Valley.
The researchers highlighted failures by dairy owners to document where waste goes and by the regulators to properly enforce reporting requirements.
Drinking water contaminated by nitrates “can interfere with red blood cells’ ability to carry oxygen throughout the body,” the Stanford experts noted.
Infants are acutely susceptible to low oxygen levels, including from nitrate impacts to water, which can lead to the potentially fatal “blue baby syndrome.”
Some counties in the Central Valley have seen 40 percent of drinking wells with nitrate levels above the safe limit established by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, posing health risks such as miscarriages and infant mortality.

The Signal Interview
Kai-Fu Leeâs AI Superpowers, an influential book published in 2018, largely predicted the current tech battle between the US and China. Now, Leeâs forecasting that AI will unleash more radical changes inside the worldâs companies than most CEOs expect â and this could reshape the competition between those two economies once again.
The former head of Google China, who has also held senior executive roles at Microsoft and Apple, understands intimately how Silicon Valley leaders think. But now that Anthropicâs Dario Amodei has called on the industry and its regulators to âpace the frontier,â Lee says he would reframe that call: âMove fast, but make sure safety keeps pace.â
Lee says he agrees with the principle that developments in AI capability must be matched by advances in safety and governance, adding that industry collaboration will be âparticularly important at this stage,â given how governance and regulatory frameworks âinevitably lag behind technological development.â
He is now deeply embedded in Chinaâs AI industry as chairman of the Beijing-based venture capital firm Sinovation Ventures and founder-CEO of 01.AI, a Chinese âAI tigerâ that has pivoted from building AI models to helping enterprises deploy the technology effectively.
Leeâs transpacific perspective has given him a unique insight into the challenges that global companies face in realizing AIâs potential. In a video interview, he says two things are clear from his conversations with other chief executives: âOne is that they all want to do AI transformation. Two is theyâre mostly doing it wrong.â
Lee is pitching his new book, AI Native, as a road map for doing it right. CEOs hoping to build an âAI-nativeâ company must take personal charge of their technology strategy, he says, and use âradical transparency,â enabled by AI, to give them unprecedented insights into what is actually happening inside their organization. That conscious echo of the management mantra of Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio, he adds, is an idea that Chinese employees will embrace faster than Western workforces.
Why transformation starts at the top
CEOs everywhere face âa Darwinian choice,â Lee says: Embrace AI or accept the consequences. They have little time to do so, he adds; companies whose assets are largely digital, like entertainment, gaming, and internet businesses, will be âdead in the waterâ if they do not adapt, he says. CEOs operating businesses further from the AI frontier â like coal mines, farms, or manufacturing plants â may have a three-to-five-year âbufferâ before they feel the pain of AI disruption.
That means executives need to ask now whether they are passing âthe earnings call test,â Lee says: If their companyâs AI efforts have not yet boosted their profits, then they are mere âAI theater.â
Where chief executives go wrong, in any industry, is when they delegate and defer to their chief information officer, Lee argues. âOnly the CEO can define the ambition, concentrate resources, redesign the operating model, remove barriers, and remain accountable for the result,â he writes in AI Native, so AI transformation âcan only be done from the top.â
That also means that each CEO needs to be using AI effectively themselves, he adds. Doing so demonstrates that the companyâs leader understands AIâs importance to the bottom line.
The radical transparency of Boss AI
Lee has taken his own advice, designing a âdecision assistantâ made up of 19 agents to help him run 01.AI. His company has since packaged this up into a product to sell to other companies, called Boss AI.
At its heart is what Lee calls a âtruth engineâ that records, organizes, and analyzes every internal meeting, sales call, and customer service request to show what is getting in the way of the company meeting its goals. That gives a CEO visibility into all corners of their company â and a âpromise ledgerâ to hold people accountable for following through on what they say theyâll do.
âMiddle managers often hope that the CEO will forget. And the CEO does forget, but the CEOâs AI does not,â Lee says. It is at this tier of most companies that the bossesâ plans meet the most resistance, he adds.
âThere are a lot of antibodies in the company, people who just donât want to do AI transformation. Middle managers feel vulnerable because theyâre not technology experts, [and] theyâre afraid the boss will put in someone who is,â he explains. Those managers also fear losing their power if their company lays off their direct reports, he adds.
Still, even as he says that AI is dividing workforces into âirreplaceable humansâ and âdisplaceable humans,â Lee does not think that CEOs should measure AI success by the number of jobs they eliminate.
âThe winners will not measure success by payroll cuts. They will measure it by what their best people, amplified 10 times, can now do that was previously impossible,â he writes in his book. Most people will not be laid off if theyâre willing to learn new AI skills, he adds, âbut they might be paid three or five times moreâ than before.
But he still believes that companies should flatten the hierarchies that protect people who resist change. âWhen the company is transparent, thereâs no need to hide, nowhere to hide, and everybody talks about the real issues and tries to solve the problems.â
Where clashing cultures meet AI superpowers
Lee presents his ideas as âexhilaratingâ for employees who are willing to sign up for them. âThe company will have a better morale, better culture, better execution, better results, better stock price, and everything will be a virtuous cycle and the company will grow,â he predicts.
Even so, Lee admits that radical transparency âtakes [some] getting used to.â Some corporate cultures will be more reluctant than others to expose themselves to the bossâ all-seeing AI, he adds, bringing his argument around to a point which converges with his earlier predictions about AIâs impact on geopolitical competition.

The Signal Insight
The combination of an Australian headquarters, a Nasdaq listing, and customers around the world means that Mike Cannon-Brookes usually has his first coffee of the day before he opens his laptop at 5 am. But Atlassianâs co-founder and CEO sees his location as one of the reasons why his enterprise software company has grown to a $48 billion valuation, making him one of Australiaâs wealthiest entrepreneurs.
Straddling the Pacific Ocean can be both a source of frustration and differentiation, Cannon-Brookes says. Sydneyâs diversified economy makes it âa great microcosm,â where Atlassian can test whether ideas hatched in Californiaâs Bay Area will work in less tech-forward cities around the world.
Even far from the âfroth and bubblesâ of Silicon Valley, Atlassian has been caught up in US investorsâ mood swings over whether AI will hurt or help software companies like his. Atlassianâs stock has leapt 230% from an April low, helped by stronger-than-expected earnings, but is still 60% below its late-2021 peak.
Cannon-Brookes says the evidence heâs seen so far suggests that customers will spend more with Atlassian as they use AI more heavily. âThe most AI-centric, the most AI-native, those are actually the customers that are expanding the fastest for us.â
Hereâs how he explains what itâs offering them, and why heâs advising other CEOs to make big bets on AI, even if they wonât all pay out.
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Whatâs your routine in Sydney?
I start most days at 5 am. I work 5 to 7, then kids 7 to 9, then work 9 to 3. Iâm not one of these early-risers that gets up, does some journaling, drinks some water, goes to the gym, that sort of thing. Itâs more like [I wake up at] 4:45 am, make an espresso, and get to the computer, which is less healthy than all the journaling and meditation kind of stuff.
Iâm interested in the challenge of building a company this big from Sydney. Youâve straddled the US and Australia for a long time, but it sounds like you think the time zone is not a disadvantage.
I travel an awful lot. When youâve got a global customer base, at some point it doesnât matter where you are [based]. But I think one of Atlassianâs biggest hidden advantages is having one foot in Silicon Valley and one foot squarely outside of Silicon Valley, in a large traditional corporate market. Sydney is a big city, with banks, insurance companies, manufacturing companies, and grocery companies. Weâre fast adopters of technology, but weâre not super technology-driven.
I always say you get the froth and bubbles of Silicon Valley. That is amazing and naive at the same time. This amazing âIâm going to change the worldâ attitude has produced some of the most incredible businesses ever. And at the same time, sometimes thereâs a lot of technology thatâs applicable between San Francisco and San Jose, and nowhere else in the world. We take the ideas from Silicon Valley, and we try to make sure those ideas apply in Sydney, which is a proxy for every other big city in the world.
Atlassian is going to be 25 years old next year. How do you describe the companyâs place in the market now?
We help companies run business processes, and collaborate around those processes in a variety of different areas that are critical glue to how a company actually runs on a daily basis. We donât handle their accounting system, their email, or their calendar. We handle all of the glue in between the systems for their business teams, their technology teams, their service teams, and their leadership teams, and try to bring that together into repeatable business processes. Which sounds naff, but a great company is just actually a collection of processes that [also allow people to] innovate and change and collaborate. People arenât robots. The intelligence and creativity of the people is what makes it a beautiful mess.
Youâve been talking about âcontextâ as the great AI bottleneck. What exactly is the context problem that your customers are dealing with?
AI models are intelligence, and you can rent intelligence from lots of different model providers. Itâs a fantastic battle [between them] that weâre all benefiting from because the intelligence power that weâre being given is going up continually. But models lack wisdom and knowledge. They have a lot of generalized knowledge. Ask any model in the world where Einstein was born, and theyâll give you the answer. If you ask, âWhen is this project due?â they have no idea because itâs not in the model; itâs in your company. So you have to bring that knowledge from the company with the intelligence of the model. Knowledge is not exactly context, because context requires you to have that wisdom of your company. What we have, for many customers, is 20 yearsâ worth of business processes, 20 yearsâ worth of workflows, and 20 yearsâ worth of decisions they made, and the outcome of those decisions.
Have you gone through the cycle many other companies have gone through of encouraging your software developers to go wild on the latest AI models and then realizing itâs costing you a fortune and reining them back in?
Iâm a bit more sanguine on this. I think thereâs a logical learning path that the world is on. If every staff member is an AI novice, and you want them to become AI-native, how do you do that? You have to encourage them to use all these tools. You have to encourage them to play, to spend tokens, and to learn. So, I think itâs natural that companies are going to say, âUse all these tools.â Then, as people start using them, theyâre suddenly going to be like, âWait, theyâre all really expensive.â I think thatâs not a bad thing. Youâve learned how to [use them]. Youâve convinced people that theyâre valuable. Youâve changed their mindset. Now you [just] have a problem of budget management. What you need to understand is how your token use relates to performance and [returns on investment].

- Published
President Donald Trump's administration says it has approved the sale of nearly 50 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a policy shift for the US that has raised concerns from some members of Congress.
Saudi Arabia has sought for years to buy the world's most advanced warplane, equipped with stealth technology that allows it to evade enemy detection.
Washington had resisted, partly because it supplies F-35s to its ally Israel, which is guaranteed under US law to receive top-of-the-range American weapons compared with those its regional neighbours can access.
Congress has 30 days to scrutinise or attempt to block the $24bn (Â£17.8bn) sale to Riyadh, which is the largest customer for US weapons.
Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, a Democrat, opposed the sale on Thursday.
He warned "it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party".
Other Democratic lawmakers and some American defence officials have raised similar concerns about giving F-35s to Saudi Arabia.
They said Riyadh might share the sensitive technology with China under a security partnership between the two countries.
The state department said in announcing the deal on Thursday that it would support US "foreign policy and national security objectives".
It said the deal would improve "the security of a major non-Nato ally that is a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf region".
"The proposed â sale of this equipment and support will not alter the military â balance in the region," the state department added.
Trump has a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited the White House last November.
The two also met in May last year in Riyadh, where a $142bn arms sale was sealed â described by the White House as the "largest defence sales agreement in history".
The latest proposed sale announced to Saudi Arabia would include 48 F-35s, which are built by the arms company Lockheed Martin.
This would place the country on a level with Israel, which currently has a fleet of 50 jets.
However, Israel's ministry of foreign affairs announced in May, external that it would procure another F-35 squadron.
This deal would double the size of Israel's F-35 fleet to 100, according to the Jerusalem Post, external.
Just one of Lockheed Martin's F-35A jets costs about $82.5m.
Congress has previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh after the murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018.
Former US President Joe Biden's administration considered supplying F-35s to Saudi Arabia if Riyadh would normalise its â relations with Israel, but that diplomatic effort faltered.
The proposed sale comes as the Saudis are engaged in fighting with the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen.
The Houthis have recently seized control of swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces.
The Saudi crown prince has personally pressed Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.
But Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, the sources said.
Additional reporting by Sareen Habeshian

The Prince of Wales has warned that the world needs to move faster to solve the biggest climate challenges.
Speaking exclusively to the BBC, Prince William called for a greater sense of urgency around ways to repair the planet.
"We're not moving fast enough," William said. "We need more businesses, investors and leaders to step up, back what works and help bring these solutions to scale."
His warning came as this year's nominees for the Earthshot Prize, the global environmental award he launched six years ago, were unveiled.
Earthshot remains one of the key priorities of Prince William's public work.
"Around the world, people are proving every day that we can restore nature and tackle climate challenges. Our 2026 finalists are an incredible example of that."
Among the 15 finalists is the entire city of Barcelona, recognised for its efforts to safeguard its Mediterranean coastline.
The city's architects were praised for "turning one of Europe's most intensively used urban coastlines into a global blueprint for climate adaptation".
The Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan was also selected, with the prize recognising how the country has embedded environmental protection into its national identity and constitution. The prize said that Bhutan had demonstrated "how a small nation's forests can safeguard water security across an entire region".
The finalists also include a range of community-led initiatives tackling environmental challenges such as waste reduction, nature restoration, and clean energy.
They include Indigenous ranger teams in Australia and an Argentinian artificial intelligence-powered wildfire detection and alert platform.
Two finalists are from India, which will host this year's Earthshot Prize awards ceremony in Mumbai.
They are Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, a leading manufacturer of electric three-wheelers, and the Mahila Housing Trust, a grassroots organisation pioneering climate resilience initiatives for low-income women.
The finalists were selected from nearly 7,000 nominations submitted across 169 countries.
Five winners, one from each of the five Earthshot categories - protect and restore nature, revive our oceans, clean our air, build a waste-free world and fix our climate - will be announced at the ceremony in November.
Each will receive a Â£1m prize to help expand their project.
The Earthshot Prize Council, which selects the winners, includes Prince William, alongside Queen Rania al-Abdullah of Jordan, actress Cate Blanchett, and chef JosÃ© AndrÃ©s.
"The solutions are here. The challenge now is scale," Prince William told the BBC.
"The progress is real. Now we need to accelerate it. That's exactly why The Earthshot Prize exists."
It has been a torrid week for the royals with allegations from Prince William's uncle, Earl Spencer about his parents.
Neither Prince William nor his brother, the Duke of Sussex, have made any public comment on the book nor the direct criticism aimed at their father, the King.
Prince William and the Princess of Wales were on the Isle of Bute on Thursday focusing on royal duty rather than family fallout.
This afternoon, Prince Harry will be in the Midlands visiting a school to look at how the stories of wounded military personnel can inspire young people as part of his Invictus Foundation.
Amidst the noise of Earl Spencer's allegations, the royal family approach will be to continue with public duty and charity engagements
Additional reporting by Daniel Wittenberg

The News
An energy price spike in Nigeria is renewing fears of an inflation rise and concerns that Africaâs top oil producer remains vulnerable to global shocks despite growing domestic refining capacity led by a giant facility owned by the continentâs richest man Aliko Dangote.
The Dangote Refinery, whose shares went on sale on Monday to kick off Africaâs largest initial public offering, raised its wholesale petrol price by 7% late last week. The move set off increases of up to 5% across pump stations in Lagos and the capital Abuja. Much larger increases are expected in northern towns and rural areas.
Nigeria Labour Congress, the top national union of government employees, warned on Wednesday that rising fuel prices risked imposing âincalculable damageâ on wages, and could cause household expenses at the beginning of a new school year to rise sharply alongside higher transport costs. The union acknowledged that the Iran war is raising global oil prices, but wondered why Nigeria had to suffer a âbleak situationâ given its domestic oil production and refining capacities.
âWe are deserving of a certain level of protection or buffer against the gales from the Gulf,â Joe Ajaero, head of the labor union that represents four million Nigerian workers, said. President Bola Tinubu ended Nigeriaâs decades-old fuel subsidy scheme in 2023. Fuel prices have risen five-fold since, sparking a cost-of-living crisis that has become a key campaign issue ahead of an election in January in which Tinubu will seek a second term.
Nigeriaâs inflation rate slowed marginally to 15.39% in August, on the back of improved food supply and exchange rate stability. The decline raises the prospect of an interest rate cut by the central bank at next weekâs monetary policy committee meeting, the penultimate one for this year.
But overall price levels tend to rise in Nigeria with higher fuel prices. Lagos-based Coronation Merchant Bank warned that âsustained higher energy costs could feed into fuel and transport prices, slowing the pace of disinflation.â Investment firm CardinalStone expects that the central bank will hold the rate steady due to a still high chance of âfurther energy-price volatilityâ in Nigeria.
Know More
Nigerians consume around 50 million liters of petrol per day. The Dangote Refinery has often insisted that its fully operational 700,000 barrels-a-day plant can fulfill this demand.
In the first six months of this year, Dangote and a handful of far smaller Nigerian refineries supplied nearly 80% of the petrol that was available in the country, according to data from Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA), the governmentâs fuel regulator. Imports, formerly Nigeriaâs main source of petrol before Dangote, declined from accounting for 60% of domestic supply all of last year to just over 20% between January and July in 2026, per the agencyâs data.
But multiple petrol price increases in Nigeria this year â including the highest rise of any country in the first weeks after the war started â point to a link between both Nigeriaâs refineries and fuel importers to global oil price increases. The price of Brent crude, the oil benchmark Nigeria favors, has risen more than 70% since January to more than $100 this month.
Up to 40% of the crude used by the Dangote Refinery comes from outside the country, while a similar share is sourced from a government scheme that sells in the local currency. A year-long rise in the oil price consequently affects both Dangote and the international oil refineries from whom Nigerian fuel importers buy their products. The latter groupâs landing costs have gone up this month after slowing during the period of Iran war ceasefires.
In the background of the dilemma over rising fuel prices, Nigeriaâs energy market remains gripped by a years-long tension tied to the uneasy co-existence of petrol imports alongside a thriving refinery sector.
Step Back
Dangote, the billionaire industrialist, has opposed imports since before his refinery began supplying fuels in 2024. His company argued in a May lawsuit against licenses issued by the regulator NMDPRA that fuel imports undermine the refineryâs investment and make the domestic market inefficient. Importers have countered that they are necessary to ensure supply diversity, security and competition.
David Bird, CEO of the Dangote Refinery, says the companyâs contention is largely over offering high quality fuels at a fair price to Nigerian consumers, and blames the regulator for the tensions. âThe tragedy for Nigerians is that there is not a regulator where you can have confidence in their institution that it is driving product quality compliance,â Bird told Semafor in an interview last week, ahead of the companyâs IPO launch.
âIf the regulator is allowing some pretty rubbishy Russian material that canât find a home anywhere else in the world, then how can we compete? Weâre against imports until we have confidence that the regulator is driving compliance to product quality,â he said.
NMDPRA did not respond to a request for comment.
Nigerian regulators should rule according to what is ultimately best for consumers, Adedayo Ademuwagun, an analyst for London-based Songhai Advisory, told Semafor. âIf an importer can supply quality fuel at a lower price, why should the government force a teacher in Lagos to pay more for locally refined fuel?â

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz faced growing pressure on his leadership ahead of state elections in which polls suggest his governing party will fare badly.

Eight state premiers, all from the CDU, backed Merz ahead of ballots being cast and Germany has little history of replacing chancellors mid-term. But moribund economic growth and his personal unpopularity have raised what once seemed an unlikely prospect for the CDU.
âThe party forgives its chairman a great deal â as long as he governs successfully,â a Handelsblatt correspondent wrote. âThe time for forgiveness is over.â

Researchers used Anthropicâs Claude technology to break into OpenAIâs ChatGPT systems, underlining the immediate dangers of AI even as regulators fret over its long-term risks. The effort, part of a bug-hunting program, was the latest in a series of cybersecurity breaches aided in large part by fast-developing AI technology, The Wall Street Journal noted.
Axios cited business executives and ex-government officials voicing worry over AI-powered cyberattacks threatening critical infrastructure, while The Washington Post noted the Pentagonâs âantiquated computer networksâ had resulted in an explosion of cybersecurity risks. As a new research paper put it, recent breaches have been the result not of a developing superintelligence as some top AI leaders warn, but of insufficient technical guardrails leaving networks vulnerable.

Discord reigned in the intensifying debate over AI safety regulation, with tech bosses taking opposing stances and government leaders sharing little common ground. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang argued at an event in Scotland that AI should not be regulated like social media, Palantirâs boss told CNBC that leading AI firms may need to be nationalized, and Huaweiâs chair called for Chinese labs to accelerate their development.
The issue will be at the forefront of talks between the US and Chinese leaders next week â OpenAIâs Sam Altman is due to join Huang and Appleâs Tim Cook at a state dinner â but Washington and Beijing have radically different ideas and goals when it comes to AI safety rules.

7b9978e96806.text: Warren Buffett will step down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, less than a year after handing over the CEO reins, the company said Friday. The big picture: The "Oracle of Omaha" is 96, and his insurance-to-railroads conglomerate is moving onto a new generation, with his son Howard as chairman. What they're saying: Buffett, in a brief letter to shareholders, said the time was right to step aside from leading the board, after transitioning the CEO role to Greg Abel earlier this year. "Greg runs the company; Howard will guard its culture and values – both worth more than anything on our balance sheet," Buffett wrote. "Think of Howard as a policy the shareholders own and hope never to claim against." Zoom in: Berkshire said Warren Buffett would become "chairman emeritus" and remain on the board of directors. Long-time board member Susan Decker, the former president of Yahoo, will remain lead independent director. By the numbers: Berkshire shares were flat in pre-market trading on the news. The stock has underperformed this year, rising just 1% versus a gain of about 12% for the S&P 500. If that doesn't change, it'd mark the fifth time in the last 10 years that Berkshire underperformed that benchmark. While Berkshire has beaten the S&P by nearly 10 percentage points since 1965, in the last decade it's lagged the index by half a point or so. Editor's note: This story has been updated with new details throughout.

Thirty-seven people accused of illegal mining in north-central Nigeria have died in custody, local officials said.
Police have set up an investigation into the deaths, which the Nigerian Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) blamed on an apparent disease outbreak.
However, an intelligence report shared with AFP news agency suggested the group died because of overcrowding and poor ventilation inside the detention facility in Niger state.
"We believe they suffocated because there was no ventilation," the father of one of those detained told the BBC.
Abdullahi Dalhatu said his son had survived because he was near a small window.
"His friend slumped and fainted, and many others also collapsed."
His son described how detainees began collapsing in the heat of the overcrowded and poorly ventilated cell, his father said.
He said the detainees repeatedly knocked on the door for help but nobody opened it.
State governor Mohammed Umaru Bago called the deaths "sad and tragic" during a press conference on Thursday.
An NSCDC commander has been detained following the deaths, Bago added.
He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections scheduled for January.
Officials had arrested the group of young men on Tuesday for suspected illegal mining near Borgu, in the mineral-rich state of Niger. The region is known for small-scale gold mining.
Two days later, 37 people detained as part of the suspected unlawful operation were found dead inside the detention centre run by the NSCDC, a paramilitary agency responsible for protecting critical infrastructure and tackling crimes including illegal mining. It also assists police with internal security operations.
The NSCDC told the BBC that illegal mining was widespread in Niger state, where artisanal miners often operate in open fields.
Its spokesperson, Babawale Afolabi, said more than 50 people were arrested during an operation earlier this week. They had not been charged because profiling and documentation were still under way before the deaths, he said.
"Illegal mining in Niger is serious," Afolabi said.
The NSCDC had earlier said the detainees were possibly victims of a diphtheria outbreak, a serious bacterial infection that can be fatal.
But the agency's national headquarters later said the cause had not been established and would require medical and laboratory tests.
"The NSCDC wishes to clarify that reports attributing the deaths to any specific disease remain subject to medical and laboratory confirmation," it added in a statement.
Dalhatu told the BBC that security officers had been pursuing suspected illegal miners in the community for several days before making arrests.
He said relatives went to the NSCDC office seeking their release but were repeatedly told to return later. "Unfortunately, the following day we got the news that our children had died," he added.
One father told Nigerian media that his son had appeared healthy when relatives took him food the day before his death and called for an independent post-mortem examination.
Another relative, whose 17-year-old brother was among those who died, said the family had visited him during his detention and questioned how a disease could have killed so many detainees without apparently affecting their guards.
Post-mortem examinations are expected to help establish what happened.
Niger's police chief ordered an immediate investigation into "the unfortunate death of suspected illegal miners while in the detention facility of the NSCDC", spokesman Wasiu Abiodun wrote in a statement.
The victim's bodies have since been taken to the general hospital in nearby Minna for examination.
It is not clear yet whether any of the suspects had been charged.
Nigeria's constitution requires anyone detained on suspicion of a criminal offence to be brought before a court within a "reasonable time" - generally within a day where a court is available within 40km (25 miles), or two days in other cases, unless a longer period is considered reasonable.
The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state has been blamed for fuelling criminal gang violence, according to officials and experts.
Much of the gold in the region is trafficked through global supply chains, a 2024 SwissAid report found.

- Published
Japan's central bank has raised its main interest rate to a fresh 31-year high as it continues to move away from decades of ultra-low borrowing costs and as the country faces increasing economic pressures.
In a widely expected move on Friday, the Bank of Japan (BOJ) increased the rate from 1% to 1.25% - a level not seen since 1995.
It comes as major central banks around the world are hiking rates as higher energy prices caused by the Iran war are helping to push up inflation.
On Wednesday, the US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time in over three years, while the European Central Bank also increased its borrowing costs earlier this month.
The BOJ has been raising the rate since 2024, when it stood at minus 0.1%. It has now hiked rates six times in the last two and a half years.
Since then the bank has been steadily putting up the rate as it tries to reach a level similar to other major economies.
When a central bank raises rates, known as tightening monetary policy, the country's currency usually becomes stronger as it makes the it more attractive to traders.
"One of the world's last sources of ultra-cheap money is disappearing," said market analyst Lale Akoner from investment company eToro.
Japan is facing several economic challenges including a persistently weak yen, rising prices and a shrinking workforce.
Official figures published on Friday ahead of the BOJ announcement showed that inflation eased slightly last month.
Core inflation fell to 1.7% in August from 1.8% the previous month but remains close to the bank's 2% target level.
While Japan's inflation rate is not high by international standards, rising prices are a relatively new development in the economy.
Until recently the country had experienced very low inflation or deflation - falling prices - for around three decades.
Global oil and gas prices have risen this year as the Iran war caused major disruptions to shipments through the key Strait of Hormuz shipping route.
Japan is particularly vulnerable to those supply interruptions as it is heavily reliant on energy from the Middle East.
The country's currency has also been under pressure in recent months.
In August, Tokyo and Washington confirmed that they had jointly intervened to halt a slide in the yen after it fell to a fresh 40-year low.
The coordinated intervention was the first since 2011, when both countries took action together to weaken the yen after the devastating earthquake and tsunami that hit eastern Japan.
Both Japan's Ministry of Finance and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said at the time that they would not hesitate to conduct more joint interventions in the future.
Bessent has also been ramping up pressure on the BOJ to raise interest rates to help support the yen, calling on its Governor Kazuo Ueda to "do the right thing".
"If [the yen] remains weak despite higher rates, the resulting inflation pressure could force the BOJ to tighten faster than markets or Japan's government would like," Akoner said.

c1ecce972ee8.text:
Yinkaâs view
The African diaspora is often discussed as a vast reservoir of capital and goodwill waiting to be tapped for the continentâs development. But that may undersell its value.
The numbers are there: the broader sub-Saharan African diaspora in the US has swelled to roughly 4.8 million people, tripling since 2000, according to Migration Policy Institute data. Nearly 50% of adults hold a bachelorâs degree or higher â outpacing both the broader immigrant population and native-born Americans.
In other words, first and second generation Africans in the US could move from âdiaspora engagementâ to âdiaspora participation,â as trade lawyer and former US government official Ufo Eric-Atuanya explained in a speech on Capitol Hill this week. The diaspora, he said, should be treated as âan economic bridgeâ carrying capital, expertise, and relationships between markets.
It is a useful concept, particularly at a moment when there appears to be growing impatience with the idea that Africans abroad should simply act as a cash machine for projects conceived elsewhere. Instead, diaspora professionals and entrepreneurs should play a more direct role in originating companies, structuring investments, building supply chains, and developing infrastructure.
One compelling example is the continentâs emerging space industry. A recent paper on African space programs points to diaspora engineers as a pool of expertise developed abroad and suggests remote collaboration and incentives for returning professionals to help build capabilities.
But the paper also cautions that such engagement âcannot substitute forâ domestic capacity. That is where the rhetoric around diaspora participation needs to be tested. It is relatively easy to invite communities abroad to conferences, solicit investment, or ask professionals to mentor young Africans. It is considerably harder to give them meaningful roles in building institutions and infrastructure.
The distinction matters because African economies do not simply need more money flowing across their borders. They need more productive capacity: businesses that can scale, infrastructure that can support them, and institutions that can retain the talent building them.
The diaspora can help supply all of those. But the goal should not be to make Africans abroad better sources of money or expertise. It should be to make them active participants in building the capacity that ultimately makes their participation less necessary.

Hollywood actor Michael Sheen said he had a "constructive" meeting with First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth over toxic dumping claims raised in his BBC documentary.
Buried with Michael Sheen explores toxic chemical dumping in 14 sites in Wales and England.
Sheen initially said an offer to meet the first minister "was not taken up" before the documentary was broadcast in August.
On Thursday, the Welsh actor said he met the first minister, speaking about how they could move forward adding it was "early days but that's really encouraging".
Speaking on Instagram, external, he said "I've just come from a meeting with the first minister.
"Talking about how we can move forward and address all the issues that Buried [the documentary] raised around the toxic dumping, and that was really constructive.
"So early days but that's really encouraging."
In the UK Parliament last week, Sheen urged MPs to back a national testing programme for historic toxic dumps to make sure sites were safe, after high levels of cancer-causing chemicals - known as PCBs - were found in soil samples and in the blood of people living near sites linked to chemical giant Monsanto.
Sheen interviewed farming consultant turned campaigner Douglas Gowan shortly before his death, who had spent decades warning that communities were at risk of toxic chemicals.
The actor later teamed up with investigative journalists Lucy Taylor and Dan Ashby who had inherited all of the campaigner's documents and research.
They set about testing 14 sites in Wales and north west England where it was thought Monsanto had been dumping PCBs, and found elevated levels at all but one.
Susan Smith, who worked at Monsanto in Wrexham, said her happy memories of working there have been replaced with fears following the documentary.
Susan and her husband Geraint's home, which they have lived in for 53 years, is separated from the decommissioned Ruabon chemical works by a thin tree line.
Geraint was diagnosed with prostate cancer 13 years ago before more recently developing skin cancer, while Susan developed breast cancer when she was 38.
While they admit they are not certain that Monsanto was responsible, the documentary has made them question the possible impact of the factory on their family's health.
Susan worked as a secretary for four years when she was 19, then returned once for temporary cover and another time to overhaul a failing system.
"Most of my time was spent in the telex office next to the warehouse. We used to send delivery notes, instructions, requests on little pieces of ticker tape through a machine to other Monsanto offices," she said.
"We had a small glass hatch that the instructions would be passed through and it was never closed because people were passing things through so often. As a result dust and powders and all sorts would blow through and coat the desks, the paper, even our sandwiches."
Susan said she wasn't given a "safety briefing, protective clothing or anything" and office staff never knew they were at risk.
Susan had her blood tested by the documentary team and while the PCB levels in her blood were not deemed high, the fact there is no safe level of PCB and the lack of accountability from Eastman â the US company which now owns what was once Monsanto â has left her with unanswered questions.
The couple have joined the Monsanto Contamination Action Group â which was set up for people in Wrexham who live in communities affected by historic industrial waste dumping.
Eastman was approached for comment.
Additional reporting Alec Doyle, LDRS reporter

Police have begun moving hundreds of migrants in Ceuta to a new tented site in the port area of the Spanish territory in north Africa.
Officers struggled to contain crowds of people jostling to secure a place at the site after weeks of living on the beaches. Shots could be heard, with reports that police fired into the air.
Several hundred migrants have now reached the camp, which has a capacity for 1,700 people.
Most of the 72,000 migrants who breached the border from Morocco in July have returned, but it is believed that more than 13,000 remain in the enclave.
The operation began at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Friday, with more than 3,000 migrants being transferred, according to the Spanish government-owned news agency Efe.
During the process, some migrants broke through the cordon along the designated 2km (1.2 mile) route to the port. Video shows young men running in the darkness as police tried to maintain control.
More than 170 police officers have been deployed, including drone technicians, Efe reported. It added that the situation was later "brought under control quickly", and the operation was able to continue.
The operation is part of the government's attempt to concentrate the migrants in facilities where they can be identified and cared for while their administrative status is individually determined.
The chaotic scenes will do little to dampen opposition criticism in Spain of Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez, who has faced strong criticism over his handling of the crisis.
Since the migrant influx, residents of the 18.5 sq km (7.2 sq miles) territory have expressed safety concerns. Some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.
Ceuta's Mayor Juan Jesus Vivas told lawmakers in the European Parliament earlier this month that the migrants had turned Ceuta into a "pressure cooker".
"The city is completely different than it was before this event, Ceutans have lost their joy and their lifestyles have been completely shaken up," the conservative mayor said.
The opposition also accused SÃ¡nchez of knowing about the influx of migrants in advance. SÃ¡nchez has insisted that it was impossible to predict, but according to government documents, its intelligence services had warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before the events happened.
Ester MuÃ±oz of the conservative People's Party said the government was "directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died".
The incident has also created diplomatic headaches for SÃ¡nchez.
The prime minister is at odds with Italy, with the two countries earlier this week extending temporary border controls imposed on each other. He is also trying to maintain his bilateral relationship with Morocco.
The influx of migrants in late July came after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta cannot be summarily returned to Morocco.
After the ruling, some social media accounts spread misinformation and offered to help migrants cross the Spanish border for hundreds of pounds.
Thousands of people then flooded across the border fence and swam around the ocean barriers. At least 100 people died during the crossing, according to local authorities.

The lone holdout juror in the trial of Lindsay Clancy has said he "didn't have any doubts" that she was criminally responsible for killing her three children.
"Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned it," Michael Desronvil said in a statement to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
The judge declared a mistrial on 4 September after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict following nearly 40 hours of deliberating.
Clancy admitted to the killings but her lawyers argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors said the killings were calculated.
Warning: This article contains distressing details
The 36-year-old was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after strangling Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home before jumping out of the second-floor window.
To find Clancy guilty, jurors had to be unanimously convinced beyond reasonable doubt that she intentionally killed her children and that she did not do so as a result of postpartum psychosis, a rare and serious condition.
The jury - nine women and three men - considered a range of options including not guilty by reason of insanity, manslaughter and first-degree murder.
Several jurors have said following the mistrial being declared that the panel was ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.
Desronvil said he believed the evidence presented in court showed she had planned the killings.
"I didn't have any doubts," he said in a statement to CBS on Thursday.
"As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented."
Paula Devlin, one of the other jurors, told CBS Mornings that the panel had spent several days trying to convince Desronvil to change his mind.
"We all worked together to convince ourselves once we got to that point where it was 10 to 2," she said.
The jury foreperson, a retired fifth-grade teacher, described not being able to reach a verdict as "awful" and an "emotional rollercoaster".
She told NBC that Desronvil had "admitted he had reasonable doubt", but as she started filling out the verdict sheets, he apparently said: "But I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity."
Another juror told local CBS station WBZ-TV that most of the jurors had been "very firm in their stance" from the start and "the stand-alone juror was not the only one that was unwilling to see things from the other side".
But they added that because Desronvil would not "follow" his reasonable doubt nor offer logical reasoning for his position, they felt Clancy had not received a fair trial.
The identities of all 11 jurors have not been officially disclosed but in the US, once a case is over, any juror can choose to speak publicly about a case and their deliberations.
Patrick Clancy, the children's father and Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband, is due to speak publicly about the case in an interview with the CBS programme 60 Minutes on Sunday.
In it, he is expected to discuss his grief, his memories of his children and the conspiracy theories that have flooded social media since the trial began.
He said he still speaks to his children "all the time", describing it as "a way I stay connected to them".
During the trial, Clancy's defence team had attempted to use her being put on more than a dozen medications in the lead-up to the killings, as well as seeking help from a suicide hotline and an emergency room, as evidence of her psychosis.
Postpartum psychosis can involve hallucinations and delusions, and her lawyers argued that she was unable to understand the nature of her actions or distinguish right from wrong.
A forensic psychiatrist who testified for the defence said Clancy experienced a "command hallucination" and a "delusion of influence" when she killed her children.
However, her psychiatrist testified for the prosecution that Clancy did not show signs of psychosis during their sessions, while another psychiatrist noted that the condition was not currently recognised by the American Psychiatric Association.
Under Massachusetts law, prosecutors had to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible for the jury to find her guilty. The defence did not have to prove her mental illness or lack of criminal responsibility.
The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial.
Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, has said he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors to avoid a second trial.
He told ABC's Good Morning America that he was upset that the lone juror would not acquit Clancy.
He said the holdout "would not apply the law of reasonable doubt" as instructed by the judge, adding: "That's not right. And that's why I was upset."
The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts.

d382c0aab809.text:
America’s centuries-old conflict with wolves took another turn earlier this month when President Donald Trump ordered the animals be stripped of federal protections across several U.S. states, claiming the action will provide economic relief for ranchers.
Alongside a suite of regulatory reviews to “promote financial viability” for ranchers, Trump ordered the Interior secretary to begin the process of removing gray and Mexican wolves from the endangered species list, and directed the Agriculture secretary to encourage states to make it easier for ranchers to shoot wolves.
But an Inside Climate News review of state and federal data indicates that wolves account for a tiny percentage of total cattle deaths. And while some individual ranchers in areas with intense wolf-livestock conflicts may face significant losses, other factors, like climate-fueled droughts, high fuel prices, persistent inflation and the Trump administration’s decision to pause levies on hundreds of thousands of pounds of beef imports are likely applying far more economic pressure to the industry than wolves.
A wolf pack’s presence near a ranch can impact a rancher’s bottom line, even if the animals don’t kill any cattle. But the Trump administration’s focus on delisting the predators and reducing their numbers with lethal management is misdirected, experts say.
“Wolves are going to be around, listed or not listed, because they are tough. So I was surprised the White House focused so heavily on wolves’ legal status when there is so much else federal agencies could do to reduce conflict,” said Arthur Middleton, a professor of wildlife management at the University of California, Berkeley. “The Agriculture and Interior departments could tweak and expand their technical and financial assistance for affected ranchers almost overnight. Focusing just on [wolves’] legal status is a big missed opportunity, and in my view, it doesn’t actually help ranchers that much.”
Gray wolves are federally protected in all lower 48 states except Idaho, Montana and Wyoming, where they have been removed from the endangered species list and are under state management. Gray wolves also live in California, Michigan, Minnesota, Oregon, Washington and Wisconsin.
In 2023, Colorado reintroduced gray wolves within its borders, a population managed by the state.
Mexican wolves have federal protection across their habitat in Arizona and New Mexico.
Inside Climate News reviewed data on cattle confirmed lost to predation by gray wolves published by states across the West. In 2025, those numbers varied from just nine animals in Washington to 155 killed or injured in California, a number that rose to 197 when including probable wolf attacks in that state. The true numbers are likely somewhat higher, as some wolf kills are never discovered and some carcasses are so decomposed that it’s impossible to determine how the animals died.
Still, wolf predation represents a tiny percentage of all cattle losses in states that are home to the predators. In Oregon, confirmed losses to wolves accounted for just 0.2 percent of total statewide cattle losses and deaths recorded by the U.S. Department of Agriculture in 2025—the highest proportion across the six Western states for which Inside Climate News found published 2025 data on gray wolf predation on cattle.
Most cattle are raised in circumstances in which they will never encounter a wolf, so those statewide figures mask problems faced by the worst-affected ranchers. Where free-ranging cattle overlap with wolf packs, the percentage of losses attributable to wolves will be much higher. But even in the counties with the most severe wolf-livestock conflicts, total losses to wolves are still relatively small.
Across the six California counties with confirmed losses to wolves in 2025, the total cattle population stood at 176,600 at the start of 2024—the most recent data available. Sierra County, with 38 cattle confirmed lost to wolves in 2025, had 6,600 head of cattle the previous year, giving it the highest proportional predation losses. That’s still well under 1 percent.

In Northern California, wolves seem to have acquired a taste for beef. In a recent peer-reviewed study from the University of California, Davis, researchers found cattle DNA in 72 percent of collected scat samples from northern California wolves in 2022 and 2023. Beef is “the predominant dietary item of wolves in Northeastern California during the summer months,” the authors wrote, though they noted that their work showed what wolves are eating, but not necessarily what they are killing—wolves could also be scavenging the carcasses of cattle that died from other causes.
Ranchers largely support wolf delisting but are having a hard time seeing how it connects to the broader economic pressures their industry faces.
“I don’t know if there’s any harm lumping them [together], but it doesn’t make sense,” said Jim Magagna, executive vice president of the Wyoming Stock Growers Association. “The rhetoric that the president’s put out in the last couple of weeks with importing foreign beef and the way he’s done it has been harmful to anybody who’s marketing cattle this time of the year.”
Last month, Trump announced his administration was temporarily pausing tariffs on 300,000 pounds of lean beef imports, claiming this would help lower beef prices for U.S. consumers. The National Cattlemen’s Beef Association, an industry trade group, released a statement opposing the decision, noting that beef markets had “already turned sharply lower” in response to Trump’s message.
“The cattle market is sort of like the stock market,” Magagna said. “It reacts as much to rhetoric as it does to reality sometimes.”

French President Emmanuel Macron has warned that the threat of hybrid attacks by Russia against Europe and France has intensified.
In a news conference at the Elysee Palace, Macron said he had called on the French government to prepare a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites in the face of this threat.
He said France had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks which would not be left "without a response".
A growing number of European leaders have warned that Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.
The French president was speaking to journalists after meeting party leaders to discuss the security impact of the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.
Macron mentioned last month's drone attack on Leipzig airport in Germany, blamed on Russia, and remarks by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggesting Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank.
"In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified," he said.
"The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine."
Macron added that the government had been tasked with protecting critical infrastructure and the "most sensitive" defence industry and technology sites against drone and cyberattacks.
He also announced that France would call a meeting of the G7 to discuss energy and raise the question of gas stocks with the European Commission.
"In the coming weeks, we will have a G7 meeting devoted to these energy issues, both to strengthen cooperation and to avoid unnecessary tensions between the G7 countries and our main partners," Macron said.
"It will also be an opportunity to consider options for a possible release or unlocking of strategic reserves."

A honeycomb-shaped pattern in marine sediments has befuddled scientists for more than 150 years, but a new study points to a potential culprit.
The formations, known as Paleodictyon, are probably burrows created by arthropods, possibly a crustacean subgroup that includes the roly-poly, researchers report August 12 in Earth-Science Reviews. The work challenges previous hypotheses about Paleodictyon, particularly that they were created by wormlike creatures.
“Our study addresses one of paleontology’s most enduring enigmas,” says Andrea Baucon, a paleontologist at the University of Cagliari in Sardinia, Italy.
Renaissance artist and inventor Leonardo da Vinci probably sketched Paleodictyon’s characteristic forms after seeing them in ancient marine sediments now on dry land. The patterns appear on seafloors today, too. In the 19th and 20th centuries, scientists attributed the patterns not only to worms, but also to chemical processes and fossilized algae, among other things.
Baucon surmised that arthropods would be a more likely cause. So he and his colleagues tested the hypothesis by investigating prior research and making observations on fossils both previously and newly discovered. Among these was a 530-million-year-old Paleodictyon — one of the oldest specimens known — that they discovered in a quarry near Torre de Moncorvo, Portugal.
They conclude that digging Paleodictyon’s sharp corners would be impossible for soft-bodied, wormlike creatures, which can only burrow where the ground is weak. In contrast, arthropods’ rigid exoskeletons and jointed appendages are well-suited to the task.
Creating such a precise hexagonal network takes mobility and cognitive skills including efficient burrowing and spatial awareness, which align with known arthropod abilities, the team concludes. Furthermore, Baucon says, Paleodictyon appears in the fossil record at roughly the same time as the earliest fossil evidence of arthropods, in the early Cambrian Period, around 530 million years ago. This coincidence in timing is not proof, Baucon says, but it is consistent with the team’s hypothesis.
Stephen Hasiotis, a geologist at the University of Kansas in Lawrence who was not involved in the study, isn’t sure arthropods are the sole creators. “Without smoking gun evidence” from across geologic time and the various marine environments where the mysterious honeycombs have been found, Hasiotis says, there is still the chance that other living things, including segmented worms, created formations past and present. Nevertheless, he says, the team’s hypothesis will doubtlessly push Paleodictyon aficionados “back onto the trail of whodunit and why.”
Baucon and his colleagues suggest that researchers could create Paleodictyon observatories to catch itsmakers in action on ocean floors. “Technologies such as artificial intelligence could help us automate the search for the creator of this mysterious structure,” he says.
