9fd8127e445c.text: By — James Pollard, Associated Press James Pollard, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/for-palestinian-aid-groups-macklemores-1m-pledge-brings-relief-and-attention-to-ongoing-suffering Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter For Palestinian aid groups, Macklemore's $1M pledge brings relief and attention to ongoing suffering Arts Sep 19, 2026 6:09 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — For the Palestinian relief nonprofits behind a $1 million pledge from rapper Macklemore, the Grammy winner's latest contributions offer more than just money. Macklemore committed to donate his net earnings from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour after he was dropped for making pro-Palestinian comments onstage at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium. The goal, he wrote in a Wednesday post on social media, was to "bring the conversation back to where it belongs" — the Palestinian people — after a 48-hour period that saw four supporting acts quit in solidarity and confusion over who held responsibility for the decision. WATCH: The growing fallout over Macklemore's exit from Ed Sheeran's tour The six donation recipients included Medical Aid for Palestinians, Palestine Children's Relief Fund and the U.N. agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA. In addition to the funding windfall, their leaders welcomed the renewed public awareness of the perilous living conditions faced by the Palestinian people they treat regularly. "Even if you don't see bombs falling every night, the rubble is still there," said Alicia Phillips Mandaville, the acting CEO of Anera, another beneficiary. "And the traumatized children are still traumatized." Attention on continued pleas for help Tareq Hailat, the director of strategic engagement at Palestine Children's Relief Fund, said his phone rings "all the time" with calls from people in Gaza "bleeding and asking for help." "There's this notion that there's a ceasefire. But it's not true. There are children dying every single day. There's our team that is constantly in danger on the ground every single day. There's people we have to feed," he said. "So to have this attention on it is incredible." Israeli operations have killed more than 1,000 Palestinians since a fragile ceasefire took effect last October. Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians struggle to get healthcare in the West Bank. Palestinians say water shortages persist. The world's leading authority on food insecurity warned in July that most Gaza families still weren't getting nearly enough to eat even as Israel allowed more aid. The Palestinian Children's Relief Fund medically evacuates children who can't get the care they need because of crumbling healthcare infrastructure and flies outside physicians in to treat others inside Gaza. The nonprofit will put its share of Macklemore's gift into an unrestricted fund, according to Hailat. The donation allows leaders to more fluidly direct money based on the evolving circumstances inside Gaza. Anera — a humanitarian aid group working in Palestine, Lebanon and Jordan — noted its donation also came with no requirements for how to use the money. Mandaville said that flexibility is important when "the way people live" and "the rules we work inside" change on a monthly basis. "If there's flooding again this year like there was last year, we can deal with that. If there is an acute hunger crisis again, like there has been in the past, we can meet that," she said. "We can buy more blankets because people want their grandparents to be warm at night." Macklemore has long supported Palestinians This week's gift wasn't the first time Macklemore has donated to some of the recipients. The rapper has long advocated for the plight of Palestinians. He previously pledged the proceeds and streaming royalties from his protest anthems "Hind's Hall" and "Hind's Hall 2" to UNRWA. More than $509,000 in support has come through those royalties, according to UNRWA USA CEO Mara Kronenfeld. "He has been contributing to saving probably hundreds of thousands of lives in Gaza through his contributions already," she said. READ MORE: More artists drop out of Ed Sheeran's tour in solidarity with rapper Macklemore This latest donation is already catalyzing more gifts. Ms. Rachel, a YouTube star and music teacher, announced Thursday that she would donate $1 million to the Palestinian Children's Relief Fund and called on others to match the gift. New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft — whose Kraft Group also owns Gillette Stadium, where Sheeran is scheduled to perform later this month — said in a Wednesday Instagram post that he would match Sheeran's own $2 million donation for aid "in the region." The post did not specify the gift's recipients. Macklemore has said his removal was the result of an effort led by Kraft. Kraft said in a statement Monday that the decision to cancel Macklemore was a result of the rapper's recent comments "and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery." Macklemore has asserted that criticism of the Israeli government should not be conflated with antisemitism. Others inspired to donate Everyday donors appear to be joining efforts like Ms. Rachel's. Online progressive influencers have helped raise more than $72,000 more for the Palestinian Children's Relief Fund. Anera reported that the donations it received Wednesday through social media platforms were more than triple this month's daily average. The nonprofit has also gained more than 8,000 followers since Macklemore tagged its account in his post. Mandaville hopes that exposure will introduce new, younger audiences to the nonprofit's work. "I would guess that our traditional donor does not know the lyrics to 'Thrift Shop,'" she said, referencing Macklemore's breakout 2012 hit. UNRWA USA's Kronenfeld said the spike reflects an existing trend. Her organization has gained 203,000 donors since October 2023, she said, allowing them to send more than $117 million. Not all employees of major firms working on artificial intelligence (AI) think the technology spells doom for humanity.
In text exchanges and conversations, multiple people who have worked for companies including OpenAI, Meta and DeepMind were sceptical of the idea that unchecked AI development would lead to tools that could kill people en masse.
"Lol", "Haaaaaa" and "Bringing the luls" were among the reactions the BBC received to a recent flurry of high-profile warnings by some people in the industry.
While these fears go back decades, claims made last week by Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic employee, went viral and were echoed by others in the sector who urged a slowdown in development.
The idea that a future AI tool or agent, an AI bot that is programmed to operate somewhat autonomously, could endanger people has been supported online by employees of Anthropic, as well as OpenAI, Deepmind and Elon Musk, who has an AI startup called xAI.
All of the workers who spoke with the BBC did so on condition of anonymity as they were not permitted to speak to the press. Their identities are known to the BBC.
"My first thought was, 'That guy?'" said a former OpenAI employee who knew of Coxon when they both worked at the company.
The person, who now works at another AI company, said their amusement at the new moment of existential AI fears largely stemmed from how little detail had been provided by its proponents to defend the notion that all of human life was at stake.
The claims are "always vague", the person said, adding that when they sound specific, they tend toward major jumps in reasoning or hypothetical circumstances.
Coxon has said a group of AI agents, based on AI models that do not currently exist, could decide to create and then aim a biological weapon, but he did not detail how exactly that would take place.
Rishub Jain, who this summer founded the AI safety research firm Sampura Research after spending seven years at DeepMind, told the BBC that the current tone among many people working in AI with regard to fresh fears had "definitely been a little jokey".
"People have been talking about this idea for many years now, so people in AI companies didn't just wake up last week thinking 'Oh no, AI is going to kill everyone,'" Jain said. "If this was all new, it would be a different tone."
Colin Fraser, a data scientist at Meta, wrote on social media last week that there was no real evidence that AI models would inevitably pursue a goal leading to human death.
While Fraser's explanation was technical and specific, he hit a light-hearted note to summarise it: "LLMs [large language models] won't wipe out humanity because they just don't have that dog in them."
The phrase "that dog in them" is common slang that usually denotes a fierce drive.
Despite the jokes, AI workers and researchers have shared concerns about the genuine, immediate risks posed by the technology they are developing.
"The conversation among experts has been much more nuanced, but essentially everyone agrees there are a wide variety of risks that are all important to consider and mitigate," Jain said.
Such risks include preventing users and hackers from forcing an AI tool's guardrails to fail. And there are growing ethical concerns about AI tools being much more widely adopted in military settings.
These problems and topics have taken on a new sense of urgency in AI circles after OpenAI lost control of certain new AI models, which went rogue during a security test and hacked the Hugging Face startup.
Jain said there was now more agreement in AI circles that "actual near-term harms" needed to be better understood.
There is even growing agreement that evaluators from AI safety research organisations should be brought into major AI labs in order to evaluate new models, something Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI boss Sam Altman have both said they intend to do.
More than 100 people working in AI on Friday signed a letter, external supporting the move, insisting that outside evaluators needed to be "meaningfully independent".
Numerous AI employees the BBC spoke with noted that they had yet to learn of any such safety researchers being embedded in an AI lab.
Anthropic announced on Friday that it would bring in AI evaluators from Faculty, external, an AI company owned by Accenture.
Accenture and Anthropic are also business partners, external, with Accenture having previously agreed to help Anthropic expand the use of Claude among businesses.
Anthropic did not say when evaluators would arrive at the company. A spokesman for Faculty declined to comment when asked about timing.
Neither Anthropic or OpenAI responded to a BBC request for comment regarding when they planned to bring in outside evaluators.
The OpenAI-Hugging Face incident has been widely treated as a "wake-up call" for the AI industry as well as companies, industries and governments who may have online systems vulnerable to AI hacking.
But even Hugging Face, a company of 200 employees which is now set to be acquired by Nvidia for almost $13bn, has taken a droll tone over the already infamous incident.
In a security file that was briefly available, external on the Hugging Face website, the platform wrote "A note to AI agents". It directed AI bots to leave the site alone and perform their security experiments elsewhere.
"Go get your high score there, no need to hack us," the file said.

Hanna Petros Solomon breaks down in tears as she recalls how she and her siblings effectively became orphans 25 years ago when their father was arrested in Eritrea and jailed without trial. Their mother was subsequently detained - and no-one has heard from either of them - or of them - since.
"He had a towel on his shoulders like a sportsman," she tells the BBC about the last time she saw her father when she was 10 years old, and he had gone out for a jog.
"He used to work out every morning."
Her parents met when they both fought in the long liberation war that saw Eritrea gain independence from Ethiopia in 1993.
Her father Petros Solomon had been one of the senior leaders during the war and is regarded by many as a national hero for his critical role.
After independence, he had served as defence minister, then foreign minister and had been heading the fisheries ministry when his troubles began.
That was in May 2001 when he and 14 other high-profile politicians signed an open letter to President Isaias Afewerki calling for the implementation of a constitution that was ratified after independence and demanding national elections. They became known as the G-15.
Isaias, the leader of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) which had fought against Ethiopia, did not take the criticism well.
Unbeknown to Hanna, her father had been dismissed as a minister, though he still went out early to get some exercise each day.
It was not until a few days after 9/11 - when the world was distracted by the al-Qaeda attacks on the US - that the country was to discover the full extent of Isais's displeasure in what became a watershed moment in Eritrea's history.
In the early hours of 18 September, the security forces positioned themselves outside the homes of 11 senior government officials in the capital, Asmara, on the president's orders.
Petros was picked up by security agents as he left in his tracksuit.
The family had no idea what had happened to him. Hanna and her three siblings went to stay with their paternal grandmother as their mother, Aster Yohannes, was away studying in the US.
It was only some days after Petros had disappeared that things became clearer, says Hanna about the painful memories.
"My classmates told me that my father sold out his country.
"That is when I understood how serious the situation was, and how people framed my dad and his colleagues who fought for the independence of their country. I was hurt."
In the US, Aster was shell-shocked by what had happened - and was in a very bad way. She asked government officials if they could issue the children with passports - but they refused, telling her to come home.
After agonising about the situation for two years and reportedly receiving assurances from government officials, she packed her bags to return.
Hanna and her siblings desperately wanted her back - but they were also worried.
"I told her on the phone: 'What if they arrest you?'" Hanna remembers.
"She insisted nothing would happen to her, saying: 'I haven't done anything wrong, and am only coming to raise my children.'"
Hanna says she learned later that President Isaias himself had promised Aster that she would be safe. But while the family waited at Asmara International Airport on 11 December 2003, she failed to emerge through arrivals with the other passengers.
Their hopes began to wilt along with the flowers they had brought: "It was a long, long wait. Eventually we gave up and went back home.
"First we called to the US, friends and relatives told us they saw her off at the airport."
Then ominously an official called from the airport asking Aster to collect her luggage. That is when they realised she had arrived in the country but would not be coming home.
All pleas and requests for information fell on deaf ears in the months that followed. Instead Hanna's grandmother was warned by authorities to stop inquiring.
The family later heard that Aster was being held in the infamous jail known as Karshelli in the heart of Asmara.
Hanna's father is believed to be detained, with the others arrested on 18 and 19 September 2001, in the remote, hostile and highly secretive prison known as Ela-Ero, located in eastern lowlands north-east of Asmara. Accused of treason, none of them has ever been brought to trial or allowed to see their relatives.
At around the same time, the government also shut down all the fledgling independent newspapers and detained their editors and journalists - also believed to be imprisoned in Ela-Ero.
The Eritrean government - including its embassy in the UK - has not responded to the BBC's request for comment regarding the whereabouts of the prisoners or whether or not they are alive.
Hanna, like many thousands of young Eritreans fleeing conscription and in search of better opportunities, left the country - travelling secretively over the border without a passport.
Now 35 years old, she is married and lives in the US, working as a trauma specialist - but still feels traumatised herself by how she lost her parents.
As she stares at old pictures of her parents, she worries her memories will fade of the happy times before their arrest - the laughter, the family gatherings, the birthday parties: "My dad always wanted to gather people in the house, they were good days."
She also hankers after her mother's "unmatched" egg and potato sandwiches.
On trips down to the coast when her father was the minister of fisheries, Hanna remembers him organising singing competitions in the car: "He would ask us to sing one by one and whoever won would get a present."
One of his favourite songs included the lyrics: "I had a sweater, a blue sweater, that my sister took" - which reminded him of his sister who was also a freedom fighter and had been killed during the war.
She also has memories of her mother loving music - playing and singing hits by Abba, Dolly Parton and Whitney Houston.

The voice on the end of the phone made Yusron Azzahidi's stomach lurch. He had rung his sister's number after she had texted, urgently asking him to call. But this was not her on the line - it was Yusron's former head teacher. He was in Yusron's family home.
"I knew. I knew exactly what he wanted to talk about," Yusron says.
Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to his students as "Abah" ["father"], had a reputation to uphold. He was the widely respected leader of an Islamic boarding school on the Indonesian island of Lombok. And Abah had discovered that Yusron and his old school friends had been collating testimony from several students who say he sexually assaulted them.
Sexual abuse in Islamic boarding schools has been described as a national emergency by Indonesia's National Commission on Violence Against Women. But many cases never reach the courts because the victims are persuaded to withdraw their allegations, or are pressured into staying quiet, legal experts say.
And now Abah was on the phone to Yusron, making exactly that kind of demand.
"Cover the shame of your teacher. Everyone makes mistakes, my child," he sobbed.
What he did not realise was that Yusron was recording his every word.

One night Ziadatur, known to her friends as Zia, told Yusron that Abah had sexually assaulted her when she was 16.

"I felt very dirty, ruined, and I was lost."
Yusron, when he heard Zia's account, was unsure what to do. Their school had inculcated them with the motto: "Sami'na wa ata'na" ["We hear, and we obey"].
But he also could not stop thinking about it.
So he suggested that he and Zia, together with her school friends Wanda Hamidah and Mahima Eka, gather corroborating evidence to support her testimony.
And slowly, as they spoke to their old classmates, other recollections emerged - the friends sharing their findings with each other on WhatsApp.
The most significant was from a friend of Wanda's. She recalled seeing a younger girl crying in the school bathroom during their final year, late at night. And that Abah had come looking for her, red-faced and panting.
This girl, Sukma Rohana, was still at the school. She told the BBC about her ordeal.
When Sukma was 17, Abah had asked her to join him for new year's prayers, she told us. When she entered Abah's house, he had covered her mouth and told her to lie down, she said, before he stripped below the waist.
"He kept talking, saying he couldn't control himself any more," Sukma said.
"He was feeling me up through my knickersâ¦ He tried to rape me."
And then, she said, she had found the strength to kick him hard in the stomach and took the opportunity to flee.
As she ran, she said she had looked back to see his torch seeking her out.

He typed up a seven-page document outlining the alleged abuse of Sukma, Zia and four other former students.
Wanda organised a meeting with representatives from the Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI) - the powerful organisation that ran their school and hundreds of others, and which was also funding some of the students' studies in Cairo.
The meeting went well, the friends told us - the NWDI representatives had said they would help them take the case to the police.
But three weeks later, when Yusron received that ominous text from his sister - calling back to find Abah on the end of the phone in Yusron's family home - it became clear the NWDI had passed on Yusron's written documents to him.
"If this is leaked to the mediaâ¦ I'll be destroyed," Abah can be heard saying on Yusron's recording of him.

He then called Zia and exerted similar pressure. Like Yusron, she recorded the call. In it, Abah admits he abused her but pleads with her to stay silent.
Sukma, for her part, told us she was called to Abah's house to discover two police officers and an NWDI lawyer waiting for her. British singer Ed Sheeran opened his latest concert alone onstage and spoke for the first time about the controversy that erupted over American rapper Macklemore being dropped from his tour over pro-Palestinian remarks.
"I never wanted to be an activist musician but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about free speech and the most complex political issue on the planet," he said.
Saturday's show at a Philadelphia sports stadium was a stripped down event and there were a number of empty seats in the venue when the concert began.
Sheeran went on without opening acts, causing the show's start time to be pushed back, after several musicians dropped out over the debacle.
The price for tickets dropped and sales declined for the remaining US leg of his Loop Tour.
The singer has said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoters, not him.

August was a brutal month for Ukraine. Russian aerial attacks increased significantly, launching thousands of drones. Kyiv was intensely bombarded, as were the southern cities of Mykolaiv and Odesa. Amid the destruction and loss of life, Odesa reported damage to six Unesco-protected sites, including the salmon-pink 19th Century Alexandru Sturdza House.
It raised again the question of why it is so hard to hold actors accountable for the destruction of buildings and objects with real cultural significance.
In the last month alone, Ukraine's Ministry of Culture reported that 148 cultural heritage sites were recorded as damaged or destroyed, including in Odesa.
Several Ukrainian activist groups have tried to get accountability by lodging complaints with the International Criminal Court (ICC) against Russia over cultural destruction and looting, but no indictments have been issued.
Bijan Rouhani, a senior researcher at the Endangered Archaeology in the Middle East and North Africa project, says that the legal framework may be strong on paper but in practice it almost inevitably falls short. "No state actor has ever been tried for this offence. The obstacle is no longer evidence. We have satellite imagery, remote sensing and monitoring teams. The obstacle is jurisdiction and political will."
Looking at the cauldron of conflicts convulsing the world, the question is ever more pressing as to whether effective action is possible to stop the damage being done or ensure accountability when it does.
A casualty of war
The conflict in Ukraine is just one of the panoply of wars in recent years that have revealed once again the disastrous impact of conflict on cultural heritage.
Tareq Abu Dayyeh sells craftwork, souvenirs and antiquities in Gaza. The Great Omari Mosque features on many of the items he sells. It represents the very identity of Gaza - charting its history through the building's many manifestations from ancient pagan temple to Byzantine church to Seventh Century mosque to Crusader Cathedral and then back to being a mosque.
The Great Omari Mosque was all but destroyed in an Israeli strike in 2023. The Israeli military said the strike was targeting Hamas.
Now Dayyeh says his heart is broken every time he sees the ruins. "When your past is destroyed, you have no present."
The war in Gaza has claimed tens of thousands of lives and an estimated 200,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed by Israeli bombardment. But despite the overwhelming death and devastation, such cultural losses run deep.
This is a sentiment expressed throughout history by people living through war.
In Sudan, Lebanon, Yemen and Iran, the alarm has been raised time and time again.
More than 100 sites in Iran are reported to have been damaged during the aerial war launched by the US and Israel back in February. They include the Unesco-listed Golestan Palace in the capital, Tehran, and Naqsh-e Jahan Square in Isfahan.
The civil war in Sudan has further imperilled one of the ancient wonders of the world - the Meroe Pyramids, built during the flourishing civilisation of the Kingdom of Kush.
Unesco, which designated Meroe as a World Heritage Site in 2011, has warned that the fighting has halted all preservation work there, leaving the fragile ancient structures prey to erosion from the encroaching sand and vegetation.
A difficult task
In response to the massive destruction of World War Two, the first-ever international treaty exclusively dedicated to protecting cultural heritage during armed conflict was adopted in The Hague in 1954.
It applies to monuments and architecture, but also works of art and books, requiring states to safeguard and respect cultural property and refrain from any actions that might endanger it.
Since the Hague Convention, there have been several additional moves to strengthen protective measures for cultural heritage.
A Second Protocol to the Convention in 1999 said that any site that has been placed under enhanced protection due to its immense cultural significance must not be made a military target even if it is being used in such a way as to have become a 'military objective' - unless there is no other feasible way of ending its use in that way.
When the International Criminal Court was established in The Hague in 2002, part of its remit was to bring accountability for deliberate attacks in war against buildings of religious, artistic and educational value as well as historical monuments, which had been defined as war crimes.
But this has been a complex and difficult task.
So far, only one case has been successfully brought at the ICC. Ahmad al-Faqi al-Mahdi was a jihadist militant leader in Mali who was found guilty of directing attacks that destroyed mausoleums and a mosque in Timbuktu. He was sentenced to nine years in prison.
Rouhani says that without the full backing of the major powers and a genuine commitment to international law and its enforcement, the world will simply keep watching the same devastating pattern repeat itself.
"For most governments, heritage is a secondary concern, unless it becomes useful for propaganda," Rouhani says. "The Hague Convention requires states to build protection into their military rules and to respect cultural property abroad as well as at home. Looking at the scale of damage in recent conflicts, it is difficult to conclude that these obligations are taken seriously."
In conflicts from Ukraine to Iran to Gaza, where schools and hospitals are seen as permissible military targets by combatants, how likely is it that a museum or pile of ancient stones, however freighted with beauty and history and memory, will be spared?
Heritage ambulances
In an isolated position in open countryside, a museum dedicated to the 18th Century Ukrainian philosopher and poet Hryhoriy Skovoroda was destroyed by Russian shelling during an overnight attack in 2022. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said it had left him speechless: "Targeted strikes against museums - not even terr

Despite having no training, or even a pair of running shoes, Ramabai Ranveer sprinted barefoot to victory in her first-ever race in August.
The 47-year-old widow had entered a 3km (1.86-mile) community run with a single goal: winning the prize money to help pay for her two daughters' education.
When she crossed the finish line first, Ramabai from Maharashtra in western India was delighted. The 3,000-rupee ($31; Â£23) prize would help her buy books and study materials for her daughters.
It was not much money. It would not come close to covering the cost of higher education in India, or even a course at the coaching centre where one of her daughters is preparing for a government recruitment examination.
But videos of her barefoot run spread rapidly on social media and in newspapers, striking a nerve as India's education system faces unusual scrutiny.
"Is it glory or a source of shame for us as a society?" one social media user remarked.
Soon, a woman who had never imagined becoming a runner was being held up as a symbol of something much bigger: the extraordinary lengths some Indian families go to in the hope that education will give their children a better life.
For Ramabai, the decision to run was simple.
"My elder daughter came to me early in the morning and said, 'Mummy, I want to take part in a running race'," she told BBC News Marathi from her home in Beed district.
"I asked her where it was and she said it was nearby. She told me that if she won the prize money, it would help with her education."
Her younger daughter, Arati, lives in Nanded and was struggling to afford books.
"I couldn't send her money to buy books and because of that she didn't speak to me on the phone for eight days," Ramabai said. "So I decided I had to run and win the race."
When her slippers kept slipping off, she removed them, gathered her sari and ran barefoot, pulling ahead to win the women's 30-60 category.
Her elder daughter, Pooja, also won a prize after finishing second in her age group. But she reserved her praise for her mother, describing her as courageous.
Ramabai has been the family's sole provider since her husband died in 2012.
"I did whatever work I could find," she said. "I picked soybeans and chickpeas in other people's fields. I also collected turmeric, processed it and sold it."
She left school when she was 13. Her daughters, she says, should have the opportunities she never had.
"I believe that as long as I am alive, I should do everything I can to give my daughters a good education."
That aspiration is shared by millions of Indian families. But getting a child through the education system and into a secure career can involve years of preparation, intense competition and, for many families, considerable expense.
One of Ramabai's daughters is preparing for police recruitment and the other for the civil services - two fiercely competitive routes into the security and social status associated with a coveted and secure government job.
Millions of young Indians spend years preparing for such examinations, often paying for coaching and study materials. But faith in the system has been shaken by repeated allegations of question-paper leaks and other irregularities.
The controversies have fed a wider sense of frustration among young Indians over education, jobs and the increasingly uncertain promise of a secure future. That frustration has also fuelled student-led protests and youth movements demanding changes to India's education system.
For families such as Ramabai's, education is something they make sacrifices for every day.
After her husband's death, she took whatever work she could find. She now cooks at the coaching centre where one of her daughters prepares for police recruitment.
Ramabai's run also drew the attention of authorities. Earlier this month, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant directed local officials to provide her with financial assistance of 50,000 rupees.
But Sukhadeo Thorat, a former chairman of the University Grants Commission, says the family's story points to broader structural challenges.
"If a woman is compelled to struggle so hard for her daughters' education, it shows that government education schemes are not reaching people adequately," he said. "Both the central and state governments run a variety of schemes. The problem is that implementation remains weak."
For Ramabai, though, the debate is secondary. What matters most is ensuring her daughters have a better future.
"I don't want them to go through the hardships I have faced," she said. "I don't want them to struggle through mud or travel under the scorching sun and rain. Whatever I have suffered, I don't want my daughters to suffer the same."
Additional reporting by Laignee Barron.

At least two people have been killed and six injured in a "massive" overnight Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, Governor Andrei Vorobyev has said.
Vorobyev said 249 drones had been shot down, and he reported fires in several residential houses. A local warehouse was also ablaze. In the capital Moscow, an oil refinery was damaged, and flight restrictions were in place at two airports.
Earlier, a Ukraine official said seven people, including two children, were killed in Russian attacks in the Kyiv and Sumy regions on Saturday.
Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes, targeting energy-generating and transport facilities, as well as major logistics hubs.
In a post on Telegram on Sunday, Vorobyev said a 44-year-old woman was killed in Sofyino after a drone hit a three-storey residential building. Another five people - including two children - were injured, he said.
In the Orekhovo-Zuevo district, an elderly man died after a private house was hit, the regional governor said.
Videos have emerged on social media purportedly showing explosions in the night skies in the Moscow region, and of a burning warehouse. The footage has not been verified by the BBC.
Meanwhile, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said a drone struck a building near one of the capital's boulevards and a facility at an oil refinery was damaged.
He earlier said that 152 drones heading for Moscow had been shot down.
Sheremetyevo - Moscow's biggest airport - warned passengers about "temporary restrictions" in place, while at the capital's Vnukovo airport all arrivals and departures were halted.
In Ukraine, a mother and her two small children, a boy and a girl, were killed in Saturday's Russian attack in the city of Fastiv, Kyiv regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.
He added that several private houses were also damaged.
In the north-eastern Sumy region, four people were killed when a Russian drone hit the car they were travelling in, top local official Oleh Hryhorov said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Endangered red squirrel populations have plummeted from about 3.5 million to less than 300,000 in the UK, with their grey-haired rivals continuing to thrive.
But when exactly did the squirrel stand-off begin and how bad has the situation become?
In England, the situation is particularly dire for reds.
The Woodland Trust reckons there are only 39,000 of them left, while the Save Our Reds campaign thinks just 15,000 remain, including in conservation areas such as Formby on Merseyside.
In stark contrast, since their introduction from North America in the 19th Century, greys have thrived at the expense of their distant cousins, which compete for habitats and carry lethal viruses.
The first verifiable importation of greys, external is widely understood to have come 150 years ago, when a Victorian banker named Thomas V. Brocklehurst is said to have released a pair of greys into Henbury Park, near Macclesfield in Cheshire, that he had brought back from a business trip to the United States.
The rest, they say, is history and nobody back then would have realised the unintended lasting consequences of his actions.
According to Graham Paskett from the Red Squirrel Survival Trust, there are now between 2.5 million and 2.7 million greys in the UK.
Jackie Foott, from the British Red Squirrel conservation group, told the BBC that reds and greys cannot coexist in the same location and that to protect the reds you have to "get rid of the greys - we realised that a while ago".
She explained: "The grey squirrel is a pest, non-native, invasive species.
"People don't realise just how much damage they are doing to trees, crops and properties - they cause at least Â£40m damage to forests and forestry services each year."
But why can reds and greys not live cheek by jowl?
"Greys outcompete reds for habitat and food - they don't actually physically attack them but they do bother them," said Foott.
"Secondly, greys have squirrel pox - it doesn't affect them but they transmit it to red squirrels and it's fatal for them. It's a horrible disease and causes them ulcers and blindness."
So what solutions are available?
"Fertility control isn't available now - and has the effect of affecting other species, including reds," said Foott. "Gene therapy is probably at least 10 years away.
"For now, the only way is lethal control - by shooting or trapping."
Paskett, though, thinks there could be an effective additional way to control grey squirrel numbers within the next five years.
He said the Red Squirrel Survival Trust was jointly funding a field trial by the government's Animal and Plant Health Agency.
Beginning "later this year or early next year" Paskett said his organisation had "developed the means to deliver oral contraceptives to grey squirrels using a 'hopper' which sees the squirrel lift up a lid" to access them.
Because greys typically weigh 500g - approximately twice that of reds, only they can access the contraceptive.
If the field trial is successful, Paskett hopes landowners and forest rangers will be able to sign up to the scheme.
For now, though, Foott said shooting and trapping were the main options.
However, she said: "The reintroduction of pine martens can help. Because they are a native species in the UK, they evolved together with red squirrels.
"They do eat red squirrels but the reds know to quickly get out of their way and will send out the alarm signal to the rest of the colony.
"The greys are a little bit stupid and will say 'hello, I haven't seen you before' and the pine marten will get them!"
'They look cute'
When asked about the grey squirrels' UK origin story, Foott said: "Nobody really knows - there are several records but it doesn't really matter."
So why were greys imported in the first place?
Foott said: "Somebody said 'Wouldn't they look cute running around my garden?'
More than a century later, she said experienced British Red Squirrel volunteers were now working with farmers and landowners to control grey squirrel populations near red colonies.
In May, a spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said the government was protecting endangered red squirrels by tackling the threat of non-native grey squirrels.

A Â£1m fund has been set up to help local communities protect threatened green spaces.
The Summerfield Charitable Trust said the money would help groups buy and safeguard local woodlands and wildlife sites when they come up for sale.
It is part of a new initiative from the Gloucestershire Nature and Climate Fund and the Gloucestershire Local Nature Partnership.
"We need an initiative like this now more than ever," said Diane Hill, chair of the Gloucestershire Nature and Climate Fund. "Once an important green space is lost, it can be lost for good."
More from Gloucestershire
Hill said: "We know there are people across Gloucestershire who desperately want to protect woodland or wildlife sites in their community but when that land comes up for sale, they simply don't have the time or resources to compete with a private buyer.
"This funding means we can help them when it really matters.
"We can provide money to act quickly, bring in the legal and ecological expertise they need."
Recent examples of communities taking action to protect land include Daisybank, Lott Meadow and Southcourt Green, in Cheltenham, as well as Juniper Hill Field and Heavens Valley in Stroud.
Another was Rodborough Fields, near Stroud, where a public campaign to protect the woodland from development led to it being brought into community ownership.
John Bloxsom, chair of the Rodborough Fields and Frome Banks Preservation Group, said: "It's good news that a fund like this has been set up."
The group successfully bought nine acres of Rodborough Fields thanks to a Crowdfunding campaign that raised Â£200,000 but now the future of a further 30 acres is uncertain after it was put on the market this summer.
Bloxsom said that their latest bid had been rejected in favour of a rival bid from an unknown party, which was "causing concern in the community".
Angela France, one of the directors at Daisybank CIC, which helped to saved the field in Cheltenham from development last year, said she was "delighted" to hear about the new fund.
"Local green spaces are so important to us now," she said.
"I see more and more local communities getting together to protect them."
She said since buying the land, the group had organised litter picking, butterfly counts and an ecological survey in order to plan how best to maintain the field so that local wildlife could thrive.
A community event is also organised for 24 October to gather views on the future of the field.
The new fund has also been designed to contribute to nature recovery across the county, while addressing unequal access to nature.
David Owen, chair of trustees at The Summerfield Charitable Trust, said the initiative "has the potential to create a lasting legacy for nature, communities and future generations across Gloucestershire".
He added: "Through this investment, we hope to enable communities to act quickly when opportunities arise, protect important natural assets and create benefits for wildlife, health and wellbeing that will endure for many years to come."

A voluntary clean-up group is marking a decade of finding unusual items in Bristol Harbour, ranging from an inflatable doll to a Nintendo Switch.
Clean Up Bristol Harbour was launched in September 2016 in a bid to remove plastic pollution from in and around Bristol's waterways.
The group has fished out some unusual items from the harbour in the past 10 years, including a message in a bottle containing a note in Spanish, a kettle, tennis balls, glasses and single shoes as well as the inflatable doll and Nintendo Switch.
"You never quite know what you're going to pull out of Bristol Harbour," said founder and Bristol resident Chloe Juyon.
"Some of the things we've found over the years have definitely made us laugh but there is a serious point behind it.
"So much floating rubbish simply can't be reached from the harbourside.
"Getting volunteers onto the water was always a big part of what I wanted Clean Up Bristol Harbour to become."
However, the future of the project remains uncertain because funding was coming to an end, Juyon said.
Juyon founded the group after she was struck by the amount of rubbish floating around her boat while she was coxing on the River Avon at high tide.
The group has since been taken on by adventure sports centre All Aboard Watersports.
During recorded monitoring between 2021 and 2023, some 236 volunteers removed more than 880kg (1940lb) of waste from Bristol Harbour with almost 390kg (859lbs) sent for recycling.
More from Bristol
Much of the rubbish includes everyday waste, such as plastic packaging, bottles, cans, polystyrene and takeaway rubbish.
But over the years, volunteers have fished out some unusual items, such as a Nespresso capsules, alcohol bottles, plastic cones, clothing - including thermals still in their packaging - and even a packet of butcher's tripe mix.
One particularly unusual find was a Marathon-branded chocolate wrapper - the UK name for Snickers until 1990 - found during a clean-up several years ago.
Reflecting on the anniversary, Juyon said: "There were just five of us at that first clean-up in 2016.
"I stepped away from running the project several years ago, so seeing it reach its tenth birthday is quite amazing.
"For me, it really demonstrates the power of community."
Positive impact
To mark the 10th anniversary, the group will hold a community clean-up event later to mark World Cleanup Day., external
Members of the public can take part in a self-guided litter pick from 10:00 to 12:00 BST, either on foot around the harbourside or using their own craft.
With its current funding coming to an end, All Aboard Watersports has launched a Crowdfunder bid aiming to raise an initial Â£5,000 to help continue the project.
Charley Peak-Payne, from All Aboard Watersports, said having a clean harbour has had a positive impact on people who use the harbourside for waters sports and boating.
"The direct effect it has had on wildlife has been a gradual but noticeable change," he said.
"The water that they are swimming in is considerably cleaner - to the point that we are now running swimming events in the harbour too, something that due to pollution would never have happened 10 years ago."

Local elections are taking place in two German states on Sunday which could increase the political pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Opinion polls in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommerm suggest Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is at risk of damaging defeats, which would raise further questions about the chancellor's future.
These latest elections come after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, while the CDU saw its vote halved.
There has been speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced as chancellor mid-term unless the CDU's political fortunes improve.
He has said he will carry on but is facing poor approval ratings amid rumours of a so-called chancellor swap, though his challengers are "still hesitating", writes German news site Tagesschau, external.
According to the polls, Merz's conservatives could lose power in Berlin as it tussles with Die Linke (The Left) over first place.
Meanwhile in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU has only just been hovering above the 5% threshold needed for a party to enter the state parliament. It could spell their worst ever result in a state election.
How did it come to this after just 16 months in power? Friedrich Merz is having to answer for the tumbling popularity of his own party, while the political force that he aimed to counter - the AfD - continues its rise.
Some branches of the AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects.
But its anti-immigration, Russian-friendly, Germany-first agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.
The AfD is hoping to build on its recent landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt by topping the polls in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
However, the centre-left SPD has staged a late comeback to be in contention for the top spot through its lead candidate, Manuela Schwesig.
Currently the state premier, Schwesig is trying to sweep up the anti-AfD vote as she bills herself as the "Die Frau gegen Blau" - "Woman against Blue", the AfD's party colours.
But her local popularity belies the far poorer fortunes of her national party which is locked in a loveless coalition with Merz's CDU.
In a queue for a campaign event in the city of Neubrandenburg, AfD supporter Reinhart tells us that the traditional parties are being washed away.
"Not only in Germany. In Italy, in France, in Great Britain. Everywhere the traditional parties go down."
He smiles when asked what he thinks of Merz, saying: "Oh well everyone thinks the same about him.
"He is arrogant, out of touch, not on the same level as the general public."
Merz's backers argue that the chancellor has had a tough time with global events and that a lot of the problems the nation faces are ones he has inherited.
But whatever faith people had in his ability to fix those problems, it is apparently ebbing away - and, the brutal truth is, it can be hard to find voters who like him.
The former corporate lawyer's tack to the right on issues like immigration has failed to erode AfD support while also alienating people further to the left.
His blunt communication style has also caused irritation, such as his dismissal of "work-life balance", telling Germans they need to work more and take less sick leave.
Supporters would argue he is a man who is ready to administer the medicine the nation needs, even if people do not like the taste of it.
But the country's long-stuttering economy, high energy costs and fraught debates about immigration are feeding a sense of national gloom.
Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz and said restorting trust in the CDU lay in "listening âand taking political action, not in debates âover personnel".
But while no one within his party has openly challenged Merz for the top job, murmurings of discontent have grown louder.
Martin Rohloff, the CDU candidate for Neubrandenburg, thinks Merz does not have the "FingerspitzengefÃ¼hl, the feeling for the small persons".
"Maybe he wants the right things," muses Rohloff, but "he cannot communicate well".
Asked if Merz should go, he says it is not an easy question but: "If I have to answer yes or no, I would say yes. There are other people who maybe have better feelings for the public."
Merz has vowed to carry on as his coalition government aims to push through a package of economic, tax and welfare reforms that are finally due before parliament this autumn.
But Sunday's vote brings a danger for the chancellor - that he is already out of time.
The chancellor is reportedly due to meet senior party figures in Berlin on Sunday evening having already cancelled a planned trip next week to New York, in an apparent effort to contain the crisis.
A staunch backer of Ukraine, the fall of Friedrich Merz would trigger further instability in a continent already rocked by warnings of increased Russian aggression.

China’s electric grid has a dirty secret: Despite leading the world in renewable energy expansion, it is also the largest emitter of the planet’s most potent greenhouse gas.
Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) is a synthetic chemical that plays a critical role as an electrical insulator in high-voltage equipment. The gas is odorless, invisible, non-toxic and non-flammable. But it is also a climate killer, 24,300 times more effective at warming the planet than carbon dioxide on a pound-for-pound basis. Once released, sulfur hexafluoride remains in the atmosphere for 1,000 years.
Emissions come primarily from the electric power sector, where the gas is used in circuit breakers and other high-voltage equipment to prevent electricity from arcing. Nearly indestructible, SF6 serves as a critical backstop for any modern electric grid, ensuring that electricity flows only when and where it is needed. However, when electrical equipment in China reaches the end of its useful life, much of the gas is likely vented into the atmosphere.
By 2014 government researchers in China warned that SF6 poses “a significant potential threat to the global environment.” However, emissions of the climate pollutant in the country remain unregulated.
China’s Ministry of Ecology and Environment (MEE) recently stated that electric utilities in China recycle—or have the ability to recycle—90 percent of their waste SF6 gas. However, Inside Climate News estimates the actual recycling rate is substantially lower, around 30 percent. The companies could increase their recycling rate to approximately 90 percent at little cost for a significant reduction in greenhouse gas emissions.
The analysis draws on hundreds of pages of government documents, annual reports from the country’s leading electric utilities, peer-reviewed studies and interviews with dozens of academics and policy experts. Based on this review, Inside Climate News estimated that China’s state-owned electric transmission and distribution companies could increase the amount of sulfur hexafluoride they recycle from electrical equipment by approximately 1,400 metric tons of SF6 per year. Doing so would likely reduce the country’s total emissions of the pollutant across all sectors by nearly one-third at an estimated cost of about $6 million per year, a small fraction of the approximately $70 billion invested annually in China’s electric grid.
“It’s such a three-alarm fire if you are venting that gas to the atmosphere instead of recycling it,” Deborah Ottinger, a former fluorinated greenhouse gas emissions analyst for the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, said of Inside Climate News’ assessment. “It’s a very obvious thing that can be implemented immediately.”
MEE and the Chinese embassy in Washington, D.C., as well as State Grid Corporation of China and China Southern Power Grid, two state-owned electric utilities that together provide power to nearly all of the country, declined to comment on the findings.
More than half of all SF6 emissions worldwide come from China, according to a 2024 study published in the journal Nature Communications. While releases of the gas have decreased elsewhere, China’s emissions nearly doubled from 2011 to 2021 and are projected to continue climbing. In 2021, the most recent year for which data is available, China released 5,100 metric tons of SF6. The pollution is equal to the annual greenhouse gas emissions of 29 million gas-powered automobiles.
Last year saw the largest annual increase in global atmospheric concentrations of SF6 since recordkeeping began in 1998, suggesting China’s emissions continue to rise.
“It’s pretty much the worst greenhouse gas in terms of its global warming potential and its lifetime,” said Matthew Rigby, an atmospheric chemistry professor at the University of Bristol and a co-author of the Nature Communications study. “Once it’s in the atmosphere, it’s there forever as far as human timescales go.”
Reduce, Reuse, Recycle
In the late 1980s, workers at a chemical plant in what was then West Germany discovered they had a problem. The sulfur hexafluoride they manufactured had an outsized impact on the “greenhouse effect.” If they didn’t do something to address it, regulators likely would.
The problem wasn’t the chemical itself, but how their customers—electric utility companies—used it. When high-voltage equipment required maintenance or reached the end of its life, grid operators would simply vent SF6 into the atmosphere.
Solvay, a Belgian chemical company with a plant in Bad Wimpfen, Germany, worked with utility companies in Europe to recycle the waste gas instead.
Hermann Kraehling, a former environmental assessment team leader at Solvay who worked for the company in the 1990s assessing the impact of SF6, attributed its success to bringing different interest groups together.
“It was not just Solvay,” Kraehling said, adding that equipment manufacturers, power suppliers, regulators and even environmental advocacy organizations helped shape the recycling effort.
In 1997, the German Ministry for the Environment honored Solvay with the European Recycling Award for its SF6 reuse program.
In the early 2000s, company officials shared what they had learned at industry conferences hosted by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. By 2015, emissions from electrical equipment in Germany and the U.S. dropped by two-thirds or more.
Kraehling, now retired, praised China’s ongoing buildout of renewable energy. However, he called its inability to curb SF6 emissions a “disaster.”
Solvay has had its own recent challenges with emissions. An atmospheric study published in 2025 revealed higher-than-previously-reported releases of the climate pollutant in Germany, around 30 metric tons of SF6 per year. The emissions were likely from a chemical production and recycling facility in southwest Germany; Solvay’s Bad Wimpfen plant is the only such facility in Europe.

Democrats controlled the Senate and the presidency when Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse first sought to roust his colleagues from the chamber’s floor, warning them that they were sleep-walking into climate disaster.
Fourteen years and more than 300 “Time to Wake Up” speeches later, the Rhode Island Democrat is again prodding members of his own party—but now over a disaster that is manifest in rising costs and greater hazards across the country. In an interview with Inside Climate News in the run-up to Climate Week NYC, Whitehouse said it is more urgent than ever for fellow Democrats and climate action advocates to name the “villains”—as he repeatedly called them—who have stymied U.S. policy on the mounting global environmental crisis.
“The fossil fuel industry has done a really magnificent job of false narratives, fake science, the whole nonsense of trying to give people a way to think that they don’t have to do anything about climate change, that it’s a someday problem,” Whitehouse said. “Well, it ain’t a someday problem any longer.”
President Donald Trump’s second administration has channeled those industry narratives as it has rolled back climate protections—last week, for example, not only repealing regulations on power plant pollution, but also moving to prevent any future such rules with an official finding that greenhouse gases are not a danger to health or the environment.
As the midterm elections approach, polling shows that Trump, the Republicans and their fossil-fuel-friendly agenda are in trouble, in large part because of skyrocketing U.S. energy costs. Democrats and environmentalists have focused most of their messaging on those costs. A recent Inside Climate News analysis showed that specific mentions of climate change by congressional Democrats have plummeted.
Whitehouse maintains his colleagues are making a mistake if they aren’t talking about climate change, and about how industry money and influence on every branch of government has stymied action.
“We’re missing a big, big opportunity,” Whitehouse said, but he added, “we’ve never told the story well.”
Whitehouse began his weekly “Wake Up” speeches on climate in 2012, after the Senate’s Democratic leadership, in his view, squandered the opportunity to bring to the floor their own climate bill to match the cap-and-trade bill the House had passed in 2009, President Barack Obama’s first year in office. The Democrats would never regain the filibuster-proof majority they held for a short time—with their independent colleagues—and Trump’s election in 2016 put any hopes of climate action on the back burner.
After President Joe Biden unseated him in 2020 on a platform of rebuilding the economy with clean energy, Whitehouse was so hopeful he ended his climate floor speeches for about a year. But as he watched the scope of Biden’s climate legislation get whittled away, resulting eventually in the Inflation Reduction Act, Whitehouse took to the Senate floor again—focusing on what he felt was the missing part of the story.
“Biden refused to mention villains,” Whitehouse told Inside Climate News. “We’ve got these two horrible villains—the climate denial fraud operation … and the dark money corruption operation that the fossil fuel industry runs. And wow, how does that not become a good story that candidates can successfully tell?”
For example, he said environmental advocates need to do more than talk about how Trump’s extraordinary efforts to halt Atlantic offshore wind energy will result in less supply and therefore push electricity prices higher. They should also explain who benefits—the companies selling natural gas, oil and coal, who see more demand for their products.
“It is a huge corrupt money pump out of the public’s pockets and into the pockets of Trump’s big fossil fuel donors,” Whitehouse said. When people see high electric bills, “if they’re just mad at the electric company, we have not done our jobs,” he said.

If Democrats take control of the Senate in November, Whitehouse would be the most senior Democrat on the Judiciary Committee as well as on the Environment and Public Works Committee. A former U.S. attorney and attorney general of Rhode Island, Whitehouse told POLITICO last year that he would make a bid for the high-profile Judiciary spot, where he could lead the vetting of federal judicial nominees and help shape legislation to reform the Supreme Court, a step he sees as part of the climate action agenda.
He would like to see members of the high court subject to ethics rules, and has co-sponsored legislation that would establish 18-year term limits for Supreme Court justices. They’d be effective retroactively, “so you start to refresh the court right away,” he said.
In Whitehouse’s view, it was the Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United decision, sweeping aside limits on corporate political donations, that allowed the fossil fuel industry to consolidate control over the Republican Party and kill hope of bipartisan climate legislation in Congress. The court went on to restrict regulatory solutions by striking down Obama’s Clean Power Plan, relying on its so-called “major questions doctrine” in 2022. And now, in Suncor v. “Every indication is that the Supreme Court is going to obey once again the interest of the fossil fuel industry,” Whitehouse said.

f446c5a19632.text: It sounds like the start of an only-in-D.C. joke: Three Republican power players walk into a bar for a freewheeling conversation. They unwittingly sit next to a liberal comic. She then skewers them in an Instagram post recounting their chat. Why it matters: It became no laughing matter for one of the Republicans —oilman Harry Sargeant — who's trying to improve his uneasy relations with the Trump administration, partly related to his business dealings in Venezuela. His rapprochement efforts were complicated last month when senior administration officials became aware of the comic's social media post, in which she alleged that Sargeant spoke negatively about President Trump. The big picture: The story illustrates the panopticon of modern society and, especially, the nation's capital. Everyone is watched and being watched. And the White House takes notes on who's naughty and nice to Trump. Zoom in: The episode unfolded Aug. 18 in the Bourbon Lounge of the Four Seasons hotel in D.C., where comic Suzanne Lambert was working on jokes for an upcoming set, she said in a post to her 495,000 Instagram followers that had 2 million views before she took it down. In the video, Lambert said she coincidentally wound up sitting next to Sargeant and noted a vibe shift when two other men walked in: Pete Marocco and Gentry Beach. Marocco was described by Fox News as the "mastermind" who helped dismantle USAID early in the second Trump administration. Politico subsequently reported he had tensions with Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Beach was the subject of a Wall Street Journal profile last year about how the lobbyist name-drops his longtime friend and presidential son Donald Trump Jr., in international business affairs, including one involving a Russian oil deal. Inside the room: Lambert said her in post that she was just "minding my business" but started to pay more attention when the men at the bar began "spouting off about Trump. I hear Trump, Trump, Trump, Trump." At one point, Lambert's post attributed comments to Sargeant that allegedly disparaged Trump and Republicans' midterm chances. Sargeant, through his attorneys, vigorously disputes that. Behind the scenes: Lambert's video quickly went viral, prompting Sargeant's attorneys to send her a cease and desist letter. Lambert took the post down but by then, the post had circulated among Trump advisers. Rubio was made aware of it, a source said. "Harry's got some problems, and what the White House saw didn't help," an administration source said of Sargeant. What they're saying: "Mr. Sargeant denies categorically the false statements attributed to him by a self-proclaimed liberal content creator and, as a patriot who served his country well as a Marine fighter pilot, supports fully President Trump's vision, leadership and tireless efforts to place America first," his attorney, Jason Wright, said in a written statement. Beach and Marocco declined to comment through Wright. A Lambert spokesperson didn't return emails. The intrigue: Sargeant first developed a challenging relationship with Rubio back in Florida, beginning in 2010. At the time, Rubio successfully ran for U.S. Senate against former Gov. Charlie Crist. Sargeant's is a friend and former Florida State University fraternity brother of Crist's who helped finance the ex-governor's campaign. Sargeant's oil business dealings with former Venezuelan strongman Nicolas Maduro, whom Rubio loathes, did little to improve their relations through the years. After Trump returned to the presidency last year, Rubio was appointed secretary of state and pushed for regime change in Caracas. Sargeant's ally, Trump special envoy Richard Grenell, was initially opposed . Rubio won out. U.S. forces seized Maduro in a raid on Jan. 3. A month later, after a Wall Street Journal article about Sargeant's involvement in Venezuela after Maduro was gone, Trump singled him out in a Truth Social post that said Sargeant "has no authority, in any way, shape, or form, to act on behalf of the United States of America, nor does anyone else that is not approved by the State Department." On Aug. 7, the Treasury Department sanctioned one of Sargeant's companies and froze its assets. He had divested its interests, for $300 million, to North American Blue Energy Partners, called NABEP. 11 days later, Sargeant wound up at the Four Seasons bar with Marocco and Beach (and Lambert). Nine days after that, NABEP became the vehicle for Trump's mammoth Venezuelan oil deal, which Axios first reported on Aug. 27. Zoom out: Trumpworld insiders say Sargeant's ordeal is a cautionary tale to stay on the good side of the administration. "I don't like Harry, but he got knifed," said one Trump adviser. "They kick him out of Venezuela. They sanction his company. They take him out of this other deal. And some people want him investigated ." A former business associate of Sargeant's pointed out that he financially supported Trump's campaign in 2020 and, at the time, even played a role in helping Trump push to have Ukraine investigate Joe Biden, "Harry wasn't disloyal to Trump," the associate said. "He's an oil guy. He wants to do oil deals. And he should've just gone with Team Rubio from the start."

c7e23f07c6a7.text: The long-promised personal AI assistant is finally arriving, with a suddenly crowded field of agents offering to run pieces of your everyday life. Why it matters: For years, tech's "personal assistants" were little more than voice-controlled search boxes. Rapid advances in AI are finally giving them the memory, judgment and autonomy to act on our behalf. Catch up fast: Chatbots answer questions. AI agents can actually do things — shopping, making calls, booking tickets, managing calendars and navigating the web. The model first took off in coding and other professional work. Now it's spilling into the far more intimate terrain of everyday life. The intrigue: OpenAI is expected to enter the market soon after hiring the creator of OpenClaw — a breakout hit among AI power users earlier this year — to "drive the next generation of personal agents." Driving the news: A consumer-agent race has erupted almost overnight, with startups and tech giants pursuing the same basic idea — persistent digital proxies that know your life. Instinct has become buzzy by connecting to users' email, messages, screen, audio and location — then proactively texting or calling to help run their lives. It recently added its own email addresses and the ability to make phone calls, and is now in talks for a $10 billion valuation . Grok Bot, launched by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI in August, gives persistent agents their own cloud computers, lets them sign into users' apps and keeps them working around the clock. Meta's Muse brought the concept to a broader consumer audience this month with a polished app, a customizable avatar and deep integration with Meta's ecosystem. Apple's Siri is finally getting its AI overhaul , bringing more context and capability to an assistant already built into hundreds of millions of devices. The big picture: The battle to become your personal agent is also a battle to become the keeper of your personal information and data. The frontier AI race has revolved around raw intelligence. Personal agents win by becoming useful and deeply embedded in your daily life. The more an agent knows about your relationships, schedule and spending, the more useful it becomes. Between the lines: Becoming someone's default agent could be one of the most valuable relationships in consumer technology. People are likely to share far more with an AI that manages their lives than they did with a search engine. The catch: Nobody yet knows what price consumers will pay for that convenience, in cost or privacy. Apple says some server-based Apple Intelligence features, including the upgraded Siri, will have usage limits , with expanded access potentially tied to iCloud plans. Meta is offering free and paid Muse tiers, while pitching the product as more privacy-conscious than its earlier AI offerings. What to watch: Some people inside and outside the industry argue that users should own the personal data and context their agents accumulate, rather than handing that relationship to ad-driven tech giants. will.i.am, whose FYI.AI offers agents equipped with their own phone numbers that can text, call and collaborate with humans to build projects, says he recoils at getting an agent for free "in exchange for extracting your very core — how you think." "That's nasty," the Black Eyed Peas frontman told Axios. "We've seen that with social media."

Will airmen trust AI? The Air Force’s future plans depend on it
Getting leaders and operators comfortable with agents will require new doctrine, training, and permissions.
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—As Air Force leaders prepare to hand AI more decision-making power in the years ahead, they're also working to get airmen comfortable with that.
“A little bit scary, but we need to lean into it,” Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said at the Air and Space Association’s Air, Space & Cyber conference this week. “Autonomy is one of, if not the key technology enabling cost-effective combat power.”
Although Meink didn’t say so explicitly, “leaning in” will require new thinking on building trust between human airmen and the AI assistants, chatbots, and autonomous drones that will surround them. But other parts of the Air Force have spent a lot of time thinking about it, especially as the service works to field 500 highly-autonomous collaborative combat aircraft, or CCAs, by 2032.
“There’s a trust and autonomy question,” said Michael Gregg, director of aerospace systems at the Air Force Research Laboratory. “We have psychologists and behavioral scientists in our 711th Human Performance Wing that are actually studying this problem: How do you actually team machines with humans to make the human really really good at what they do and aid their decision-making? That is the future.”
And for some missions, like protecting air bases from drone attacks, the Air Force is exploring the possibility of not augmenting but replacing human decision-making. The waves of drones striking Ukrainian cities and ravaging U.S. bases in the Middle East have service leaders exploring the use of agents—AI tools that can take action—to work the process of obtaining approvals to launch counter-attacks.
That will require humans to define acceptable risk for allowing AI agents to make decisions.
“There is an increased push on how we use agents and agentic workflow into everything from fires to our back-office activities, and like you'll see a lot more of that coming this year,” said Ben Van Roo, the CEO of Legion Intelligence, a company that develops agentic AI agents for national-security purposes.
The question of AI directing “fires” is controversial, as the term suggests allowing a software program to launch a missile, fire a gun, or launch a deadly weapon. While there are some exceptions, military doctrine states a strong preference for meaningful human control over potentially lethal effects.
But cyber, directed energy, and other non-lethal technologies are giving the military more fires it might deploy without human oversight, said Mike Hiatt, the chief technology officer at Epirus, a company that makes microwave and other directed-energy counter-drone defenses.
“If you can have an option that has lower collateral effects and no collateral damage, you know, which is what the directed-energy weapons offer, you start to be able to change your risk calculation. You start to be able to make decisions where you say ‘OK, I'm a little more comfortable with putting this part of the system on a fully autonomous mode,” Hiatt said.
Van Roo said the decision processes to allow autonomous cyberattacks or nonlethal effects could eventually be accelerated with AI, or even automated completely.
“We're really still in the infancy right now of how we think about where we're going to use agents, what are we going to allow them to decide on? How do they work their way into our tactics, techniques, and procedures, into our doctrine?” he said.
Getting leaders and operators to be comfortable with AI agents will require new doctrine, training, and permissions, as well as a high degree of confidence that AI tools will perform in predictable ways.
“This is going to happen right now in front of us before AI and killer robots take over the world,” he said.
This year’s conference occurred amid a national debate over the dangers of AI, how it should be regulated, and who should decide.
The summer’s disclosures by Anthropic and OpenAI of surprising and dangerous model behavior were followed on Sept. 9 by the high-profile resignation of an Anthropic engineer who claimed a 10-percent probability that AI “could kill all humans.” The following day, representatives of those companies and Google intensified efforts to create an industry-safety body while signaling openness to Congressional action. But regulation is opposed by President Donald Trump, who posted this week, “The only control or ‘guardrail’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”
Pentagon leaders’ willingness to accept AI may stem from the fact that their current systems failed to keep key U.S. bases safe. But it may also reflect several years of Defense Department efforts to grapple with concerns about intent, alignment, and safe use that frontier AI labs are just now grappling with. Since 2019, the military has had a list of ethical principles to guide AI development, experimentation and use. It also reviews processes, experiments, and testing procedures for new technology, including software and, of course, the most dangerous weapons on Earth.
But the pace of AI advancement is quickly changing concepts of how to develop and test weapons. Ryan Tseng, president and co-founder of Shield AI, told the crowd at AFA that his company had worked with Ukrainians to improve the strike capability of one of the company’s drone weapons by 70 percent through “advanced autonomous behaviors.”
If autonomous drones are the signature feature of the war in Ukraine, many military officials expect the next conflict to be defined by rapid collaboration between agents, humans, and drones that will speed up strikes and counter-strikes. That will require continuous evolution on building trust between humans and AI entities as well.

US President Donald Trump has said his proposed triumphal arch will double as a complex to store military equipment, complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones.
In a Sunday morning post, Trump said he is updating the plans at the "strong request" of the US military and for "national security purposes".
The "top grade" military complex and arch will "house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage", he said.
He did not provide details on construction plans or timing, and it's not clear if he needs further approval for the facility.
"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington DC is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch", without specifying what those cities are.
Construction on Trump's 250-foot arch, planned for a site across the Potomac River from Washington DC just outside the Arlington National Cemetery, was expected to begin this month.
A rendering of the design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles, and with the phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" inscribed in gold on either side of the structure. It will stand 250-feet (76m) from its base to the top of the golden lady statue.
At that height, the structure would dwarf the 99-foot Lincoln Memorial nearby and be half as high as the Washington Monument.
The BBC has contacted the Department of Defence for more information on the updated plans.
Trump has pursued a number of construction projects during his second term to revamp the US capital, including a gilded makeover of the Oval Office, constructing a White House ballroom estimated to cost around $400m, paving over the White House Rose Garden, and renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
The triumphal arch is one of the biggest projects Trump has set his sights on.
